en: Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Yongjia Chanzong:
Alas! How grave indeed is the affliction of sentient beings' deluded agitation! By day they are distracted and restless, exhausting their spirits.
At night, they are restless and obscure their spiritual clarity. It is like using a lead stylus to carve through mud:
the mud is not formed, yet the stylus is daily diminished. It is like using fine wine to dispel a hangover: the hangover is not relieved, yet one’s lucidity is daily clouded.
Thus, while living, they gradually move toward death; and by dying, they only further exhaust their life. Within the cycle of the three realms, what [is there to be gained]?
The time has passed. The ascent and descent through the six realms of existence never pauses for a single day. To speak of this truly increases one’s sighs;

to contemplate it is indeed enough to move one to tears. When one is about to receive a physical form within the universe and be endowed with a nature by means of yin and yang, one follows the opening and closing of the movement of the vital breath and pursues the welcoming and sending-off of the seasons.
Thus, as days pass and evenings arrive, the heavens and earth undergo their great cycle of darkness and motion.

It is thus: spring growth and winter storage are one great cycle of obscuration and movement within the yin and yang. Exhalation and inhalation are one great cycle of obscuration and movement within the human body.
Waking by day and sleeping at night are one great cycle of obscuration and movement of this mind.

Momentary recollection and momentary forgetting are one great cycle of obscuration and movement within a single kṣaṇa. Alas, that human life should trade its twilight for a minor death in order to seek a heavy [burden].
The great sleep of the spring source brings about the minor life of morning awakening, which in turn leads to the weary life of the future. Alas!
Is the toil of delusion and movement not indeed excessive for life? Yet, is it truly the case that Heaven and Earth, Yin and Yang, cause me to be thus?
Or is it rather that my own nature—wondrously bright and awakened—causes Heaven, Earth, Yin, and Yang to be thus? If one first returns to the root...

In the future, I shall take the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as my primary authority. The Sūtra says: "The nature of awareness is inherently luminous; through delusion, it becomes the perception of luminosity. This obscuration becomes space.
Within the darkness of this obscured space, the accumulation of darkness becomes form. Form is mixed with false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and these conceptual appearances become the body."
When the mind gathers its objects and wavers within, it rushes outward in flight; this state of murky agitation is taken as the nature of the mind.

This would mean placing the spiritual essence first and Heaven and Earth second. If one prioritizes the derivative and neglects the fundamental, I shall instead take the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean) as my authority.
The *Zhongyong* says: "What Heaven mandates is called nature; following nature is called the Way. Furthermore, the Song Confucians said: "Heaven gives birth to all things..."
Only humans are most spiritually gifted; thus, they exist prior to heaven and earth and subsequently possess spiritual nature.

If one intends to plan for their convergence and unification, or their meeting and return [to the source], there must necessarily be that toward which they are directed. The *Zhongyong* says: "When harmony and centrality are perfected, heaven and earth find their places, and the myriad things are nourished.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the ten directions become void..."

All things in emptiness are subject to dissolution; life and birth are likewise subject to dissolution. Although their specific meanings differ—being first the root and later the branch—their ultimate destination is one and the same.
Yet worldly people are ignorant of this and fail to perceive it; they wander in delusion and forget to return. They do not regard it as suffering but instead take pleasure in it;
they do not regard it as a malady but instead treat it as a medicine. Furthermore, they say, "The Way lies within it," even as it is filled with afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding birth and death: how could the Way ever reach its end? After passing through tens of billions of years, there appeared a Great Awakened Sage born in the land of India, named Śākyamuni.
Having practiced for vast eons, he perfected the Way in a single lifetime. As for his Dharma-body, it encompasses the ten voids;
as for his wisdom, it penetrates the three periods of time. Furthermore, he took clarity and stillness as his essence.
Its essence gives rise to awakening and stillness as its function. It unfurls the illumination of wisdom upon the dark thoroughfare; the long night cannot obscure its brilliance.
It turns tranquil concentration back toward the net of dust; the myriad things cannot disturb its purity.

That which heaven and earth cannot cover or support, and that which yin and yang cannot displace—it is what Zhuangzi called being able to be heaven and able to be earth, able to be yin and... [able to be yang].
He is capable of manifesting yang; he is able to act as the sovereign of the myriad things. He does not wither along with the four seasons, nor does he merely discourse on principles in the void.

He truly is able to restore his original source; he is none other than the Buddha alone. It is from this that he emits light and shakes the earth; it is from this that he leaves no trace and hides his spirit;
it is from this that the Lion’s Roar resounds at Vulture Peak; and it is from this that the chamber is closed in Mahādeva’s cave. Thus it is.

To speak through silence is the very essence and its function; it is nothing other than the propagation of the school of Samādhi and Prajñā, and the elucidation of the Dharma of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā.
Indeed, medicine arises from the presence of illness, and the spirit returns through the application of medicine.

Since one treats turbidity and agitation with awakening and stillness, and restores clarity and tranquility through Samādhi and Prajñā, even the thousand Buddhas could not differ in their cause, nor could the multitude of sages [alter this principle].
It is impossible for their ultimate aim not to be identical. Since the transmission of the prediction on Vulture Peak, the frost-covered trees have remained in hidden splendor;
yet the Way arose in accordance with conditions, and the lamp was passed to Kāśyapa. Thirteen transmissions later it reached Nāgārjuna; twenty-three transmissions later it reached Siṃha.
Nāgārjuna was a fragrant elephant among the Dharma and a great dragon among men. Having already expounded the school of Prajñā through the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he further...
Using the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* to transmit the purport of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he crossed the Huai and the Yellow Rivers. Huiwen was of keen and intuitive understanding;

he revered Nāgārjuna from afar and first established the Mind School (*Xinzong*). From him, the teaching was transmitted to Mount Heng (Nanyue). At Mount Heng, he practiced the Vaipulya for seven years and maintained constant seated meditation for ninety days.

He realized them all at once and complete in a single moment, transmitting them thus to Tiantai. Having heard the teachings on Mount Ling in his youth, Tiantai attained wondrous enlightenment at Dasu.

With unimpeded wisdom, he wielded eloquent debate to proclaim [the Dharma], taking the Lotus Sūtra as the doctrine of his own school and further expounding *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) as its practice.
With both understanding and practice perfected, and both vision and feet beautiful, those who praised him said: "The Wise One (Zhizhe) possesses the eight [qualities]."
He realized the Way through these signs, and people called him the "Little Śākyamuni of the Eastern Land. He established ten dharmas as the vehicle for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
their meaning accords with the Great Buddha-Crown of the Western Heaven. This is indeed his true virtue; how could it be mere empty talk? Tiantai transmitted [the teaching] to Zhang’an;
Zhang’an transmitted it to Fahua; Fahua transmitted it to Tiangong. As for Tiangong, he was the Great Master Zhenjue’s...
He was a successor who attained realization through the path of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) and gained comprehensive mastery of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

His spiritual lineage traced back to Caoxi (Huineng), and as teacher and disciple were in perfect accord, this collection was compiled and recorded by the Great Master upon his return to the Oujiang River region.

It was intended to clarify the core intent of the mind-transmission at the moment of its bestowal; thus, he repeatedly examined every word and earnestly emphasized *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. As for that which...
This elucidation may indeed be called detailed. Alas! Now, the nature (dhātu) takes non-duality as its essence, and the mind takes the absence of differentiation as its purport;
this is what is common to both Chan and the Teachings (Dharma). Is it that Chan exists apart from the Teachings, or that the Teachings exist apart from Chan?
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Do not abandon words to speak of liberation. The *Ratnaketu-paripṛcchā-sūtra* says: "In sum..."
To "hold" is to be without words; yet words manifest the *dhāraṇī*. These two explanations are unified.
I shall further advance this by means of mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are sealed by the One Dharma. Yet, the Way is like water, and its transmission is like a current.
At the beginning, they were united and not yet separated; I shall now verify this with Śākyamuni: are they the same or different? In the middle, they were separated and not yet...
"Let us verify this with the various Chan teachings and the patriarchs who attained the Way: do they agree or differ? In the end, they will diverge and then reunite;
they will differ and then return to unity. Furthermore, I shall verify it through the True Enlightenment Master’s compilation of this collection."
I maintain that were it not for this collection, the beginning and end of Chan and the teachings would not harmonize;

were it not for this essential meaning, the heart-essence of the Tathāgata would ultimately remain unclarified. Thus, their differences lie in the traces (*traces*), while their sameness lies in the source (*the fundamental*). To be deluded is to cling to the traces and forget the source;
to awaken is to grasp the source and let go of the traces. When both source and traces are simultaneously dissolved, Chan and the teachings are merged as one.
I shall further verify this against the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) of the Great Master of Yongming. For the sake of this commentary, I have thus prefaces and traced its origins.
May readers set aside the traces to seek the source; then the Way of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* will be attained.
The layman Zhengyan of Masengma is one who has arisen as a successor to Yongjia. He felt that were it not for me, the Cloud from Tiantai, [this teaching] could not yet be preserved.
He has fully grasped the essence of the Great Master’s *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; thus, he did not hesitate to send me a letter requesting that I produce a commentary.
His intent may indeed be called diligent. I have recorded the origins of this request so that the beginning and end of this commentary may be clearly understood.
On the first day of the bright moon in the early autumn of the second year of the Huangming Tianqi era, the cyclical year being Renxu,

the śramaṇa Youxi of Mount Tiantai, a distant descendant of the lineage who transmits the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai and the lamp of the Dharma, composed this in the Eastern Hall of the Unblinking Eye at the Śūraṅgama Altar.
Collected Commentaries on the Yongjia School of Chan, Volume One.
Compiled and annotated by the monk Chuan Deng of Youxi on Mount Tiantai during the Ming Dynasty.
Collected Commentaries on the Yongjia School of Chan.

The five characters of the title should be arranged correctly, placing the person first and the Dharma second, as in the *Yǒngjiā chánzōng jí* (Collection on the Chan School of Yǒngjiā), following the precedent of works such as the *Tiāntái zhǐguān*.
The previous compilation placed the Dharma first and the person second, which was a reversal of the proper order.
"Yǒngjiā" refers to the birthplace of the Great Master; thus, the person is distinguished by his location. "Chánzōng" (Chan School) refers to the Great Master’s...

The Dharma that is taught takes the *pāramitās* as its essential purpose. In Sanskrit, *dhyāna* is translated here as "calm contemplation" (*jinglü*) and is also called "cultivation through reflection.
It is one of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Its essence is the source of all practices.

Generally speaking, *dhyāna* pertains to concentration (*samādhi*), while *prajñā* pertains to wisdom (*prajñā*); this is stated according to the distinctions between their respective dharmic characteristics. That is to say:
It is concentration that is never without wisdom; it is wisdom that is never without concentration. This is spoken of in terms of their essential nature being without differentiation.
As clarified below in the explanation of *śamatha*, when one speaks of concentration, one simultaneously mentions "quiescence and illumination.
It is said: "Quiescent yet alert is correct; mere dull quiescence is not. Is this not precisely concentration that is identical to wisdom? This serves as an analogy for *vipaśyanā*.

Śamatha corresponds to wisdom (*prajñā*), while vipaśyanā corresponds to śamatha and vipaśyanā in equal measure; there is nothing that does not involve the simultaneous fusion of stillness and illumination, with śamatha and vipaśyanā functioning interchangeably.
This is precisely because the essence of samādhi is pervasive and unobstructed: śamatha is itself vipaśyanā.

Therefore, throughout the verbal explanations of this entire section and the methods of cultivation, all take both samādhi and prajñā as their primary focus, and both stillness and clarity constitute the fundamental principle for realizing the nature.
This is that which presides over the attainment of Buddhahood. It is here to which Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s forty-nine years of teaching ultimately point.
It is here to which Nanyue and Tiantai transmitted from master to master. It is here into which Great Master Zhizhe (Zhenjue) attained awakening upon entering the Heavenly Palace.
It was here that he traveled south to Caoxi to seek confirmation, and it was here that he received that confirmation.
This is it. Upon returning to Dong’ou, I have expounded this very teaching for the benefit of both monastics and laypeople;

it is this that has been taught. From this, one attains awakening and entry. This constitutes the Perfect and Sudden Supreme Vehicle. Any practice other than this is that of the Lesser Vehicle or external paths.
How can practitioners of the末代 (final age) fail to revere it?
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuánjué of Yǒngjiā during the Táng dynasty.
"Táng" is the name of the state. Gāozǔ Shényáo Huángdì, whose personal name was Yuán and courtesy name was Shūdé, belonged to the Lí clan.
He was a native of Chéngjī in Lǒngxī and a descendant of Wǔzhāowáng Gǎo of Xīliáng. His grandfather, Hǔ, served the Western Wèi and achieved distinguished merit.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Longxi. His father, Zhao, had been enfeoffed as the Duke of Tang during the Zhou dynasty. Yuan succeeded him and inherited the title of Duke of Tang.

At the end of the Sui dynasty, he raised an army, received the abdication of the Gaozu Emperor, and ruled the world with the virtue of Earth. He established his capital at Chang’an and founded the state named Dàtáng (Great Tang).
The Master was born during the reign of Emperor Taizong and passed away during the reign of Emperor Ruizong; he was a disciple of Tiāngōng (Tianqing).
He studied under Master Lang of Zuoxi and Master Ce of Dongyang. Yongjia is the name of a commandery; it was called Dong’ou during the Han dynasty and was renamed Yongjia during the Jin dynasty.
During the Song and Yuan dynasties, it was all called Wenzhou, named for the abundance of mildness and warmth in its terrain.
To this day, there is Wenzheng to the east and Wenxi to the west, both belonging to the jurisdiction of Yongjia. "Śramaṇa" is a term from the Sanskrit language. [The full term is]...

"Sāman" (娑迦懣那) is now abbreviated as "Shamen" (沙門). A renunciant who diligently cultivates morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and extinguishes greed, anger, and delusion—meaning one who has stilled the mind and reached the fundamental source—is therefore called a Shamen.

The Master’s courtesy name was Yuánjué (元覺), his posthumous title was Dàshī Zhēnjué (真覺大師), and his secular surname was Dài (戴). Having traveled abroad by ship, he went forth from home and extensively investigated the Tripitaka.
He refined the perfect and wondrous Dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Amidst the four modes of deportment, he constantly remained in accord with meditative contemplation.
Inspired by Master Lang of Zuoxi, he subsequently traveled together with Chan Master Yuance of Dongyang to Caoxi to meet the Sixth Patriarch.
The details of their dialogues and karmic conditions are fully recorded in the biographical account (*xingzhuang*) composed by Yang Wenyong. Observing his display of eloquence, one sees...
He was quick-witted and discerning. Although it is said that he received formal certification at Caoxi, he actually attained realization in the Celestial Palace.
Therefore, the dharma-gates he expounded were entirely based upon the Three Contemplations; that the pond is deep and the flowers are large can be known all the more clearly from this.
The Master had a younger sister named Yuanyi, who also left the household life and realized the Way; her account is recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
Commenting on this compilation of texts, it is divided into two major sections: first, a general presentation of the ten chapters; second, a detailed explanation of the ten meanings.
Regarding the first section, the general presentation of the ten chapters, it is further divided into two parts: first, rectifying the sequence and correcting errors in the compilation;
second, re-editing the order and providing a detailed explanation. As for rectifying the sequence and correcting errors, this work must have been produced by the Great Master himself.
These are previously scattered drafts, or writings whose composition was left unfinished. The scholar Wei Jing lamented that these were like flowers strewn before him;

thus, he strung them together and compiled them. Lacking the skillful hands of the palace tailors of the Sui dynasty, and further deprived of the marvelous ingenuity of the Dou family’s palindrome compositions, he has often mixed the *udumbara* flower with the *vāsaka*. Consequently, the Bodhisattva...
Regarding the causes for this prediction [of enlightenment], the brushwork of Tianre Baozhi’s *Fanjiu* (Intermingled Translations) was such that readers lamented its state.

Now, following the formal conventions of the two traditions, I have corrected its unstable arrangement. It is a rule that when masters from India and China compose treatises, they invariably begin with a verse of taking refuge in the Triple Gem;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Vipaśyanā-citta-śāstra* serve as examples of this.
Furthermore, it is now contrary [to logic] to place the verse on taking refuge in the Triple Gem as the tenth; this is the first inconsistency.

First, the principles followed by this compilation are all based upon *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Within the five summaries of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the cultivation of the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*) is primary.

This is followed by the cultivation of Great Practice, the realization of Great Fruit, the tearing of the Great Net, and the returning to the Great Abode. Now, to prioritize the cultivation of the Great Resolve...
To vow to establish the Great Mind (mahācitta) at the very end [of one's practice] is the second impossibility.

First, if one examines this using the ten chapters of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, then this collection on the "Ritual for Aspiring to the Way" (*Mùdào zhīyí*) and the "Ritual for Serving the Teacher" (*Shìshī yízé*) both correspond to the section on the "Five Conditions" (*wǔyuán*) within the twenty-five expedient means (*upāya*) of the sixth chapter of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the precepts against luxury and extravagance, one should censure the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) and renounce them.
Regarding the matters among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*): one should purify the three karmas and practice one of the five tasks.
These are all listed at the outset, yet the general intent for cultivating dhyāna is not clarified; this is the third impossibility.

Furthermore, if one examines this by means of the ten stages of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, then first one ought to contemplate the realm of principle (*li-jing*) in order to harmonize the mind, and only thereafter arouse the resolve (*cittotpāda*) to broaden it.
Only after harboring [this understanding] can one apply effort to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Now, you place the non-duality of phenomena and principle in the eighth [section];

this is the fourth impossibility. As for the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles, it concerns the clarification of the partial and the complete, and the distinction between the provisional and the real, within the ten major chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Now, you place it in the seventh; this is the fifth impossibility. Moreover, you intend to use it to exhort friends.

To transcribe non-urgent writings and clutter the collection, thereby bringing blemish upon my upright friends and causing a flawless jade to be ultimately marred by a minor flaw—this would be the sixth unseemly thing.
Nevertheless, this work has been in circulation from the Tang dynasty to the present for over a thousand years;
it has already been engraved into the Great Canon and esteemed by the worthies of both past and present. Thus, I, a piece of withered and useless wood, [dare not refuse].
What insignificant person am I to dare to "blow on a hair" to seek out flaws, or to point out blemishes to deprive one of their jade?
This is something those who would "rise with a drawn sword" most dread. However, as I was annotating the text, my pen lingered; this has indeed become an obstruction to its circulation.
I have now withdrawn these and written them separately as a letter of exhortation to a friend. Furthermore, I have split the *Pranidhāna* (Vow) text into two parts, the first of which is:
I take refuge in the Triple Gem. Second is the making of great vows. As for all other matters of advancement or retreat, each has its proper place;
they are neither excessive nor deficient, lacking nothing and having no surplus. They are like the full moon in the sky or the *maṇi* jewel in the great ocean.
Why must one enter a spring pond to compete for tiles and rubble, or descend an ancient well to pull out a toad? It is simply by means of this.
I submit this to the Great Master of True Enlightenment; he too will surely nod his head in approval within the realm of the eternally quiescent light.
This great treatise is divided into ten sections: (1) Taking Refuge in the Triple Gem; (2) Making Great Vows; (3) Drawing Near to Teachers and Friends;
(4) Admonitions on Food and Clothing; (5) Purifying the Three Karmas; and (6) The Gradual Progression of the Three Vehicles.
Sixth, the non-duality of phenomena and principle; seventh, distinguishing and indicating the partial and the perfect; eighth, the correct cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
ninth, the ten gates of contemplating the mind; tenth.

First is taking refuge in the Triple Gem. Throughout the ages, from India to China, whenever venerable elders of the past and present intended to compose treatises or write commentaries, they invariably first paid homage to the Triple Gem to seek its manifest and hidden blessings, so that no errors might arise;
therefore, it is placed first. Second is the making of great vows. Now, practice cannot be essential without vows, and vows...
If even practicing [the path] alone cannot guide one, how much less so for the myriad practices of a bodhisattva, which must benefit both oneself and others?
If one lacks a vow, one cannot restrain the mind; therefore, it is placed second. Third is "drawing near to teachers and friends":

for the Way is not clarified without teaching, and teaching is not transmitted without a teacher. Furthermore, through the teacher’s model, one is fashioned into a vessel of the Dharma; thus, one must know well—
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is ranked third because it serves as the complete condition for attaining the Way. Regarding the fourth precept on clothing and food:
clothing is used to cover the body and food to fill the belly; these are indispensable for this dependent physical frame.

Nevertheless, one must remain far removed from the four and five perversions, clearly understanding the eight impurities and the eight purities; only then can one transcend the cage of worldly existence.
Nirvana can be hoped for; therefore, it is placed fourth. Fifth, regarding the pure cultivation of the three karmas:
although the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are the foundation for ascending purity, they are also the ladder for sinking into decline.
If one does not cultivate them with purity, how could one restrain the deviant and enter the correct? Therefore, it is placed fifth. Sixth, the three...
Regarding the successive stages: the seventh concerns the non-duality of phenomena and principle; the eighth distinguishes and demonstrates the partial and the perfect;
and the ninth concerns the actual cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Now, phenomena are not established without principle, and principle does not stand without teaching.

Because the teachings are both sudden and gradual, the principles are accordingly distinguished as partial or perfect. Nevertheless, the sudden is not revealed without the gradual, and the gradual is not harmonized without the sudden.
At the beginning, one clarifies the gradual stages of the Three Vehicles; at the end, one awakens to the perfect and sudden principle of the One Vehicle.

Only then can wondrous understanding be perfected and wondrous practice be established. Now, observe how the [Threefold] Truths manifest as the basis, and how the [Threefold] Virtues are revealed through the causes.

For those who are deluded regarding the Three Virtues, the three afflictions (trivisa) thereby become chaotic; for those who awaken to the Three Truths, the three contemplations (trisamādhi) arise as a matter of course. As for their essence:

Fundamentally, it is neither vertical nor horizontal; its cultivation has from the beginning been neither unified nor differentiated. If one attains the one while losing the two, the essence of the perfect *ī* (the three-in-one) is violated.
If one is preoccupied with that while clinging to this, the delusion of the *akṣa* fruit (the three-in-three) will accumulate.
Furthermore, how could it suffice to describe the perfect cultivation? Therefore, the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth [chapters] follow one another to clarify the doctrine, principle, and practice.
As for the tenth chapter, the "Ten Gates of Contemplating the Mind," this is a re-examination of the path of principle.

Once again, this gateway of cultivation is elucidated, so that the nature of the perfect fusion of the three virtues may be ultimately and fully revealed, and the practice of the clarity and subtlety of the three contemplations may be finally and completely manifested.
As for their mutual correspondence, these are all subtle realizations of the stage of fruition;
as for their wondrous accord with the primordial source, these are the secrets within the realm of the Great Beings (Bodhisattvas). It is by means of this that the conclusion is reached.
To summarize the great purport of this work: it is certain that it should be placed at the end.
I take refuge in and pay homage to the Three Jewels, first:
I bow my head to the Perfectly Omniscient One, The source of quiescence, equality, and primordial truth.
The marks and signs are uniquely majestic, neither existent nor non-existent; Wisdom’s brilliance shines universally upon lands as numerous as motes of dust.
"Buddha" in Sanskrit means "the Awakened One. Herein, one takes refuge in the one who fully possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*).
First is the Awakened One of Perfect Universal Knowledge, which is the *Sambhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). In Sanskrit, it is called *Vairocana*, which means "Universal Radiance."

This leads to the perfection of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) through the cultivation of *prajñā*. Pervading the entire dharma-realm, there is nothing it does not perceive and nothing it does not know.
This body dwells in the self-enjoyment land (*svasaṃbhogakṣetra*), adorned with the true recompense. In terms of the three truths, it belongs to the truth of ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*);
in terms of the three contemplations, it belongs to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Now, I wish to elucidate the purport of this śamatha-contemplation of emptiness.
Therefore, one first takes refuge to seek their protective empowerment. Next, regarding "the source of quiescence, equality, and fundamental reality": this is the *dharmakāya*.
In the Sanskrit language it is called Vairocana, which here means "pervading all places. Because it is primordially pure, it is called "quiescent.
Because there is no distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas, and because matter and mind are non-dual, it is called "equal. It serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening...
The fundamental source is the true basis from which Buddhas arise; hence it is called the "original true source. It belongs to the primordially existing Dharmakāya.

When discussing the pervasiveness of awareness, it is no different from the Saṃbhogakāya. However, while the wisdom of the Saṃbhogakāya is regarded as the means of realization (*sādhana*), this Dharmakāya is that which is realized (*sādhya*).
Therefore, Master Tiantai clarified that the nature of sentient beings is *li-ji* (identical with) Buddhahood, stating: "This..."
This is perfect wisdom and perfect enlightenment; all phenomena pervade every place without anything being unclear. It is through this that one knows: how could there be any separate substance?
Cultivation is entirely within the nature—is this not what is meant? This body dwells in the land of eternal quiescent light.
In terms of the three truths, this belongs to the Middle Way, the Truth of Ultimate Meaning; in terms of the three contemplations, it belongs to the Middle Contemplation.
Now, wishing to expound and clarify the principles of the Middle Contemplation within *ubhayatobhāga-pratisaṃvid*, I first take refuge and seek its hidden empowerment.
That which is adorned with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and is neither existent nor non-existent is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
In Sanskrit, Śākyamuni; in this [language], it means "Capable Sage" (*Nengren*) and "Tranquil Silence" (*Jimo*). This refers to the so-called Śākyamuni Buddha of the thousand-billion response bodies.

There are two types: first, the superior response body; second, the inferior response body. The superior response body is, for example, the ten-thousand-fathom body in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The inferior response body...
For example, there is the body of sixteen feet at the Deer Park. These two types of manifestations are both adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

A body of a thousand feet is extraordinary; a body of sixteen feet appears ordinary. However, there are cases where the inferior is concealed and the superior is manifested, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

There are cases where the superior is concealed and the inferior is manifested, as in the Deer Park. There are cases where the inferior and the superior are identical, as in [the manifestation at] Ling...

Mountains meet with the fundamental principle; this is what the Dragon Girl perceived. It is simultaneously supreme and simultaneously inferior; this is what the Śrāvakas of the *Avataṃsaka* perceived.
That which is praised in the present text is neither existent nor non-existent, yet its wisdom shines universally.

This precisely refers to the Dharma-body of the Middle Way, which, in union with the Reward-body and Wisdom, serves as the foundation. It is entirely like the Medicine Master [Bhaiṣajyaguru]: majestic and magnificent.

The Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) is like Mount Sumeru, manifesting within the great ocean; therefore it is said that his marks and signs are uniquely adorned, being neither existent nor non-existent, but rather belonging to liberation.

He possesses this body which, descending, responds to the three lands: responding to the Land of Real Reward, it belongs to the Body of Other-Enjoyment (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), also called the "Supreme Response";
responding to the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, it belongs to the Supreme Response; responding to the Land of Common Dwelling, it belongs to...
The "inferior response" (lèshèng) is also merely a provisional description. To speak more precisely, the responses in all three lands possess both superior and inferior aspects;

however, it is simply that a single body appears differently according to the capacities of those who perceive it. In terms of the Three Truths, this belongs to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);

in terms of the Three Contemplations, it belongs to the contemplation of the provisional (prajñapti-vipaśyanā). Now, wishing to elucidate the principle of the contemplation of the provisional within vipaśyanā, I shall first...
I take refuge to seek his secret empowerment.
I prostrate to the湛然 (zhànrán) [serenely still] and truly wondrous enlightenment, the profoundly deep twelve *sūtras*—neither text nor letter, beyond all verbal expression;
a single sound that is clearly understood by all according to their kind.
In the Sanskrit language it is *dharma*; here it is translated as "Dharma" (法). There are two kinds of Dharma:
first, that which is signified, namely the profound, true, and wondrous awakening; second, that which signifies it, namely the extremely deep twelve *sūtras*.

Both of these possess the sense of being a standard for emulation; therefore, both are called "Dharma. That the signified possesses the sense of being a standard for emulation refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The nature [of phenomena] constitutes the virtue of the Dharmakāya. That which can express this meaning of having a standard to follow consists of language and written characters;
these can express the nature of all dharmas as the *vyañjanakāya* (body of phonemes) and *padakāya* (body of phrases).

There are no Buddhas on the stage of the causal ground who do not take this as their standard to achieve perfect enlightenment. Therefore it is said: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is what is called the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, all Buddhas...

It is also eternal. It is neither text nor letter, nor is it expressible by words; this praise of the expressive [means] is itself free from letters, which is precisely the expressed reality—the *dharmatā*.
Thus, while being within letters, it is free from letters. Vimalakīrti said that there is no liberation apart from letters.
Therefore, regarding the statement that "a single sound is clearly understood according to each type," this praises the subtle resonance of the Buddha’s voice as he preaches the Dharma.
It is wondrous. It accords perfectly with the minds of people; though there is but one sound, there are diverse understandings, each being different. This is what Vimalakīrti meant when he said:
"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind. To speak of this in terms of the three virtues:
This belongs to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. The aforementioned Buddha-Jewel belongs to the virtue of *prajñā*. Although these are a single virtue, each necessarily possesses the three.
Its very substance is pure and illuminating, free from all defilements of delusion; thus, these three virtues constitute that which is illuminated.
The Buddha-Jewel, as the object of the three truths, is that which illuminates—the wisdom of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), which is entirely the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).
This is what is meant by the statement: "The cultivation that arises is entirely cultivation within the nature.

Now, wishing to expound and clarify the wondrous wisdom of the three contemplations within one mind, I first take refuge in the treasure of the single object and the three truths, seeking their secret empowerment.
I prostrate to the pure and noble sages, And to the Saṃgha of Arhats in the ten directions who are in harmony.
They uphold the prohibitive precepts without transgression, Shaking their mendicant staffs and carrying their alms bowls to benefit all sentient beings.

The Sanskrit term *saṃgha* translates here as "the harmonious assembly. First is harmony in principle (*dharma-sāmagrī*), referring to those above the stage of seeing the Truth (*darśana-mārga*). As for the body...

Although they differ from one another, the principle realized is the same, and these two matters are harmonized. This refers to four or more persons performing the same *poṣadha* (*śīla-uddeśa*) and *karmavācanā*.
However, there are both Bodhisattva Saṃghas and Śrāvaka Saṃghas; from the stage of self-enlightenment (*svayambhū*) downward, they constitute the Bodhisattva Saṃgha.

Those from the stage of the four fruits downward constitute the Śrāvaka Saṃgha; this is the Saṃgha-ratna in its distinct characteristics. If, however, one considers the Three Jewels as a single essence:
"Buddha" means awakening, which is the Buddha-ratna to which one previously took refuge;

"Dharma" means non-awakening, which is the Dharma-ratna to which one previously took refuge; and "Saṃgha" means harmony, which is the Saṃgha-ratna to which one now takes refuge. These are the Three Jewels.
To speak by summarizing "one as three": within the aforementioned Buddha Jewel, the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is the Buddha Jewel;
since "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*), the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) is the Dharma Jewel; since "Dharma" means non-awakening (*abodhi*), the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is the Saṅgha Jewel;
since "Saṅgha" means harmony, it is the merit that harmonizes with the *dharmakāya* and manifests everywhere in response. Thus, these are contained within this single Buddha Jewel.

This constitutes the essence of the Three Jewels. Within the second jewel, the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*): the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is the Dharma Jewel, for its nature is wondrous provisionality, which is primordially complete.
Thus, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is the Buddha Jewel, for the ultimate can dissolve the conventional and remains free from defilement.
Thus, the middle truth (*madhyamasatya*) is the Saṅgha Jewel, for it can harmoniously integrate the two extremes and cause them to be in accord. Within this Dharma Jewel, there is one...
This is the embodiment of the Three Jewels. Within the third, the Jewel of the Sangha, the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra regards the governance of the great assembly as the Sangha Jewel.
Thus, the governance of principle (*li*) in harmony is the Buddha Jewel; the governance of phenomena (*shi*) in harmony is the Dharma Jewel;

and the governance of phenomena being identical to principle, and the governance of principle being identical to phenomena, constitutes the Sangha Jewel. Within this Sangha Jewel, there is the Three Jewels in One Essence (*yiti*). Now, wishing to...
I clarify here the three virtues of the single essence, the three truths of the single object, and the three contemplations of the single observation;
therefore, I first take refuge to seek their secret empowerment, so that what I shall expound may accord with both principle and the capacity of beings.
II. Making the Great Vow:
Beings born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; Those with form and those without form;
those with perception, without perception, or neither-perception-nor-non-perception— Of these diverse classes, circling through the six realms of existence without a moment’s rest.
I now prostrate and take refuge in the Triple Gem, universally giving rise to the Bodhi-mind for the sake of all sentient beings.
May all beings submerged in the sea of suffering be uprooted from their pain through the power of the Buddhas, Dharma, and Sangha, and through the skillful means of compassion;
may you not abandon your great vows to deliver all living creatures.
With the sovereign power of transformation, they deliver beings without end; Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges shall all attain perfect enlightenment.
These twelve lines of verse are the formal arousal of the Four Great Vows, namely: "Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them.
"Afflictions are innumerable; I vow to sever them. "Dharma gates are immeasurable; I vow to study them. "The Buddha-way is unsurpassed..."

This refers to the fulfillment of these vows. These four vows are based upon the objects of the Four Noble Truths; externally, compassion is able to bestow happiness, and pity is able to extract one from suffering.

Although the present text speaks of the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, revolving within the three worlds without a moment’s pause, it urges one to take refuge in the Triple Gem and rely upon the power of compassion and skillful means to extract one from the truth of suffering.
Indeed, the fruit is achieved through the cause; therefore, if one wishes to uproot the fruit of suffering, one must first eliminate the cause of suffering.
This entails gathering the two vows: the vow to deliver all sentient beings and the vow to sever all afflictions. Thus, one does not abandon the great vow to rescue all living beings.

The power of transformation is sovereign and its deliverance is infinite. The three phrases regarding the establishment of all beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in perfect enlightenment constitute the single vow of "I vow to attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, while one desires to bestow the fruit of happiness, it is also necessary to teach them to first cultivate the causes of happiness;
this constitutes the two vows of "I vow to study all dharmas" and "I vow to attain Buddhahood. Moreover, the Four Noble Truths correspond to these four [vows].

The teachings differ regarding whether [the four truths] are progressive or not. Since the subsequent text explains the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* based on the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), this vow is thus formulated in reliance upon the realm of the unconditioned four truths (*anabhisaṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Having understood this, all that follows shall be judged by means of the four truths and the four great vows, whether they are complete or deficient.

There is nothing that does not conform to the compass and the square. Furthermore, regarding the four great vows (catvāri mahāvratāni) above, one has already perfected both self-benefit and the benefit of others;
as for what is manifested below, one first acts for oneself and subsequently for others—all of these, without exception, are matters contained within the four great vows.
Having spoken these verses, I again prostrate myself and take refuge before all the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Sanghas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Having already paid homage previously, I now take refuge once more to manifest my earnestness and to have something upon which to rely. Indeed, the triple world...
In this ocean of suffering, only the Three Jewels can serve as a vessel for crossing over; they provide both self-deliverance and the deliverance of others, and their teachings are fully complete.

Therefore, among the vows made below, one first acts for oneself and subsequently for others. Within the practice for oneself, one first vows to diligently seek unexcelled Bodhi with a resolve that never regresses.

Relying upon the power of the Triple Gem, I make this vow with a sincere heart: to cultivate unexcelled Bodhi, from this present life until the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment, I shall resolutely and diligently seek it without ever retreating.
One should diligently seek [the goal] without retreating. For example, in a previous life, Śākyamuni was a girl named Maitrīhṛdayā (Compassionate Heart).

She resolved to go to the great ocean to retrieve a wish-fulfilling jewel in order to relieve the suffering of the poor. Her mother, out of affection, would not let her go. As she was about to depart, her mother clasped her daughter’s feet;
though the girl insisted on leaving, she inadvertently injured one of her mother’s hairs. Only then did her mother release her and allow her to go.
When the signs of the Great Ocean Hell appeared, a glowing iron wheel descended from the sky to scorch her head.
The woman made this vow: "May all the sufferings of all sentient beings in the world gather upon my crown; may I undergo them all on their behalf.
Having made this vow, the iron wheel vanished of its own accord. Thus, there is a verse that says: "Even if a glowing iron..."
"May the wheel spin upon the crown of my head; never for the sake of such suffering shall I retreat from the bodhicitta.
Such should be the resolve in seeking the Way."

Before attaining the Way, one shall not suffer from untimely illness, nor shall one’s life be cut short prematurely. When the end of one’s natural lifespan arrives, one shall see no evil omens and be free from all terrors;
no inverted views shall arise, the body shall be free from pain, the mind shall not be distracted, and right wisdom shall be clear and lucid.
They do not pass through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). They do not enter the hells, nor the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, or those that move upon water, on land, or through the air.
Neither celestial Māras, non-Buddhist paths, nor the spirits and ghosts of the dark underworld—none of these various forms shall they ever assume.

Before attaining the Way, one’s status is extremely vast. For now, let us consider the period prior to severing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), and before emerging from birth-and-death within the limits of the mundane world (*paricchinna-utpāda-vināśa*).
During this time, one cannot avoid the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and the transmigration through the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).
Among these six destinies, it is only within the human realm that one can cultivate the Great Path of Bodhi; therefore, one should make the vow to be born [as a human] life after life.
Passing through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one does not enter the three miserable realms in successive lifetimes. One does not take birth among those who travel by water, land, or air;
nor among celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, or the ghosts and spirits of the dark realm; nor among any of the various hybrid forms. As the scholar Pei said:

"Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of deep obscurity and sorrow; birds and beasts harbor the grief of frantic flight; the Asuras are in the midst of rage; and the devas are in the midst of pleasure."
One may thereby rectify the mind and thoughts and advance toward Bodhi; only the human path is capable of this.

Yet, even though one’s resolve is thus established, there is the obscuration of the "darkness between births" (*ganyin*) upon taking rebirth. Therefore, one must first vow to be free from sudden illness, to avoid untimely death, and to exhaust one's lifespan through right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
One should be free from inauspicious signs, from terror and delusion, and from the distraction of physical suffering. Right...
With clear and lucid wisdom, may the objects of the hidden realm not manifest before you; thus, there shall be no occasion for even a fleeting thought to follow after them.
May you long obtain a human body—intelligent, upright, and honest—not born in an evil land, nor encountering an evil king, nor born in a frontier region.
They shall not undergo the sufferings of poverty; nor shall they ever be born as slaves, women, eunuchs, or those with dual sexual organs;

nor as those with yellow hair or black teeth, the dull-witted, the dark-minded, the ugly, the deformed, the blind, the deaf, or the mute. Indeed, anything loathsome shall ultimately never arise for them.

Among the six realms of existence, a human body is the most difficult to obtain. To cultivate bodhi, one must further ensure that the three karmas are fundamentally free from evil and consist solely of goodness;
by constantly extinguishing evil and giving rise to good, one shall long maintain a human form, endowed with intelligence and integrity.
This person is fundamentally without evil and possesses only goodness. Not being born in an evil land, they are not led astray by evil.
Not encountering an evil king, they are not compelled by evil. Not being born in a frontier region, they have no faction of false views.
Not suffering the hardships of poverty, they lack the causes for creating evil. As for the forms of slaves and women—[this is]...

One shall never be born blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired; indeed, nothing loathsome shall ever arise. There shall be no retribution for evil karma, and the obstacles to leaving the household life shall be severed.
One shall be born in a central land, into a family of right faith, always obtaining a male body with all six sense faculties complete, upright and fragrant.

Free from all defilements and impurities. The preceding passage clarified that there was originally no evil; this statement declares that there is only goodness. As the Sūtra says: "A human body is difficult to obtain;

birth in a central land is difficult; the arousal of faith is difficult; and the possession of the six sense faculties is difficult. Since one is upright and fragrant and pure, and furthermore free from defilement—
Once purified, one may become a vessel for the tools of renunciation and a receptacle for receiving the Way.
With a harmonious and elegant will, and a tranquil body and mind, one is free from greed, hatred, and delusion; the three poisons are forever severed, and no further evils are committed.
"Constantly contemplating all that is wholesome.

All that follows speaks of constantly extinguishing evil and giving rise to the wholesome. The five phrases beginning with "the mind and will are harmonious and elegant" clarify the constant extinguishing of evil;
the single phrase "constantly contemplating all that is wholesome" clarifies the constant giving rise to the wholesome.
He did not serve as a royal minister, nor did he act as an envoy; he had no desire for honor or adornment, but lived out his life in contented poverty.
Although royal ministers are noble, they lack the aspiration for renunciation, and thus he did not wish to become one.
Long ago, a certain official asked the Patriarch, "Your humble servant also wishes to leave the household life. The Patriarch replied, "Renunciation is the task of a great man."
This is not something that generals or ministers can achieve; thus, one knows that leaving the household life (renunciation) is no easy matter.

Even if one were appointed to a mission, it would lead to the fault of flattery and sycophancy, so I do not wish to undertake it. Though the splendors of honor may be beautiful, they give rise to a heart of greedy attachment;

therefore, I do not seek them. As for the previous statement that one does not accept poverty and suffering, and the present statement that one dwells in poverty while passing through this world—now, as for those who are poor, they are [the true] scholars.
This is a constant principle. That the gentleman remains steadfast even in poverty serves as an aid to entering the Way; thus, he is able to find peace in poverty while advancing toward the Way.
The petty person, however, when in straits, becomes excessive; instead of being content, they are burdened by the pursuit of food and clothing and lack the will for long-term vision.
As the ancients said: "Whether one is capable or not depends on oneself; whether something is acceptable or not likewise does not depend on external things. This is precisely what that means.

Furthermore, they have few desires and know contentment; they do not amass stores, but rely on food merely to sustain the body. They refrain from stealing, do not kill living beings, and do not eat fish or meat.
They respect and love all sentient beings as if they were no different from themselves.
The Sūtra says: "One who knows contentment is peaceful and happy even when lying upon the ground; one who lacks contentment finds no satisfaction even while dwelling in heaven.
For those who study the Way, clothing need only suffice to cover the body and food need only suffice to fill the belly.
For if one accumulates excessively, desire becomes insatiable; and if desire is insatiable, one will inevitably resort to theft.
Regarding theft, up to the killing of sentient beings and the eating of fish and meat—few instances of taking life or harming living creatures do not originate from a lack of contentment.
Nevertheless, those who study the Way must not only refrain from killing and eating; they must furthermore regard all things and themselves as no different, embracing them with compassion.
Having already loved them, they must also revere them; having loved them, they must treat them with respect.

Thus, they become my field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*); to revere them is to treat them as my field of respect (*guru-kṣetra*). When the field of compassion is universal, humans and animals are nurtured alike;

when the field of respect is universal, one views living beings and Buddhas with equal regard. This is the vast and expansive resolve for salvation, serving as the gradual entry into the Ultimate Way.
Their nature and conduct are gentle and supple. They do not seek out the faults of others, nor do they boast of their own virtues. They do not contend with things;
they treat enemies and kin with equality, giving rise to no discrimination and producing neither hatred nor attachment.
When one's nature and conduct are supple, one is then constantly gentle, harmonious, and compliant, rather than abrupt or violent. This is the source for blocking transgressions.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Abiding on the ground of patience; by patience one attains the ground. Once the ground is attained, insults cannot enter.
Even if they do enter, one already possesses that ground and does not succumb to abruptness or violence. This is what is meant by: "In moments of haste, one must necessarily..."
In this regard, those who seek out the faults of others not only fail to see their own faults, but they inevitably conceal the virtues of others.
When one does not see their own faults, their own transgressions increase day by day; when one conceals the virtues of others, their own virtues diminish day by day.
Those who extol their own virtues do not merely boast of their own goodness, but they inevitably suppress their own [shortcomings].
This is evil. To boast of one's own goodness causes one's goodness to diminish daily; to conceal one's own faults causes one's faults to increase daily.
This is the means to block the source of evil and the gradual way to give rise to goodness;

therefore, the Great Master has taken great care to speak of it, intending that one must never contend with others, treat enemies and kin with equality, refrain from giving rise to discrimination, and not harbor hatred.
Through love, hatred is severed and goodness arises. One does not covet the possessions of others nor begrudge one's own wealth;
one takes no pleasure in aggression or violence and always maintains integrity and straightforwardness, so that the mind is never impulsive or violent.
Always delighting in humility is the severance of the root of greed. Not begrudging one’s own wealth is the destruction of the root of stinginess.
Taking no pleasure in aggression is the means to cut off desire. Constantly harboring sincerity and straightforwardness is the blocking of the gradual onset of depravity. The mind does not...
Sudden violence is the cause of distant anger; constant delight in humility is the gateway to the arrival of goodness.
If one can truly act in this way, what evil would not be severed, and what goodness would not arise?
There is no evil speech in the mouth, no evil conduct in the body, and no crookedness or deceit in the mind; thus the three karmas are pure.
This is the summary, which constitutes the place where evil is severed and goodness is produced. It does not go beyond the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
When these three karmas are pure, they become a forest of the ten wholesome virtues; when the three karmas are defiled, they become a deep pool of the ten unwholesome transgressions.
Whether one follows or opposes [the path] depends on the person.
Wherever they dwell, they shall be peaceful and secure, free from all obstacles and difficulties, such as thieves, bandits, royal law, imprisonment, shackles, staffs, and chains.

Swords, spears, arrows, and lances; fierce beasts and venomous insects; falling peaks and drowning in water; being burned by fire or blown away by the wind; startled by thunder and struck by lightning;
trees breaking and crags collapsing; halls crumbling and rafters rotting; the terrors of being beaten and struck; being pursued, surrounded, seized, and bound.
Furthermore, they falsely slander and maliciously entrap one with crooked accusations; yet none of these difficult circumstances will be experienced.
The three calamities and eight difficulties are all summoned by evil karma; since there is no evil karma, how could there be any difficulty?
Although no [karmic] deeds have been committed in this life, I fear that past retributions have not yet been extinguished.

I pray that the power of the Triple Gem may provide secret assistance and manifest protection, so that none [of these karmas] shall be experienced, and that they may not become obstacles on the path of practice.
May malevolent spirits and flying calamities, celestial poisons and pestilences, and demons, goblins, and specters— whether by rivers or seas,
on lofty mountains or remote peaks, or tree-dwelling deities— whosoever among these numinous beings hears my name or beholds my form, shall give rise to the bodhicitta.
May they all protect one another and not harm or disturb each other, remaining peaceful and secure day and night, free from all alarm and fear.

May their superior vows be entirely unharmed, and may they simply remain far removed from such calamities. Now, I pray that upon hearing your names and beholding your forms, they will resolve to protect you.
Furthermore, may you lead them toward the good and instruct them in the Way, so that both themselves and others may together ascend to that [state of liberation].
This is the armor (*saṃnāha*) of the Bodhisattva Śrīpūrṇa.

His four great elements are robust and healthy; his six sense faculties are pure; he is unstained by the six sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); his mind is free from distracted thoughts and devoid of dullness or stagnation.
They do not give rise to nihilistic views; they do not cling to emptiness or existence; they remain far removed from all signs. They faithfully serve the Muni and do not grasp at their own opinions.
Their understanding is clear and lucid; they practice in every birth. Their right wisdom is firm and steadfast, and they are not captured by Māra. At the time of their great passing,
Peaceful and joyful, as they cast off one body and receive another, may they have no enemies or adversaries; may all sentient beings become their virtuous friends.

May this vow keep them far from malevolent spirits and demons, and cause them to always return to the Right Path. Within the human realm, before renouncing the world, may it be thus in every birth, and so in every place.
In whatever place I am born, may I encounter the Buddha and hear the Dharma; may I leave the household life as a pure youth and serve in harmony with the Sangha.

May my body never be parted from the *kāṣāya* robe, and may my vessel for food never deviate from the *pātra* bowl. May my resolve for the Way be firm and steadfast, and may I never give rise to arrogance—this is the true vow of the Great Master.
If I do not cultivate the Great Path of Bodhi, then so be it; but if I wish to cultivate it...

This cannot be achieved except through leaving the household life. Indeed, becoming a śramaṇa by leaving the household life is the first step toward transcending the mundane world and the initial gateway for entering the Path.
It is to join the orthodox stream of the Triple Gem and board the Dharma-ship of the Six Perfections.
However, if one is born in a place where it is impossible to encounter a Buddha or hear the Dharma, one will not know the excellence of leaving the household life. Unless one is a child...

This is true renunciation. Furthermore, one must not merely be a monk of outward purity; having already left the household life, one must be a member of a harmonious and non-contentious Saṃgha, a practitioner pure in the observance of the Vinaya.
Therefore, I vow that my body shall not be separated from my robes and my food shall not be separated from my bowl;

thus, throughout this lifetime, the precepts shall remain unimpaired, providing a foundation for the multi-storied pavilion of concentration and wisdom, while simultaneously strengthening the resolve for the Way.

Firmly, one does not give rise to arrogance; as steadfast as a vajra, yet yielding like a bridge, with hardness and softness complementing one another, there will be no place one enters where one does not find fulfillment.
Revere the Triple Gem; constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); draw near to enlightened teachers; follow virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); have deep faith in the True Dharma;
diligently practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); and read and recite the Mahāyāna.

This and the subsequent passages all refer to the practices to be cultivated after leaving the household life. First, one must revere the Triple Gem, for they are the field of merit that provides excellent protection and serve as the foundation upon which one relies.
Second, one must constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), progressing toward purity so as not to be defiled by the dust of the world.
Third, one must draw near to enlightened teachers and follow virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for their guidance and transformation.

First, one must be guided and led, for by seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one attains realization. Second, one must cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, for by contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, one abandons all delusions. Third, one must practice the four right efforts, for by severing unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome ones, one attains liberation.

Fourth, one must have deep faith in the True Dharma and walk the direct path, for it is free from all perversity and deviation. Fifth, one must diligently practice the six perfections, for by crossing the ocean of the six realms of birth and death, one reaches the six infinite virtues (pāramitās).
Sixth, one must read and recite the Mahāyāna, for by penetrating the perfect principle, one is able to transport oneself out of the three realms.

Walking in meditation and prostrating; with exquisite flavors, incense, and flowers; with sounds of chanting and hymns; with lamps, candles, pavilions, and towers; with mountains, seas, forests, and springs;
in the air and on level ground—whatever exists in the world, from the size of a mote of dust upward, they are all brought forth as offerings. Thus they gather and unite all merit.
Dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment:
the Ten Great Vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva begin with "paying homage to all Buddhas," followed by "extensively cultivating offerings.
Thus, whether it be walking the path, prostrating, or various forms of making offerings, they are all matters of this practice, culminating in dedication.
"Bodhi" refers to the tenth practice of universal dedication; by mentioning its beginning and end, the intermediate vows are likewise encompassed.
Contemplating the definitive meaning, one should aspire to solitude and tranquility, remaining pure, simple, and silent, disliking clamor and distraction, and taking no pleasure in living in crowds.
One should always prefer solitude and seek nothing at all, concentrating the mind on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
This constitutes the correct cultivation of one's vow. Contemplating the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) takes understanding and liberation as its foundation.

The five phrases beginning with "resolving to delight in seclusion" correspond to the fifth of the five conditions: dwelling in a quiet and secluded place. "Seeking nothing at all" refers to concentrating the mind.
Concentration and wisdom constitute the dharma-gate of the correct cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they transform and deliver sentient beings; according to their heart's wishes, they act with sovereign mastery and without obstruction, bringing all myriad practices to fulfillment.
Exquisite and infinite; upright, circular, and luminous.

To resolve to attain the Buddha-way is the vow to learn all Dharma-gates. To be fully endowed with the six supernormal powers and to transform and deliver sentient beings is the vow to deliver all sentient beings.
To cause them to become upright, circular, and luminous, and to resolve to attain the Buddha-way, is the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way. [The afflictions...]
The vow to sever [afflictions] is also included therein. Thus we know that although vows are many, when summarized they do not exceed the Four Great Vows.
For if a vow does not rely upon these four, that vow is deluded; yet to not make a vow at all is to fall into folly.
Rather than being foolish, it is better to be deluded; by correcting that delusion and returning to the right path, the Bodhisattva’s resolve is fulfilled, and the Six Perfections—
By practicing this cultivation, the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi may be hoped for.

I vow that by means of these roots of goodness, they shall extend universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions—reaching upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and downward to the Wind-Circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
To all beings within the heavens and the human realm, to those with bodies in the six destinies, and to all conscious creatures: may all my merits be shared together with all sentient beings.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as atoms, not only for a single sentient being, but for all who possess roots of goodness corresponding to my own, may they all be universally suffused and adorned.
This demonstrates that through the merit of making vows, one further redirects those vows from oneself toward others and shares them with all sentient beings;
it truly manifests the universality of the Great Master’s vows and the fulfillment of the Bodhisattva’s pledge.
The suffering and affliction within the hells: *Namo buddha-dharma-saṃghāya*. By invoking the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, may all beings attain liberation.
The suffering and affliction among the hungry ghosts: *Namo buddha-dharma-saṃghāya*. By invoking the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, may all beings attain liberation.
The suffering and affliction among the animals—homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. By invoking the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, may all beings receive liberation.
Gods, humans, asuras, and all sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who are tormented by the eight sufferings—homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
By virtue of these roots of goodness of mine, may all be universally freed from their fetters. Homage to the Buddhas of the three periods of time;

homage to the Sūtras, the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas, and the Sangha, and to the assembly of all holy ones as numerous as motes of dust. May you not abandon your original compassion, but graciously receive and protect all classes of sentient beings.

The Great Master’s vow was fundamentally to deliver sentient beings. Although the vow was established, his practice had not yet been fulfilled; although his practice had been fulfilled, his delusions were not yet exhausted;
because his delusions were not yet exhausted, the Way was not yet perfected; and because the Way was not yet perfected, the boat was not yet secure.
To attempt to ferry many people across the ocean of evil with a boat that is incomplete and insecure is such that both self and others will inevitably drown—this is the necessary principle.
This is the profound admonition of Tiantai and the deep insight of the Great Master. However, it is precisely when sentient beings suffer most acutely that the time is ripe;
at such a moment, the mind’s resolve to deliver them is urgent, yet one lacks the leisure for self-reliance and must instead rely upon the power of others.
Only the Triple Gem serves as the vessel for the world and the excellent medicine for the sick; therefore, one must urgently invoke their names to seek swift salvation.
May all sentient beings throughout the void take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; may they leave suffering behind, escape the three miserable realms, and swiftly transcend the triple world.
May each of them give rise to the bodhicitta and practice Prajñā day and night; in every birth, may they exert diligent effort, always as if their very heads were on fire.
When first attaining Bodhi, one vows to deliver others through transformation.
One makes a vow to take refuge in the Triple Gem oneself in order to seek the liberation of sentient beings;

yet it would be even better to wish that each and every being individually takes refuge in the Triple Gem, for those who are thus delivered will find it easy. This is because the Triple Gem of the One Essence is inherently possessed by all living beings. Due to...
Beginningless ignorance causes one to be deluded and unaware of oneself. Because one is unaware of oneself, one is deluded regarding the Buddha Jewel;

because one fails to realize what is inherently present, one is deluded regarding the Dharma Jewel; and because the beginning and the fundamental are separated and not unified, one is deluded regarding the Sangha Jewel.

Thus, one is like someone who mistakes their head for a shadow and pursues it, abandoning their father and fleeing from home, wandering through the six realms of rebirth without end. Therefore, they have no father and no home.
Without support and without refuge, they now vow that all sentient beings throughout the empty realm shall each take refuge in the Triple Gem.

This is solely for the purpose of their awakening to the fact that the original, single essence is the Triple Gem, so that it may serve as their refuge, their reliance, their salvation, and their protection. Thus it is said:

by taking refuge in the Buddha, one does not fall into hell; by taking refuge in the Dharma, one does not fall among the hungry ghosts; by taking refuge in the Sangha, one does not fall among the animals.

When one maintains meditative equipoise through the power of both self and others, such that the initial and fundamental awakenings are unified as one, only then does one become a true refuge in the Triple Gem.
I practice the Way and pay homage; I recite the sutras and mindfully recollect the Buddha; I cultivate morality, concentration, and wisdom. *Namo buddhadharmasaṃghāya*.
I universally pray that all sentient beings may fully attain the path of Buddhahood. We, all conscious beings, shall resolutely seek Bodhi;
we pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and vow to quickly achieve perfect enlightenment.
Within this, the making of vows is expressed through three types of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). "I practice the Way, perform prostrations, and so forth" refers to the cause;

"may all [beings] attain the Buddha-way" refers to the fruit. This is thus the dedication of the cause toward the fruit. Furthermore, regarding "I practice the Way, perform prostrations, and so forth":
"Self" means: universally wishing that all sentient beings shall all attain the Way of Buddhahood. "Other" means: turning oneself toward others.
Furthermore, my own practice of the Way, such as prostrations and so forth, is the phenomenon (*shi*). That "all shall attain the Way of Buddhahood" is the principle (*ri*).

This is returning the phenomenon toward the principle. If there were no cause, the fruit would not be consummated; if there were no self, there would be no universality for others; if there were no phenomenon, there would be no integration with the principle.
Third is fulfillment. When the bodhisattva’s practice is perfected, one therefore makes a vow to ultimately attain it.

Furthermore, in such a vow, there is practice within the vow; as vow and practice rely upon one another, they are neither excessive nor solitary. They occupy the foremost position prior to formal cultivation.
This marks the beginning of its publication.
○ Chapter Three: Drawing Near to Teachers and Friends.
First, one contemplates the three realms in order to give rise to weary detachment.
All who wish to depart from the home of the triple world must give rise to a mind of weary detachment (*saṃvega*).

To give rise to a mind of weary detachment, one must contemplate the realm of no-abiding security, as in the Parable of the Burning House: the head is the palace, the belly is the hall, and the back is the dwelling—all are impermanent.
High yet perilous, suffering is without end. The foundations of the pillars have crumbled and rotted; life does not...
Long has the consciousness served as the guiding beam and ridgepole; now ruined by manifold sufferings, it is truly pitiable.

Past karma serves as the foundation and steps, yet decrepitude and decay—how can they be endured? The four elements are joined together like a wall; when it crumbles and collapses, they disperse in all directions.
As the plaster falls away, the skin becomes a festering sore; the thatched roof of hair falls in disarray, turning yellow and withered.
The rafters and eaves are askew and detached; the joints are rigid and stiff. The surrounding walls are crooked and winding, evoking a sense of desolation.
Various impurities fill every corner, lacking any purity or fragrance. Owls, hawks, and vultures are long on arrogance; crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons are strong in pride.
Vipers, snakes, and scorpions flaunt their anger; centipedes and millipedes display their fury with haughtiness. Lizards and many-legged insects are foolish and base; weasels...
The field of ignorance is filled with wildcats and mice; what can the various evil insects do to resist it? They scurry about in confusion, their movements vast and chaotic.
This realm of the four inversions is a place of foul excrement and urine, overflowing with impurities in manifold ways.

Upon it gather dung beetles and various other worms, which mistake the impure for the pure, clearly exposing their own corruption. There are also jackals, foxes, and wolves, gnawing and devouring [the corpses].
Trampling corpses at their side, greed draws things toward itself; it does not act with reason, like a pack of dogs vying with one another to seize and maul.
Emaciated by hunger and seeking food, the mind is filled with terror; it hoards the five sensory objects without knowing when to stop.
How powerful and arrogant is this greed! It fights, tugs, snarls, and barks—such is the doubt of man.
Delusion is likewise not good; everywhere there are *chimei* and *wangliang* ghosts. Such sharp faculties give rise to long-standing attachments.
*Yakṣas* and evil ghosts devour human flesh, and poisonous insects likewise feast upon them.

Denying both virtuous causes and their evil fruits, they sweep everything away at once like a walnut trampled by a staggering ox. Various evil birds and beasts breed and multiply, each guarding its own hoard.
The deep embankments are overrun as yakṣas vie with one another to seize and devour [the corpses]. Their malevolent intent grows ever more intense, their clamor resounding far and wide.

Holding wrong views, they deny both good and evil; they destroy the principles of cause and effect, acting in accordance with those same [corrupt] ways. The kumbhāṇḍa spirits crouch upon earthen mounds.
They move about one or two feet above the ground, sporting wantonly and grasping the paws of dogs; they strike them down for their own amusement until the dogs lose consciousness.
Such is the state of these outsiders when born in heaven. When the Mlecchas see them, they sometimes bow or nod.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with massive bodies, naked, black, and emaciated, dwelling in their midst; they let out great, evil cries, calling out for food. The multitude...
To give rise to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is also inauspicious. Vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, it is likened to something vast and long.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with needle-like throats; their bellies are as large as mountains, yet they starve their own entrails. The danger of the non-conceptual nirvāṇa is like this:

the two attachments to annihilation and permanence obstruct one another. Their hair is disheveled and extremely fierce; driven by hunger, they repay their karmic retribution. Such are the various views.
The initial turning is not yet fixed; they attack one another’s strongholds on the frontier.

Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil beasts, driven by hunger, peer through the windows and casements in all four directions. With false wisdom, they observe and cling to the four extremes; how immeasurable is their fear of various calamities!
When the fire of the burning house breaks out and blazes on all sides, the beams, rafters, and pillars crackle and burst, collapsing and falling.

How lamentable their fall! The walls and fences have crumbled; how can anything endure forever? Such is the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet my children remain unaware and frolic in joy.
The elder, moved by compassion, established a bridge and ferry; he enticed them with three carts and led them outside the gate.
