As a True Dharma King, he bestowed great carts equally upon all. The three vehicles are gradual stages and not the ultimate; in reality, phenomenon and principle are non-dual.
Fasiliang was weary of suffering and delighted in joy; he cultivated the three contemplations and rode this precious vehicle to travel through the four quarters.
Next, he associated closely with virtuous friends in order to seek the way out. Next, he inquired after them morning and evening to maintain the proper etiquette.
Next, he examined whether they were well or unwell to ensure their proper care and nourishment. Next, he asked what they were doing to show his close attendance to their affairs. Next, he observed...

One looks upward with tirelessness because of the arising of profound reverence; one repeatedly resolves upon the essential points for the sake of correct cultivation; one presents a concise analysis according to one's understanding in order to distinguish between the erroneous and the correct;
one examines one’s own capacity to know whether [the practice] has matured; one observes the arising of defects and gives rise to doubt so as to be able to advance to the sublime medicine;
one reflects with meticulous scrutiny to seek what is truly accurate; and one applies oneself with diligence day and night, fearing that conditions may diverge.
To focus single-mindedly on one practice is for the sake of accomplishing one's task; to forget one’s own body for the sake of the Dharma is for the sake of repaying kindness.
This chapter does not go beyond these two intentions: first, contemplating the three realms to give rise to weary detachment; second, associating with virtuous friends to seek the way out.

Within the category of associating with virtuous friends, there is both the manifestation of what is correct and the exclusion of what is incorrect. Regarding the manifestation of what is correct, there are ten [points].
Third: The first phrase, "intimately associating with virtuous friends," serves as the general heading; the remaining twelve phrases constitute the specific details.

This is because there is no such thing as seeking the path to liberation while not intimately associating with virtuous friends. Regarding the practice of inquiring after one's health at dawn and dusk as a matter of formal etiquette, this refers for now to the conventional norms of human society, such as the constant duty of a son serving his father;
thus it is said that one "maintains the rules of etiquette. Next, one must examine...
Regarding the phrase "how to appropriately attend to one's needs," this refers precisely to the actual practice of a disciple attending to their teacher.

This involves the morning and evening inquiries of well-being (*ding-sing*), following the protocol of ancient sages who would ask of their teacher: "Are you free from much illness? Are you free from much distress? Are the four great elements in harmony?
All such methods are established as models within the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya*. As for the matter of harmonizing [the body], [the instructions are as follows].
Providing food and drink, and adding to the bedding and coverlets—these are all matters in which a disciple ought to exert their utmost sincerity. Next, one asks what tasks have been performed;
this clarifies those who have personally received instructions. When a disciple serves a teacher, there must be specific tasks to be done;
by carrying out these orders, no discord or deviation occurs. This is like Śākyamuni serving Devadatta, gathering firewood and fruits as required.
To offer with reverence at that time is the proper procedure. Next, regarding "gazing up without indolence so as to give rise to earnestness":
the three preceding points all concern the act of gazing up. If indolence arises, the mind will not be earnest;
if the mind is not earnest, the resolve for the Way will not be urgent. How then can one resolve upon the essentials to constitute right practice? Therefore, one must maintain this.
Regarding "Laziness": it refers to those who have repeatedly resolved to engage in correct cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Since the preceding section on serving the teacher was entirely for the purpose of resolving upon the essentials of correct cultivation, this follows immediately after the explanation of serving the teacher.

This is what is meant by "keeping the sublime Dharma in mind," whereby body and mind are free from indolence and weariness. One who loses correct cultivation is one who merely practices these resolutions of intent.
Understanding. Understanding is like having eyes; practice is like having feet. When eyes and feet assist one another, one can reach the cool pond.

Therefore, repeatedly resolving upon the essential points of the mind is established for the sake of correct cultivation. Now, people say that practice alone is sufficient; what need is there for understanding?
How is this any different from walking without eyes? If they say, "I am well-versed in knowing the passable and the obstructed," I do not grant them permission. Furthermore—
[The opponent] says: "Awakening and understanding are sufficient. What is the use of practice? How is this any different from having eyes but no feet?

[The author] replies: "I have already ascended to the Jewel Island; yet, that is not yet enough. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains admonitions regarding practice, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides the analogy of the eyes and the feet.

I address this to those who seek perfect cultivation: do not fall into partiality. Next, in accordance with my understanding, I present this brief note to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

Therefore, the mind is resolved through a teacher, while understanding relies upon one's own progress. A single sound may be interpreted differently, for awakening is attained according to individual capacity.
If one does not employ one's own discernment to investigate under a master, how can one know whether one’s realization accords with the Buddha’s intent?
Therefore, one must present one’s understanding to the teacher to request their discernment: that which is correct should be preserved, and that which is erroneous should be discarded;

that which is perfect (*yuan*) should be cultivated, while that which is partial (*pian*) should be ceased. In this way, one will not fail the aspiration of having left the household life and serving a teacher.

Next, regarding "verifying the perfect cultivation to know whether it is mature or immature": once one has recognized the erroneous and the correct, as well as the partial and the perfect, and is further able to construct practice based on that understanding, [one may proceed].
The power of this [spiritual] energy must further be verified through a teacher. As for what is called "energy" (*bala*):
there must first be energy before there can be power. It is like a seed entering the earth; it acquires the vital energy (*ojo*) and is thus able to generate power.

However, before branches and leaves appear, one must necessarily first produce roots. Therefore, the Dharma-gate employs the analogy of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); only when there are roots can growth occur.
The power [of the sprout] draws up its stalk, breaking through the earth; branches grow and leaves spread; flowers bloom and fruit forms.

Whether it is raw or ripe during this interval can only be known by questioning experienced gardeners. It is the same with the study of the Way: stillness has power and serves as the vital energy of the ground for attainment;
illumination has power and achieves the merit of emerging from the soil. If stillness is usurped by dullness, and illumination is overcome by agitation, [the seed will not flourish].

If the wholesome seeds have already begun to rot and decay, how could they possibly give rise to the five faculties, attain the five powers, blossom with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, or bear the fruit of the eightfold noble path?
Therefore, one must request a teacher to examine whether the vitality of these seeds has matured;

only then can one avoid the calamity of scorching and ruin. Next, seeing that the illness has arisen and harboring doubt as to whether one is fit to receive the wondrous medicine, [the teacher] first—

I request that the Master examine whether [the mind] is raw or ripe. If it is raw, there will be illness; or perhaps doubt arises because of the illness, in which case one should treat it with the medicine of the Dharma.
If there is doubt, shatter it to give rise to faith. If it becomes dull through stillness (*śamatha*), arouse it with illumination (*vipaśyanā*);
if movement arises through illumination, nurture it with stillness. For stillness is the initial gateway for subduing the fetters (*saṃyojana*), while insight is for severing delusions.

This is the essential point: *śamatha* (calm abiding) is the excellent resource for nourishing the mind and consciousness, while *vipaśyanā* (insight) is the wondrous technique for stimulating spiritual understanding.
This is because although mental afflictions are many, they do not transcend dullness and agitation; and although the medicinal teachings are numerous, they do not transcend *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
As the subsequent text states: "If there is an excess of stillness, it easily gives rise to drowsiness; if there is an excess of alertness, it easily gives rise to delusion."
"Thought: 'Tranquil yet alert'—this is it; thus, drowsiness and sleep will not arise. 'Alert yet tranquil'—this is it; thus, distracted thoughts will not arise.
This is precisely what is meant. Next, regarding "thoroughly and specifically examining with careful thought to seek what is true and correct":

having already presented your understanding and proven its efficacy above, you have requested the application of the Dharma-medicine. Next, you must yourself thoroughly and specifically examine with careful thought, necessarily seeking that which is to be cultivated.
The path of practice culminates in a single point: returning to what is true and correct. That which is not [true] is illuminated so as to become correct;

that which is correct becomes quiescent, thereby giving rise to the various [qualities]. Only then do the five faculties arise, the five powers are perfected, the five hindrances are shattered, and one enters the three gates of liberation.

To "practice with diligent effort day and night, fearing that conditions may diverge" means that although the aforementioned process involves shattering what is non-correct to establish what is correct, it must nevertheless not be neglected.
Confused and lacking refinement; remaining stationary and failing to advance; entering into worldly toil; following divergent paths with disparate conditions;

causing one to walk the Middle Way only to abandon it halfway. Those who practice a single path with focused intent for the sake of accomplishing their task—indeed, the Way prizes unity and dreads multiplicity;
the mind prizes refinement and dreads confusion. If there is multiplicity or confusion, then the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) will not succeed.
Success! The illness of delusion and agitation grows daily; by what means can the gates of worldly toil be opened? By what means can one escape from the house of the three realms?
To forget one's own body for the sake of the Dharma is to know gratitude. As for those who are but followers of worldly toil:

The body is heavy while the Dharma is light, because one lacks the resolve to transcend the mundane world. For those who study the Way, the Way is heavy while the body is light, because they possess a mind focused on the conditioned Dharma.
Those who recognize their debt of gratitude will surely forget their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma;

those who do not recognize their debt of gratitude will surely forget the Dharma and value their own bodies. Indeed, the teachings expounded by the Master are the very heart-mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The Thesis: The wondrous nature of all sentient beings is the pure *dharmakāya*, from which it arises; the life-force of *prajñā* wisdom grows by means of it.
Its kindness exceeds that of one’s biological parents, and its virtue is more profound than that of the closest of kinsmen ordained by heaven.

Therefore, one ought to recognize this kindness and hold this Dharma in high esteem. Now, there are many kinds of teachers: those who possess the fullness of understanding, practice, and realization are the highest. There are also those who possess [only] understanding...
To practice without attaining realization through understanding is mediocre. To possess understanding without practicing is inferior.
If one possesses practice but lacks understanding, this is the lowest of the low.
When a disciple seeks a teacher, if they cannot find a superior or mediocre teacher, then rather than mere practice, they should seek understanding; for practice depends upon the teacher, whereas...
The understanding lies within oneself, yet its realization depends upon the teacher. It is like gold wrapped in tattered cloth;

one does not discard the gold because the cloth is worn and fail to take it. The same applies to serving a teacher: one does not refuse to accept the understanding simply because the teacher’s virtue is meager.
In this degenerate age, it is essential to seek a teacher through the lens of understanding. Only when both understanding and practice are complete should one seek [a teacher].
A teacher is not easily found with certainty. Thus, the Great Being of the Snowy Mountains abandoned his entire body for the sake of a half-verse to serve a rākṣasa;
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, lowered his banner of pride for the sake of the Buddha-dharma and prostrated before a jackal.

When the ancients honored their teachers for the sake of the Dharma, they forgot their own bodies to repay their kindness in such a manner. Those of later generations who aspire to the Great Way should take this as a model.
This serves as a mirror for reflection.

If one’s power of faith is feeble, the mind lacks single-minded resolve, conduct is coarse, and understanding is shallow, then one will drift according to circumstances. When encountering an event, the mind arises because of that event;
when there is no object, one rests the thoughts upon that absence. Since this is not the contemplation of equality between movement and stillness, then—
One follows the gains and losses inherent in existence and non-existence; yet the Way is not ascended at random, but is traversed according to one's merit and station.

The preceding text clarifies what is correct, while this section excludes what is erroneous. If one’s power of faith is slight and one’s intention lacks single-minded resolve, then not only will there be a lack of propriety in serving the teacher, but one’s study of the Way will also lack dedication.
Consequently, the realization that arises within such a person will be shallow. Its...

The practice is still coarse. When encountering conditions and confronting objects, the mind drifts and follows the current; when withdrawing the thoughts to contemplate the mind, delusions arise according to the stimuli.
"Stimulus" (*jī*) refers to the subtle; it is the very beginning of movement. This means that in the arising of the mind and the stirring of thoughts, there is entirely no method for subduing them;
hence it is said that one "drifts and follows the stimuli. When contacting phenomena, the mind arises because of those phenomena, yet the conditions themselves have no [fixed nature].
Thus, for one who relies on the cessation of thought through non-existence:

because the primary cause consists of coarse conduct and shallow understanding that float loosely according to circumstances, whenever they encounter various matters, the mind arises due to those matters. Since this phenomenon arises, various kinds of minds arise.

When they take emptiness and non-existence as their object, they rely on non-existence to cease their thoughts. Since this phenomenon ceases, various kinds of minds cease. This is precisely because...

The mind has no sovereign ruler; it pursues objects and flows along with them. The arising of the mind does not arise from non-abiding, and the cessation of thought does not cease through the knowledge of illusion.

If one arises from non-abiding, one must first be able to realize that the nature of objects is fundamentally empty, and only then, relying on emptiness, give rise to mental activities and practice the perfections.
If one ceases through the knowledge of illusion, one must first be able to know that all phenomena are like illusions, and only then, by means of illusion...
Thus, one extinguishes all discursive thoughts. This means that knowing illusion is itself detachment; no further expedient means are required.

Detachment from illusion is itself awakening; it is likewise not a gradual process. It is to contemplate movement and stillness as equal, and to arrive simultaneously at both existence and non-existence.
How could there be right and wrong, gain and loss, capable of leaving a trace within such a state? The final line concludes: "However, the Way is not ascended in vain. Follow...
Regarding those whose practice has reached the various stages: this further admonishes them not to give rise to arrogance toward higher levels, nor to become discouraged or retreat.

Because principle is identical to phenomena, the gradations of the stages remain distinct; because phenomena are identical to principle, the distinction between ordinary beings and Buddhas vanishes. Because they vanish...

Sentient beings are themselves Buddhas; this is because they are already so. Without realization, one cannot ascend to this state. Therefore, by understanding the Tiantai doctrine of the "six stages of identity" (*liu ji*), one may practice accordingly.
Thus, the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) is itself the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), and the sequential arrangement is itself the path of perfect fusion.
One can grasp this and put it into practice, ensuring that every action accords with the compass and the square.
IV. Admonitions on Food and Clothing Regarding the origins of food and clothing:
they involve nurturing and cultivation, tilling the soil and digging the earth, salting, boiling, and silkworm-rearing, as well as the ripening and processing [of materials].
They injure living beings and cause others to suffer death, providing for themselves while fearing only hunger and cold, yet failing to contemplate the suffering of death.

They kill others to sustain their own lives—how painful and lamentable! Furthermore, they employ the labor of agriculture and accumulate great strength; why do they alone take the lives of sentient beings?
Moreover, even the offerings of the faithful are difficult for them to digest. Though they have left the household life, what virtue do they possess?
In this context, clothing and food are first mentioned as the causes of merit and transgression.

If they are used to sustain the physical body so that one may enter the Path, they constitute merit; if they are used to indulge the four elements (the body) so that one creates karma, they constitute transgression.
For clothing is produced through extensive cultivation, which involves boiling salt-water silk worms; food is achieved through planting, which involves tilling the soil.
Digging the earth and tilling the soil involves inadvertently harming the lives of creatures. Boiling silkworms and moths with salt constitutes the intentional killing of sentient beings.
Thus, one brings about the maturation of karmic actions that injure life and cause others to undergo death, while providing sustenance for oneself.
These words describe the locus of the transgression; what follows is a formal admonition. Therefore it is said: "One fears only hunger and cold, yet does not contemplate death."

It is suffering. To kill others to sustain oneself—how painful and lamentable! Shi Bi said: "One worries for one's own hunger and cold, seeking food and clothing to the full, yet remains devoid of shame;
alas, this harms all living beings. The *Jiaojie jing* (Sutra of Precepts) says: "If one lacks a sense of shame, there is no difference between such a person and the various birds and beasts.
Furthermore, it does not stop at this alone; they also employ agricultural labor, accumulating great effort and depth of toil.
Thus, these robes and this food both originate from the blood and sweat of farmers and the fat and marrow of donors.

If one lacks the power of the Way, how can one bear such gifts? Therefore it is said: "Not only do sentient beings risk their lives [to provide for us], but the faithful offerings are also difficult to digest.
If this is the case, then even though one has left the household life, what virtue does one possess? When we speak of this, how could it be otherwise?

It does not cause heartache. Thus, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* says: "If one receives the faithful offerings of others but uses them contrary to the Dharma, allowing the mind to become negligent and abandoning the practice of the path, one will enter the three miserable realms and undergo the retribution of heavy suffering."
Alas! Those who wish to transcend the Triple World have yet to practice the severance of worldly dust; they merely possess the body of a man, yet lack the resolve of a true hero.
Day after day they are distracted by turmoil, night after night they remain shrouded in darkness. They have not cultivated the Way and its Virtue, yet their food and clothing are consumed in vain.
Above, they fail to propagate the Great Way; below, they neglect to benefit living beings; in between, they betray the Fourfold Debt of Gratitude—this is truly a cause for shame. Therefore...

The wise person reflects upon this: would it not be better to die with the Dharma than to be born without it? To do otherwise is merely to be deluded by oneself, holding one's own body in high esteem while disparaging the Dharma.
Having already used these matters to offer admonition and warning, I now seek to rouse his resolve; therefore, I first utter a sigh of lamentation to serve as an exhortation.
After this, he corrected him with these words to inspire him: "Generally speaking, those who speak of 'leaving home' (renunciation) mean leaving the home of the triple world (triloka).
Now, the triple world is the effect and the afflictions (kleśa) are the cause; this has been so from time immemorial.
If one now wishes to leave this triple world, it cannot be done without severing the dust [of worldly attachments]. Furthermore, renouncing the household life is the duty of a man of integrity."
It is truly admirable that you are able to sever affectionate attachments and cut off worldly toil.

If you merely allow yourself to be distracted by worldly toil without ceasing your delusions, remaining in a state of dull stupor throughout the night without regulating your sleep, then while the Way and its Virtue remain unaccomplished, your food and clothing will be squandered.
That you have been born with the body of a man and possess the resolve of a true hero—how much more so for one who has left the household life!
For such a person, there are three urgent priorities: first, to propagate the Buddha-Dharma; second, to benefit sentient beings; and third, to repay the four debts of gratitude.
If you do not apply yourself to these, but instead devote yourself solely to wealth, sensual pleasure, fame, food, and sleep, then reflect upon this and truly consider it a cause for shame.
One who can reflect in this way is a person of wisdom. Thus, it would be better to die while maintaining the Dharma than to live without the Dharma.
For example, there were once two śrāmaṇeras who traveled together to visit the Buddha. Having journeyed a long distance, they became hungry and thirsty;
encountering water containing insects, they had forgotten to bring their water-strainers. One śrāmaṇera said: "It would be better to endure thirst and die than to break the precepts."
He drank water containing insects. One novice monk said, "I would rather break the Buddha's precepts than lose my life and fail to see the Buddha.
Let those who are thirsty die on the road; let me live to go forward and see the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him, saying, "People take the precepts as the Buddha;
they do not take seeing [me] as the Buddha. You have broken the precepts to see me; this is not truly seeing me."
Furthermore, if one observes the precepts and beholds me, they truly behold me. For the Buddha constitutes the Dharma-body through the harmony of the five aggregates.
That novice who observes the precepts has already beheld the body of the precepts; how much more so the foundation for the fivefold multi-storied pavilion [of the other aggregates].

Having thus made firm the foundation of the precepts, the body of concentration, the body of wisdom, the body of liberation, and the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation will likewise be established.
One must know and see the body; only then can one be said to have fully beheld the Buddha-body. The final sentence concludes by stating:

"Those who are merely deluded and foolish, who value the body and despise the Dharma. This implies that those who awaken and thereby give rise to wisdom will necessarily value the Dharma and despise the body, whereas those who are lost in confusion and fall into folly are those who value the body and despise the Dharma.
V. Purifying the Three Karmas:

Fifth, [one must purify] the three karmas of greed, hatred, and wrong view; the karma of the mind [consisting of] false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech; the karma of the mouth [consisting of] killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
and the karma of the body. Indeed, one who aspires to seek the Great Way must first purify these three karmas.

The activities engaged in during the daily life of human existence are but three: namely, those of body, speech, and mind. These are like the great earth, which may either cause one to fall or cause one to rise.
If one cultivates the ten wholesome deeds of these three categories and takes them as the cause for transcending the world, then it is "causing one to rise."

If these are categorized as the three grades of the ten evil deeds, then the sequence of causes is inverted. Therefore, for those who have transcended the mundane world, the three karmas must be cultivated;
they must not fail to be purified, and they must reach the stage of ultimate purity.

Thereafter, within the four modes of deportment, one gradually enters the Way. Even when the six sense faculties encounter their respective objects, one attains thorough understanding according to conditions;
object and wisdom are both quiescent, merging in silent accord with the wondrous ultimate.

The preceding statement that purifying the three karmas constitutes the auxiliary practice (*upāya*) means that entering the Way through the four modes of deportment constitutes the primary cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The virtues of this primary cultivation do not transcend object and wisdom (*ālambana* and *jñāna*). Wisdom is the subject that contemplates; the object is that which is contemplated. Regarding these object and wisdom:
Furthermore, this does not lie outside the midst of daily life, for it concerns that which is encountered by the six sense faculties.

Thus, when *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* clarify the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* fully sets forth its twenty-five gates, these are none other than these very matters. However, the method for correct cultivation lies in the subtle art of attaining thorough realization in accordance with conditions, such that both object and wisdom are simultaneously stilled.
This is what is explained in the following passage regarding the non-duality of phenomena and principle, and the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
The principle of single-mindedness is thus perfected through cultivation; only then does one accord with the wondrous intent.

How does one purify the physical karma? One should deeply reflect for oneself upon the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—and restrain the three transgressions therein:
namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

Within the purification of bodily action, there are both specific and general explanations. Both the specific and general texts include the cultivation of restraint (*śīla*) and the cultivation of wholesome conduct.
Within the specific explanation, killing comes first, followed by stealing and sexual misconduct; in the subsequent text, it first speaks of the cultivation of restraint regarding killing.

Nurturing with compassion, do not harm the lives of sentient beings. Whether moving in water, on land, or through the air—all conscious creatures, regardless of whether their lives are great or small—protect them with an equal mind.
Let no wriggling or flying creature be destroyed.

Regarding the karmic action of killing with respect to the body, both the wholesome practice of desiring to act and the wholesome practice of refraining from acting must first take compassion and nurturing as their foundation.
Next, they take the non-injury of living beings as their practice. "Aquatic, terrestrial, and aerial" clarifies the vastness of the places where living beings depend for their existence.
"All sentient beings" refers to the multitude of living beings who are the subjects that depend [upon those places]. Life is not [limited by] size.
"Small. This refers to the equal mind of loving protection; it signifies the thought of safeguarding living beings.
To ensure that no creature, whether wriggling or flying, is ever harmed is the greatest of all virtues.
For those caught in the flow of peril and distress, one diligently rescues them and employs skillful means to deliver them, causing all to attain liberation.
This clarifies the practice of goodness: it means not only refraining from killing, but also being able to release living beings.
Regarding those in peril and distress, the scope of those rescued is vast; as for all forms of life, whether human or animal, if they are in danger, there are none who are not [rescued].
He diligently rescues them and employs skillful means to deliver them, causing all to attain liberation. This involves two intentions:
first, liberation through the cause, which is to redeem their physical lives and release them to roam in freedom;

second, liberation through the fruit, which is to chant the names of the Buddhas and take refuge in the teaching of the Dharma, thereby planting the seeds of the "cause of realization" so that, at the end of life, they are reborn in heaven and obtain flowers.
This is the joy of retribution: receiving a prediction of future enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and obtaining the cause for attaining Buddhahood.

Although the aspirations of those who practice the Way may be vast and universal, their strength has its limits; therefore, one should act according to one’s capacity. To fulfill this completely is the highest standard.
If it were otherwise, it would be better to let previous karma suffer a deficiency than to fail in one's subsequent duties. For who among the living does not die? To merely redeem one's life in vain—
One merely escapes from this single lifetime; yet death has its causes. For by hearing [the Dharma], one ultimately transcends eternal death.
Regarding the wealth and property of others, one does not take what is not given—even down to a single needle or a blade of grass belonging to spirits or deities—one never takes it.
There is no intentional transgression.
Within this karma of stealing, one merely practices virtue: not taking what belongs to others when it is not given. Thus, the precept that is observed is broad;
even regarding a single needle or a blade of grass, one never intentionally transgresses. Thus, the objects restricted by the rule are strict. Ten.
In the recitation of the Vinaya, there are six kinds of thievery of mind: taking by means of harsh treatment; taking by means of a piteous appearance; taking with contemptuous behavior;

taking by manifesting an air of authority; taking under another’s name—claiming, "I am a virtuous friend"; taking by forceful confrontation—meaning to coerce others into submission through arrogance and abuse;
taking what has been entrusted—meaning to misappropriate what has been deposited with one in a state of confusion; and taking by lending out money.
Regarding those who criticize others’ livelihoods, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* lists four types: a deceitful mind, a crooked mind, a hateful mind, and a fearful mind.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* lists ten types: a darkened mind—meaning ignorance of cause and effect; a perverse mind—meaning failure to recognize correct principles;
a crooked and distorted mind—meaning sycophancy; and a fearful mind—meaning the dread of losing [one's gains]. Constantly...
Regarding the intent to steal another's property: since it is said that this intent is always present, it does not matter whether the amount is large or small; one certainly desires to steal.

One definitely takes possession of it. Whether by taking it through forceful means regardless of the other's consent, or by taking an entrusted object, or by taking it through intimidation—meaning to frighten them with words, such as speaking of the terrors of the hells to shake them—and thereby seizing their wealth, or by taking it upon merely seeing it. This refers to:
One observes for an opportune moment to take it by theft. "Taking through reliance" means to borrow or exploit power and influence.
According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, there are three types: taking by force, taking through gentle speech, and taking back what was given; all constitute violations of the precept against stealing.
To a poor beggar, one gives with a respectful heart according to what one possesses, bringing them peace and security without seeking any reward for their kindness.
This is the practice of virtue within the context of the karma of stealing; that is to say, not only refraining from theft, but further being able to practice generosity.

However, while the act of giving performed in both the mundane and supramundane realms is the same, the mental state employed differs. Regarding the poor beggar, one gives according to what one has...

To give to such a person is to bring them peace and security; thus, by means of that field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*), one fulfills the mind of great compassion (*mahā-karuṇā*) that uproots suffering and the mind of great loving-kindness (*mahā-maitrī*) that bestows happiness.
One who gives with a reverent heart is able to regard that field of compassion as equal to the field of reverence (*guru-kṣetra*).
Furthermore, by not seeking gratitude or recompense, the mind has no fixed abode and does not cling to the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*). This...
This is what constitutes the supramundane gift. He reflects thus:
"The Buddhas of the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, practiced the giving of *dāna*, bestowing elephants, horses, and the seven treasures."
From my head, eyes, marrow, and brain, even unto my very body and life, I shall give them away without stinginess. I am now likewise;
whatever I may have to bestow, I shall joyfully offer it with a heart free from any sense of attachment or regret.

Shibei said: "To emulate the supreme sages, one must remain steadfast for a long time. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The foolish practitioner may practice for but a short time, yet they have been idle and doubtful for a long duration;
whereas for the holy scriptures, practicing with diligent hardship for immeasurable kalpas is but a mere moment."
Regarding the forms of women, his mind is free from defiled attachment.
Within the context of sexual karma, this first clarifies the goodness of restraint (*saṃvara-kuśala*). Regarding the forms of women, it first points to the objects of desire;
"the mind is free from defiled attachment" is an admonition not to give rise to greed.

Ordinary worldlings are inverted; intoxicated by desire, they are addicted, deluded, and confused, unaware of their own transgressions—like one who grasps the stem of a flower without realizing it is a venomous snake.
This says that fools are deluded by desire, and because of it, they give rise to transgressions.
Those who are inverted perceive the impure as pure, like mistaking a head for a tail. Those intoxicated by desire take form (*rūpa*) for wine;
drinking it, they do not realize their intoxication. Thus, the foolish people of the world add desire upon desire, becoming addicted and lost in confusion.
They are in disorder and do not recognize their transgression; it is like being intoxicated and then adding more wine, becoming dazed and delirious, unaware of what is wrong.

It is like grasping the stem of a flower without realizing that a venomous snake is coiled around it—this is a metaphor for those who are addicted to sensual pleasures and disregard the evil realms. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"It is like the stem of a beautiful flower with a venomous snake coiled around it. For example, there is a person whose nature loves the color of the flower, yet they do not see [the snake]."
Regarding the dangers of poisonous snakes on flower stalks,
the wise man observes that even the mouth of a venomous snake, the paws of a bear or leopard, or fierce fire and glowing iron cannot serve as adequate metaphors for them.
Upon copper pillars and iron beds, their backs are scorched and their entrails are seared; flesh and blood are crushed and disintegrated, with pain penetrating to the heart and marrow.
Contemplating in this way, one sees only suffering and no joy.
Previously, the characteristics of the fool were clarified; now, the contemplation of the wise is explained.
One regards the mouth of a woman as the mouth of a venomous snake that stings a person; one regards the hand of a woman as the paw of a bear or leopard that endangers life;
and one regards the body of a woman as a fierce fire or glowing iron that burns a person when embraced. Furthermore,
By means of a woman’s body, the sensations of cold, warmth, and smoothness become copper pillars and iron beds that burn, scorch, and dissolve her very form.
Why is this? As for the cause, it can ruin a state, destroy a family, bring about the loss of one's body and life, and lead to ailments such as emaciation and chronic exhaustion.
As for the result, it becomes the burning of copper pillars and iron beds in hell.
Regarding the retribution of burning the body and so forth: one who is able to contemplate in this way will see only suffering and no pleasure.

It is like a leather bag filled with excrement, a mass of pus and blood; externally it is falsely adorned with fragrant ointments, but internally it is nothing but foul stench, with impurities overflowing.
It is not even comparable to the dwelling places of maggots and grubs, nor to the stench of a fish market or the holes of a latrine.
The former was merely a provisional contemplation; this is now a direct, actual contemplation. "A leather bag filled with filth" refers to everything contained within the intestines and stomach;
"a congealing mass of pus and blood" refers to everything contained within that leather bag. Even if one were to apply external perfumes and ointments as a support...
It conceals shame. Within, it is foul and filthy; it is filled with impurity and evil. Impure fluids overflow, becoming more exposed as they are more concealed.
It is the dwelling place of maggots and worms, sharing its residence with such creatures. Even the stench of a rotting fish market or a latrine hole cannot compare to it.
The impurity of the human body is described in extreme terms; even the stalls where dried fish are sold or the holes of latrines cannot be compared to it.

Once, a person who had attained the first fruit of the path (srotāpanna) forgot his realization during an interval between lives, and his lust became so intense that his wife could no longer endure it.
Her family regularly made offerings to a holy monk, so the wife went to him and told him of her suffering. The monk instructed her, saying: "When he desires you..."
He addressed her, saying, "Is this how a person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna (*srotāpanna*) should act? The wife explained it according to the Way.

Thereupon, the man recognized his past lives; a sense of revulsion toward desire arose within him, and he forever severed his attachment to female beauty. Seeing that her husband had long since ceased his pursuit of her, the wife desired to regain his affection.
Her husband took a painted jar, filled it with excrement, sealed its mouth tightly, and commanded his wife to treasure and protect it.
He said to her, "If you can hold this without losing it, I shall give it back to you as before.
The wife joyfully took it, but after a short while, she lost her grip and it fell, spilling foul filth. The husband asked his wife, "Did you not love this jar in the past?"
He replied, "I truly loved it. [The man asked,] "Can you still love it now? He replied, "In the past I did not know it; therefore, I cherished and loved it.
Now that I have seen it, I no longer love it. The man said, "In the past, before I had attained awakening, my affection for you was ever more profound.
Now that I have attained awakening, I no longer love you."

The wise person contemplates it and sees only hair, body hair, nails, and teeth; thin skin and thick skin; blood, flesh, sweat, and tears; mucus, saliva, pus, and fat; tendons, veins, the brain, and the meninges;
yellow phlegm and white phlegm; liver, gallbladder, marrow, and bones; lungs, spleen, kidneys, and stomach; heart, adipose tissue, bladder, and urethra;
large intestine and small intestine; the raw viscera and the cooked viscera; excrement, urine, and the foul-smelling place. Each of these things—[he sees them] one by one.
It is not a person.
That which causes humans to be greedy is their grasping at the existence of a self and others.

Now, from the crown of this body down to the heels, if one observes all that exists within it, it does not exceed thirty-six things; their solid and obstructive nature returns to earth, and their moisture...
Moisture returns to water; warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind. At the beginning, these are gathered together to form the body;
at the end, they disperse and return to their source. If one seeks them in the interim, not a single part is "self. Now, regarding this delusory body, which among its parts could be said to be it?
Observing it in this way, ultimately there is no body. Since there is no body, it is merely a provisional name.
Human beings are equal to illusions; both men and women are illusory, and both subject and object are empty. Where, then, can there ultimately be lust or a lustful person?
Why, then, do you construct evil karma within the void and bring about the suffering of the three miserable realms?

Stirred by the winds of consciousness, false speech arises; one feigns friendship while being in truth envious and hostile. This ruins virtue and obstructs the Path, constituting a most grave transgression;
one should distance oneself from it as one would avoid an enemy or a thief.
This explains the doubts of certain individuals regarding the preceding passage. Those who doubt say:
"If this body is empty and void, and if there is no person within it, how can it speak and engage in mutual intimacy? Therefore, he explains it thus:

"The ability to speak is nothing more than the initial entrustment of a single thought of consciousness, wherein illusory conditioned breaths accumulate; this consciousness [unites] with the father..."
The mother’s own retribution-wind resides below the navel wheel, like a furnace bellows.
This consciousness-wind is struck by it to produce speech through the throat, tongue, gums, and palate; it is not the throat, tongue, gums, and palate alone that can produce speech.
If it were merely the throat, tongue, gums, and palate that could produce speech, then since the tongues of those who have died still remain, why do they not speak?
As for those who appear to be close friends, their intimacy does not go beyond the four great elements; they feign friendship while in reality harboring enmity and jealousy toward me.
It is like someone who forms a close bond with an enemy; though he does not immediately carry out the act of killing, [the danger remains].
It is only because the body incites one to commit various unwholesome deeds that it causes the ruin of virtue and obstructs the Path, acting as the primary culprit and the cause of death.

The same applies to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Though they coexist for a hundred years, feigning friendship, there is no act of lust, killing, theft, or falsehood that does not arise from them;
their transgressions are most grave. Therefore, the wise should distance themselves from them as they would avoid an enemy or a thief.
Therefore, the wise observe them as being like venomous snakes. It would be better to approach a venomous snake than to become intimate with female beauty. Why is this?

A venomous snake kills a person, resulting in death once; but female beauty binds one for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, with various forms of torment and suffering that are inexhaustible.
Upon careful examination and deep reflection, it is difficult to draw near to her.

Previously, because of female form, one clearly understood that the human body is impure, characterized by suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and the deluded attachment to a self—all of which constitute faults.
Now, having identified the faults of the human body, they are specifically traced back to female form.
One should observe this with wisdom: it is like a venomous snake and must not be approached.
Therefore, the wise person thoroughly examines these three faults, reforms the past and cultivates the future, turns away from evil and follows goodness, refrains from killing and stealing,
releases living beings and practices generosity, does not engage in sexual misconduct, and constantly cultivates pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Previously, the two virtues of cessation (*śamatha*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) were explained separately according to the three types of action (*trikarma*).

Now, they are explained collectively. The essential point is to constantly and earnestly examine these three faults: to reform what is evil and to practice what is good. This also refers generally to the two virtues of cessation and cultivation. Within the specific explanation:
abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitutes the virtue of cessation; releasing living beings and practicing giving constitutes the virtue of cultivation.
"Brahmacarya" means practicing goodness. However, there are cases where one practices goodness by merely abstaining from it; as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Not drinking alcohol or eating meat, yet giving alcohol and meat [to others]; not wearing flowers or perfumes, yet giving flowers and perfumes—such is the practice of giving."
Without spending a single word’s worth of wealth, one earns the title of a "Great Donor" (Mahādānapati).
This is because the Buddha, seeing that people of the world are able to practice giving but unable to maintain the precepts, praised the precepts while perfecting the great gift.

This was intended to make people understand the excellence of giving—that nothing is greater than the precepts—but it does not mean that one should maintain the precepts while dispensing with the practice of giving.
Day and night, they were diligent and tireless, practicing the Way and performing prostrations, taking refuge in and relying upon the Triple Gem, and aspiring for liberation.
Regarding their bodies, lives, and wealth, they cultivated the three steadfast dharmas.

The above has clarified the two virtues of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). These are still merely the virtuous precepts of humans and devas—unstable dharmas that are insufficient to serve as the cause for transcending the world.
One must necessarily be diligent day and night, aspiring to seek liberation, regarding one's body, life, and wealth [as impermanent].
One should cultivate the three dharmas of firmness. This requires relying upon the four types of samādhi through śamatha and vipaśyanā and fully practicing the ten great sovereign vows;

only then will one accord with this dharma. The three dharmas of firmness are set forth in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (Original Text Sutra). First is the non-firmness of wealth: one should trade non-firm wealth for firm wealth.
That is to say, all worldly material goods are by nature not solid; their accumulation and dispersal are impermanent and cannot be relied upon.

Kubo. If one can take these and practice giving to those who lead the pure Brahma-faring life—whether seeking the unsurpassed peace and bliss of Nirvana, or seeking the fruits of happiness among humans and devas in the future—then this becomes a firm wealth that shall never perish for all time.
This [previous wealth] is unstable wealth; it is used to trade for firm wealth. Second, the unstable body is traded...
It is easy to make the body firm. This refers to the body born of one's parents, which is a provisional combination of the four great elements.
It is precarious, fragile, and insubstantial; its nature is not solid. Subject to arising and ceasing, it is impermanent and cannot endure for long.
If one can maintain the five precepts, remaining pure and untainted, and cultivate the unsurpassed path to Bodhi, one will thereby realize the indestructible Vajra-body.
This body is the exchange of a non-firm body for a firm body. The four great elements are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
The five precepts are: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, and not speaking falsely.
Do not drink alcohol. Third, do not trade that which is impermanent for that which is permanent. This refers to the life-span received by persons:
though longevity and early death differ, all are alike in being like dreams and illusions; their substance is not solid, they are suddenly impermanent, and cannot be preserved for long.
If one can thoroughly understand the Four Noble Truths and practice the True Dharma, one will transcend birth and death and continue in the eternal state.
This imperishable life of wisdom is the exchange of a non-substantial life for a substantial life.
Knowing that the body is illusory and lacks intrinsic nature, and that form is itself emptiness—who is there that could be called "I"? Thus it is with all phenomena.

There is only a provisional name; there is no fixed reality that can be identified as "this is my body. Among the four great elements and the five aggregates, not a single one is the self, nor does their combination constitute it.
When sought internally and externally, it is like a mass of foam, a floating bubble, a mirage, a plantain tree, or a magical illusion.
Like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water, they are ultimately devoid of any person. Yet, through ignorance and lack of realization, one falsely clings to them as a self.

Amidst what is unreal, one recklessly gives rise to craving and attachment, committing acts of killing, stealing, and debauchery in wild confusion. From night until dawn, one labors incessantly to create karma.

Although it is not ultimately real, the retribution for good and evil follows one like a shadow follows a form. When contemplating in this way, one does not seek sustenance for the body and life through unwholesome means.
This Great Master exhorts practitioners that they must not sustain their physical lives through evil means. Why is this?
It is because worldly people fail to realize that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are empty; they regard body and life as truly existent.
For this reason, they seek and crave excessively to sustain their bodies and lives, unaware that the body is not truly existent and that life cannot be prolonged. How [could they otherwise know]?
With this illusory human body, one commits truly real sins that lead to hell; with this fleeting life in Jambudvīpa, one bequeaths the long-lasting causes for rebirth in the evil realms;
and with the fleeting pleasures of the five desires, one is afflicted by the suffering of the body and mind being broken and crushed.
The text contains both the Dharma and parables, and the conclusion contains a reprimand; these can be understood through careful examination.
One should observe one's own body as being like a venomous snake. For the sake of treating the illness, one accepts the four requisites: wearing clothing upon the body is like bandaging an ulcer;
consuming flavors with the mouth is like a patient taking medicine. One should exercise restraint over the body and moderation in speech, so that luxury and extravagance do not arise.
Hearing it said that one should have few desires, one deeply delights in the practice of cultivation.
This passage and those that follow are exhortations for the practitioner to accept the four requisites for the purpose of treating illness.
Indeed, the human body is a great sore upon the *dharmakāya* and the life-force of wisdom. This bodily sore fears cold and is unsightly; thus, clothing is required.
If one does not treat it with medicine, an oral ulcer will not be cured by merely fearing hunger or famine; nor will it be cured by medicine that is not for food and drink.
Therefore, it is said: "The body wearing clothes is like wrapping an abscess. Since medicine is prescribed because of illness, one should not cling to the medicine and thereby incur further illness.

One should regulate the body and be frugal with the mouth, having few desires and knowing contentment, rather than giving rise to luxury and extravagance, and should take deep delight in [simplicity].
Regarding practice, a sutra states: "One who possesses few desires and practices *dhūta*, and who well understands contentment, is able to enter the path of the noble ones (*ārya*).
The intent of this cited passage is that if one wishes to cultivate the practice of few desires and contentment, one must honor the *dhūta* ascetic practices to shake off [defilements].
This teaching is fully detailed in the *Dvādaśadhūta-sūtra*.

Since one relies upon the practices of dwelling in an araṇya, at the foot of a tree, in a cemetery, in the open air, and remaining seated without lying down, one is able to cultivate contentment regarding one's dwelling place and bedding.
Since one relies upon the practices of begging for food regularly, eating in a single sitting, and begging in sequential order, one is able to cultivate contentment regarding food and drink.
Since one possesses only the three robes and rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*) and does not store any extra clothing, one is able to practice contentment regarding garments.
Since one relies on medicinal decoctions from decayed matter to treat illness, one is able to practice contentment regarding medicine.
This constitutes the gateway to the path for a bhikṣu, and is the hallmark of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles.
Why is this? Beings in the evil realms pass through immeasurable kalpas lacking clothing and food, crying out in agony, tormented by hunger and cold until skin and bone are joined together.
Compared to that, my current temporary lack is not even sufficient to be considered suffering.
An ancient worthy said: "For one who has left the household life, three things are always insufficient: clothing, food, and sleep.

It is precisely through this insufficiency of these three that one truly attains fulfillment for the sake of the Way. If one gives rise to much negligence because these are satisfied, one will remain negligent throughout life;
yet there are also practitioners of the Way who, having already undertaken the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) and austerities, certainly do not [neglect] these three constant needs."
This is sufficient. When a person is in a state of insufficiency, they should contemplate the suffering of the evil realms; though lacking, they should always maintain contentment.
Therefore, the wise value the Dharma and despise the body, diligently seeking the ultimate Way without regard for their physical form or life. This is called pure cultivation.
Regarding physical action:
the fool necessarily prizes the body and despises the Dharma; thus, he places the body first and the Way last, looking only to his physical form and life.
The wise person necessarily prizes the Dharma and despises the body; thus, he places the body last and the Way first, seeking only the Great Way.
The gap between the ignorant and the wise is such as this. Whether one follows the Way or not is likewise determined by this. How does one purify the karma of speech?
One should reflect deeply upon the four faults of the mouth: they are the root of birth and death, they increase all manner of evils, and they overturn the myriad practices.
Because people alternately engage in mutual criticism and contention, the wise who wish to uproot these faults must sever them at their source.
It is false. One should cultivate the four kinds of truthful speech: upright, gentle, harmonious, and according to reality. These four forms of speech are practiced by the wise.
In all cases of purifying the karma of speech, one should reflect for oneself: regarding the words that issue from the mouth, there are both faults and merits.
As for faults, these are the four evil karmas of speech: namely, frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*), and false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
These four types of speech can alternately affirm or deny others, increasing faults and evils, overturning the myriad practices, and forming the root of birth and death; this constitutes a fault.
Furthermore, foolish people nourish its roots with the four evils; therefore, the foundation of birth and death increases day by day.
Wise people uproot its source with the four realities; therefore, the nature of nirvana grows day by day.
Why is this? Those who speak with straightforwardness are able to eliminate frivolous speech; those who speak with gentleness are able to eliminate harsh speech;
those who speak with conciliatory words are able to eliminate divisive speech; and those who speak according to reality are able to eliminate false speech.
Once the practitioner has understood that the merits and faults of verbal karma differ according to what is right or wrong, they must further understand how these functions eliminate transgressions.

Just as medicine can cure a disease only when it is diametrically opposed to the illness, so it is with verbal karma: uprightness is the opposite of frivolous speech because it is free from deviousness;
gentleness is the opposite of harsh speech because it is free from coarseness; and harmony is the opposite of... [text truncated]
Divisive speech is the opposite [of its counterpart], for it lacks the quality of not inciting strife. False speech is the opposite of truthful speech, for it lacks sincerity.
Furthermore, these four modes of speech necessarily proceed in mutual dependence. Why is this? For if one possesses straightforwardness but lacks the other three, one errs toward rigidity;
if one possesses gentleness but lacks the other three, one errs toward sycophancy; and if one possesses conciliation but lacks the other three, one errs toward...
If, as you say, there were truly no three [vehicles], one would fall into the error of the crude and uncultivated.
It is precisely because one should take the One as the host and the three as the guests, with both host and guests acting in concert, that it is both good and beautiful.
There are two aspects to right speech (*samyag-vāc*). First is speaking in accordance with the Dharma. This instructs those who hear it so that they may attain clear understanding and faith.

"In accordance with the Dharma" means relying on phenomena as they inherently exist. By clearly discerning the specific characteristics of these phenomena, one enables those who hear it to attain clear understanding and faith.
Second is the discourse that accords with principle, which causes all who hear it to eliminate doubt and dispel delusion.

"Principle" refers to the text and its nature. By analyzing according to the text and speaking in accordance with its nature, one is able to cause people to sever doubts regarding the provisional and give rise to faith in the real.
Gentle speech is also of two kinds. The first is consoling speech, which causes those who hear it to feel joy and draw near.
The reason people distance themselves from others and do not wish to associate with them is that those others speak with hostility and reject them.
Now, because one offers consolation, one is able to cause people to feel joy and draw near.
Second, the tones and melodies are refined and elegant, causing all who hear them to delight in and practice them.

"Gong" and "Shang" represent two of the five musical notes. If a person’s speech accords with these five notes and their phrasing and eloquence are likewise refined and elegant, who among those who hear it would not delight in and practice it?
Furthermore, among the four types of speech, there is that which is [effortful yet] acceptable...
Among those who study, there are those who strive in their studies yet fail to achieve mastery; this is because the harmonization of *gong* and *shang* tones is difficult to perfect.
This is due to the fact that people come from the North or South, their voices are clear or dull, their speech is eloquent or stammering, and their breath is fluent or obstructed.

To seek such a person among a thousand is as rare as finding one in ten thousand; I cannot encounter them morning or evening. Alas! Regarding those who skillfully expound the Dharma, as for their voice—
The way of sound is indeed difficult! There are two types of harmonious speech:

first, reconciling those who are in conflict; seeing people engaged in strife, one offers counsel and exhortation to make them desist from it, refrains from self-praise, and remains humble and respectful toward others.
To see people engaged in strife and to exhort them to desist, speaking words that firmly bring about reconciliation— furthermore,
not seeking merit or claiming one's own virtues while refraining from self-praise, and being concurrently humble and respectful toward all things— this is the ultimate harmony of harmonies.

Second is the harmony of principle: seeing those who have regressed from the bodhicitta, one earnestly exhorts them; one is skillfully able to discern that bodhi and afflictions are of one identical mark in their equality.
Regarding those who regress from the bodhicitta: because it is mutually antagonistic with the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are like water and fire placed in the same vessel.
Consequently, the water of bodhi is unable to extinguish the fire of afflictions;
instead, it is boiled away by the fire of afflictions. Since the afflictions prevail, the bodhicitta therefore regresses. This is because... [the other...]
Hitherto, we have not heard the teaching that afflictions are themselves bodhi—the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden.

Now, one is able skillfully to discern that bodhi and afflictions are of one identical mark in their equality; when these marks are brought into harmony as a single entity, they are in accord without contention.
Those who speak according to reality are also of two kinds. First, those whose words accord with facts: if something exists, they say it exists; if it does not exist, they say it does not exist;
if it is so, they say it is so; if it is not so, they say it is not so.

That existence and non-existence do not exceed his words is surely the true speech of a man of the Way; that right and wrong are never absent from his mouth is surely the candid speech of one who has left the household life.
This must pertain to a discourse on the principles of things, merely not overstepping the bounds of right and wrong.
Second, regarding the ultimate truth: all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is eternally abiding and unchanging.
This "language of ultimate truth" is spoken in accordance with the nature of reality:

that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and are no different from the Buddha, such that birth is itself non-birth; and that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is eternally abiding and unchanging, no different from birth.
Thus, the source of cessation does not cease.
For this reason, the wise practice the four truthful words and contemplate those sentient beings who, throughout kalpas past, have been subject to these four transgressions.
Thus they fall into perversion, sinking into the cycle of birth and death, from which it is difficult to escape.
A wise person who wishes to transform their goodness through pure cultivation must contemplate evil and recognize their transgressions.
Sentient beings sink into suffering due to the four perversions; I shall follow the four right paths to achieve liberation.

I now wish to uproot its source. Observing that vocal karma—the lips, tongue, teeth, throat, and resonance from the navel—I see that consciousness and wind strike together, and sound issues forth from within them.
To stem its flow, one must uproot its source. To uproot the source, one must trace the current upstream to find it;
once the source is found, it can be uprooted, and the flow may be stemmed. As for this "flow," it refers to the four types of unwholesome speech.
Speech relies upon sound, and sound, in turn, arises from the lips, tongue, teeth, and so forth. Tracing outwardly from these back to the navel, one reaches the out-breath at the navel.
Wind. Thus, when it strikes upward, it forms sound and issues forth as speech. Furthermore, the breath is governed by consciousness;
therefore, it is said that "consciousness stirs the wind. Consequently, if one wishes to still the sound, one must still the breath; if one wishes to still the breath, one must still the mind.
This does not mean that one should remain entirely silent, but rather that the mind, as the sovereign, maintains rectitude to preside over [the senses].
It is so commanded.
Due to the causes and conditions of the mind, there is a distinction between the false and the real. The real brings benefit; the false leads to diminution.

The real is the root from which goodness arises; the false is the basis from which evil is born. The roots of good and evil are expressed through the medium of speech. As for words that express goodness—
Those termed the "Four Right [Efforts]" are words that define evil; those termed the "Four Wrong [Efforts]" lead to suffering, while the right lead to happiness.
Goodness is the condition that assists the Path, whereas evil is the root that ruins virtue.

The Emperor commanded that one trace the source by going upstream; having already grasped their minds, if he wishes to uproot [their afflictions], he must first know their merits and faults, correcting them where necessary and following them where appropriate.

By abandoning the four perversions and returning to the four rectitudes, it is not merely a matter of generating goodness and attaining happiness, but can also serve as assistance on the Path toward the realization of Truth.

Therefore, the wise person must support the mind with correctness and establish themselves in truthful speech. They recite the sutras, mindfulness of the Buddha, and contemplate the true nature (*dharmatā*) of speech.
With no attachment remaining in their words, they regard speech and silence as equal; this is called the cultivation of verbal karma.
Previously, the cessation of evil through verbal karma was clarified; now, furthermore, the cultivation of goodness through verbal karma is also clarified.
By advancing in both cessation and cultivation, one is able to extinguish evil and give rise to goodness. Moreover, one must contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of speech:

it is neither existent nor non-existent; speech and silence are equal; there is neither excess nor deficiency. One should not cause loss by speaking excessively, nor should one practice the "dumb method" [of total silence].
To avoid inciting reproach is what is called purity of verbal karma.

How does one purify the cultivation of mental karma? One should deeply reflect that the source of both good and evil arises entirely from the mind. Through the conditions of false thoughts, all manner of evils can be produced;
through the conditions of right contemplation, all manner of virtues can be produced.
Regarding the causes and conditions of the three types of karma, the mind is the root. If the mind harbors a thought, body and speech follow it accordingly.
Furthermore, one who seeks to properly regulate these three types of karma must first be cautious regarding the karma of the mind, taking it as the foundation.
Therefore, a sutra states: "In the three realms there is no separate dharma; it is created solely by this one mind. One should know that the mind is the root of all dharmas.
In the cited proof, it is first stated that the mind creates all dharmas, but it has not yet been said that all dharmas are solely the mind.

What is wrong mindfulness? It is the failure to understand due to ignorance, the false grasping at a self, the firm adherence to the view of a self, and the arbitrary conceptualization of all things through greed, hatred, and wrong views, thereby giving rise to various defiled attachments.

All manner of erroneous thoughts do not fail to originate from ignorance (*avidyā*). Failing to understand that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are without self and that all phenomena (*dharma*) are fundamentally empty, one consequently clings tenaciously to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Human beings stand in opposition to one another, recklessly calculating and becoming defiled through attachment due to greed, hatred, and false views.
This is what is meant in the *Awakening of Faith*: "From the non-awakening of ignorance, the three subtle states arise; with objective realms as conditions, the six coarse states develop.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because of the existence of 'self,' there arises 'what belongs to self'; thus, the sixty-two views of annihilationism and eternalism are produced."

"Self" (*ātman*) refers to the divine self as conceived by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). "What belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which are the locus upon which that divine self depends.
At times, they may conceive of form (*rūpa*) as being the self; or that the self is distinct from form;

or that the self is large while form is small, with form abiding within the self; or that form is large while the self is small, with the self abiding within form. These four [conceptions] apply to each of the [five] aggregates.
The other four [views] are likewise; thus they total twenty. When distributed across the past, present, and future, they total sixty.
Adding the fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, there are sixty-two.
The views and afflictions continue in succession; the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) cause the cycle of birth and death within the three realms to revolve without ceasing.
The sixty-two views mentioned above are produced only by non-Buddhists who have attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Now, as for the eighty-eight latent tendencies of the view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), when combined with the ten latent tendencies of the thought-delusions (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), these are shared in common by ordinary worldlings and all non-Buddhists alike.
One should know that wrong thought is the root of all evils; therefore, the wise restrain it and do not follow it.
Since beginningless time, there has been no sentient being who does not possess wrong thoughts. The foolish follow them and do not restrain them, and thus they become deluded.
The wise restrain them and do not follow them, and thus they achieve wisdom.
What is correct contemplation? It is that self and other are without distinction, and form and mind are not two.

Regarding the method of correct contemplation: first, one realizes that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only. If they are mind-only, then others and oneself are of one essence; who then is "that" and who is "this"?
If they are consciousness-only, then the environment and its inhabitants are not two; what then is "form" and what is "mind"?

When "who" refers to that and "who" refers to this, the discrimination between self and other is forgotten. When there is neither form nor mind, the subject-object duality of form and mind is severed.
Enemies and kin are equalized, merging into the source of the Dharma-realm; object and wisdom are perfectly interfused, becoming quiescent within the ocean of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
With internal delusions no longer arising and external objects entirely relinquished, what further cycle of afflictions and karma could there be?
How could there be any turning away from this?
Awakening and affliction are fundamentally no different in their nature; birth-and-death and nirvana are equally illuminated as one.
Birth-and-death is itself nirvana; affliction is itself awakening. This is originally from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, upon which Tiantai established the Perfect [Teaching].
The fundamental principle of the Sudden Teaching (Dunzong) relies upon this; even the Great Master’s awakening and entry from the celestial palace were attained through this.
As stated above, self and other are without distinction, and form and mind are not two; were it not for this, the essential meaning would have nowhere to return.

Therefore, if one can realize that these two are fundamentally no different in their original nature and perceive them with equal, singular illumination, then every thought will be free from dependence and every moment will be perfectly interfused.
Thus, more than half of the correct cultivation of the three contemplations has already been accomplished.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Detaching from 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' one contemplates equality. Both 'self' and nirvana are empty.
If one does not even slightly detach from 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' one cannot contemplate equality;
if one does not even slightly contemplate equality, one cannot detach from 'self' and 'what belongs to self. What is called "equality" means that both 'self' and nirvana are empty.
One should know that all phenomena exist merely as names; thus a sutra says: "Even nirvana exists merely as a name.
It further says: "The nature of written characters is detached, and names are also empty."
All phenomena exist merely as names; thus, names have no substantial reality. Since names have no substantial reality, their essence has no substantial reality.
In this way, afflictions are not afflictions, and awakening is not awakening; birth-and-death and nirvana are likewise so.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* asks: "Who possesses afflictions such that one could say that vipaśyanā can destroy them?"
[It is] affliction (*kleśa*). Now then, who possesses bodhi such that one could say that affliction can obstruct bodhi?
Since the two natures of bodhi and affliction are both empty, all phenomena (*dharma*) and nirvāṇa exist only as names. Furthermore, the nature of words is transcended.
Thus, names are also empty; both name and reality are empty. Therefore, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are equal. Why is this? Phenomena do not name themselves;
it is through provisional names that phenomena are expressed. Since phenomena are not [inherently] phenomena, names are also not [inherently] names.
Names do not correspond to phenomena, and phenomena do not correspond to names. Since names and phenomena have no correspondence, all things are empty and quiescent.
Dharma Master Zhaol said: "The name has no power to summon the essence; the essence has no reality to correspond to the name.

Since there is neither name nor reality, where can name and reality abide? Indeed, all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds are merely names provisionally established through the deluded conceptualizations of sentient beings;
they then cling to them as being real. Consequently, by following names to seek appearances, they chase after shadows while forgetting the substance."
As for form: since one realizes that phenomena are not phenomena and names are not names, both are equally without application; they are fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Thus, a sutra says: "Phenomena have no names, for language is cut off."
Provisional names cannot express ultimate reality, because the provisional and the real are not the same.

Therefore, sublime marks transcend names, and true names are beyond characters. Why is this? Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is quiescent and extinction; it is supremely subtle and wondrous, transcending characteristics and departing from names.
The paths of mind and speech are cut off. One should know that correct contemplation is the essential means for tracing back to the source.
The wondrous marks merely transcend names; it is not that the true essence is non-existent. The true name merely transcends characters; it is not that the true name is non-existent.
This is because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is quiescent and extinguished, reaching the ultimate subtlety and mystery; therefore, it transcends marks and is detached from names.
It is that which names cannot name, where the paths of mind and speech are cut off, and which thought cannot reach. Only by observing correctly in this manner can one trace back to the source.
Therefore, when the wise correctly contemplate causes and conditions, the myriad delusions are all dispelled; object and wisdom are both forgotten, and the source of the mind becomes pure.
This is called the pure cultivation of the mental faculty.
"Conditions" (pratyaya) refers to the objective realm that is observed; this is precisely what was explained above: the form and mind of self and other, as well as enlightenment and affliction.
"Correct observation" (samyag-darśana) refers to the principle that performs the observation;

it is the wisdom that can integrate phenomena so as to return to the principle—namely, the non-dual state of equality where both name and reality are simultaneously forgotten, as explained above. To be able to observe in this manner [is correct observation].
The myriad delusions are dispelled of themselves without being cast aside; object and wisdom are forgotten of themselves without being intentionally let go.
When delusions are dispelled and contemplation is forgotten, the source of the mind becomes vividly clear and pure.
This is the sixth stage of the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles.
Now, the wondrous Way is profound and subtle; its principle transcends the realm of names and forms. The ultimate truth is empty and still; its measure exceeds all categories of number.
