Although the intent was originally to explain it clearly, one first speaks of "no-explanation" to establish the foundation. For indeed, "no-explanation" is the very principle of what is explained.
Some say it refers to the teaching that can express [the truth]. To be able to realize that there is no speaking does not preclude the existence of speaking.
Thus, one may speak fervently all day long while remaining silent, or remain profoundly still and soundless all day long while preaching the Dharma.
This is what is meant by "speaking in silence" and "silencing while speaking"; within this great gate of giving, there is no obstruction.

Yet, through his compassion that is without objective conditions, he responds to beings according to their capacities; through the principle of non-duality, he distinguishes teachings according to their faculties and natures.
Following things while forgetting self-concern, he bestows [benefits] without creating [karmic action]. Though he teaches and explains all day long, it is no different from silence;
though he establishes many paths of instruction, they do not deviate from the single standard.
Shibei said: "Without haste yet swift; moved, it immediately penetrates. Thus, one is able to shine forth with primordial illumination, reflecting upon that which has not yet taken form.
The Tathāgata, riding upon the non-dual true mind, proclaims the manifold and diverse teachings.

That which remains consistent despite these divergences—surely this can only be the Sage! He further said: "In accordance with things and reflecting worldly customs, he forgets his own being to reflect the Truth. At last...
The daily acts of giving all ultimately return to the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Therefore, the Great Sage, out of compassion, benefits beings according to their capacities; he synthesizes their profound essence, so that the various scriptures do not differ in their ultimate aim.
Compassion benefiting all beings arises from the essence to manifest as function; it is that which, being originally without differentiation, manifests as differentiation.
The profound principle is not distinct [from the essence], for it is function that is simultaneously the essence; it is differentiation itself that is non-differentiation.
Those of middling and inferior capacity contemplate the truths and conditions to diminish their own [self-clinging]. Those of superior capacity ride upon the six perfections to achieve greatness.

The three vehicles cross the river by gradual stages; Tiantai classifies this within the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). If discussed in terms of time, it corresponds to the two stages of "unripe" and "ripe" butter.
If discussed in terms of the method of transformation, it belongs to the Gradual Teaching. If discussed in terms of the indeterminate, it is as the Tathāgata’s inconceivable [wisdom].
Regarding the power of deliberation: when a single sound is expounded, understanding is attained according to individual capacity.
From the perspective of the secret [teaching], the Tathāgata may preach the Four Truths to one person, or preach Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and so forth to another;

these do not mutually know one another. The present text precisely clarifies this indeterminacy; therefore it says that those of middle and lower capacities achieve their own [results] while those of high and superior capacities achieve the Great. How could this be...?
Is it not that the distinction between the superior, middling, and inferior vehicles lies in the capacity of the practitioner and not in the Buddha?

Because these various classes of beings are deluded and unable to understand by themselves, they may attain awakening and comprehension through the Buddha’s teaching; therefore, they are called *śrāvakas* (Hearers).
This clarifies the origin from which those of inferior wisdom derive their name. It means that they awaken to the Way upon hearing the sounds of the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, they are called Śrāvakas (Hearers).
Examining what they cultivate, the Four Noble Truths constitute their fundamental practice.

This clarifies the foundation upon which those of inferior wisdom practice. That is to say, they are able to know suffering, sever the origin [of suffering], aspire toward cessation, and cultivate the path.
They contemplate impermanence and give rise to fear; they reflect on emptiness and stillness to seek peace; they dread the saṃsāra of the six realms and loathe the three [poisons].
Regarding birth and death within the realms:
this clarifies the fundamental aspiration of those with inferior wisdom who are directed toward these states. Birth and death are indeed impermanent, yet the Bodhisattva dwells therein without fear.
Nirvana is indeed peaceful and secure, yet the Bodhisattva yearns for it but finds no leisure [to rest], because he possesses compassion.
This is because of their great resolve born of compassion. Therefore, they dwell with equanimity within the six realms of existence and the three worlds.
The śrāvakas, being the opposite, give rise to fear and dread of suffering therein; they seek pleasure and strive for security.

Seeing suffering, they constantly harbor a sense of weary detachment; severing the origin of suffering, they always fear its arising; realizing cessation, they alone accord with the unconditioned; and cultivating the path, they concern themselves solely with their own liberation.
This clarifies why those of inferior wisdom contemplate the Four Noble Truths and thereby become Śrāvakas. Indeed, this is the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths.
The four teachings are applicable in common; one must simply observe how their faculties and natures progress and what they understand.

The Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) also contemplates the Four Truths, yet why is it uniquely termed "unconditioned" (*wu zuo*)? It is because it can realize that birth-and-death is itself nirvana, and afflictions are themselves bodhi.
This is not the case for the śrāvakas. It is like empty space, which is fundamentally free of thorns; therefore...
Seeing suffering, one constantly harbors weary detachment to uproot it; seeing its origin, one always fears its arising to sever it.
Since even empty space is fundamentally unobtainable, one therefore aspires to cessation and uniquely accords with it;
one cultivates the Path and uniquely transcends it—this is why it is called "inferior wisdom. However, this refers only to the Tripiṭaka Teaching (Zàngjiào). As for the Shared Teaching (Tōngjiào):
The teaching is not like this, for it is able to explain that form is itself emptiness, rather than emptiness resulting from the extinction of form.

Because their great vow has not yet become universal, the Way of gathering and transforming beings is not yet practiced; because reverence according to the six harmonies is empty and void, the compassion toward the three realms is not yet exercised.

Consequently, the myriad practices are neglected and the fruit of perfect permanence is lacking; since the six perfections have not been cultivated, how can such a state be anything other than that of the Small Vehicle?
Such is the way of the śrāvaka. Their great vows are not universal;
this is spoken of with deliberate ease. If one were to challenge them with harsh words, it would simply be to point out that their vows are not universal.
Since their vows are not universal, how can they exercise the transformative power of gathering and converting others? This is what is meant by "leaping alone like a deer, without looking back."
The latter refers to the group of followers. Regarding the "Six Harmonies and Respects," the Shibi commentary states: first, harmony and respect in the common precepts;
second, harmony and respect in common views; third, harmony and respect in common conduct; fourth, harmony and respect through physical kindness; fifth, harmony and respect through verbal kindness;
and sixth, harmony and respect through mental kindness. I say: it is not that the Śrāvakas lack these six harmonies and respects; rather, they simply subsume them within emptiness.
Since their six harmonies are already empty and their compassion does not function, if a bodhisattva wishes to perfect the fruit of myriad virtues, they must follow the causes of myriad practices.
If the causal practices of a śrāvaka are at variance with this, how could the qualities of the fruit not be deficient?

With the six perfections left unpracticed in such a vast void, what category would they not belong to other than that of the Lesser Vehicle? For this reason, they are judged to have entered the Śrāvakayāna.

There are those who, without depending on the teachings of others, personally realize impermanence; because they encounter conditions that disperse [delusion] and realize the true nature, they are called *pratyekabuddhas*.
In the Sanskrit language, this is *pratyekabuddha*, which is translated here as "Solitary Realizer" (*dujue*) and also as "Conditionally Awakened" (*yuanjue*).

"Not depending on the teachings of others, personally realizing impermanence" refers to them solely as Solitary Realizers. "Encountering conditions that disperse [delusion] and realizing the true nature" refers to them as Conditionally Awakened.
If one traces the origin of what has been practiced, the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) constitute the fundamental practice.

These twelve links of dependent origination are of three kinds: those spanning the three periods of time, those of a single lifetime, and those of a single moment. Herein, we shall first discuss those of the three periods of time.
Contemplating ignorance, one finds it is immediately empty; realizing all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one sees they are without volitional action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Since these two causes are not its karma, how could the retribution of the five fruits be requited? With craving, grasping, and becoming free from blemish, what burden could even old age and death impose?

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and formative forces (*saṃskāra*): these two factors of the past are the causes. For those who follow the teachings common to the *pratyekabuddhas*, they are able to realize that afflictions are empty and that karmic bonds and activities are without action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*): these five factors of the present are the fruits. Since the causes are empty, how could the fruits be obtained?
Therefore it is said: "The two causes are not karma; what fruit could the five results repay? Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*)...
There is. The three links are present causes. Because there are these three present causal links, the two future links—the fruits of old age and death—are brought about.
Since craving and grasping are already free from defect, one is no longer burdened by old age and death.
This is the method for entering the Path by contemplating the mark of cessation within dependent origination.
Thus he was able to transcend freely and alone, dwelling in seclusion in a pure place. Observing the transformations of things, he realized their impermanence;

beholding the withering of autumn leaves, he entered the True Way. His four modes of conduct were composed and orderly as he restrained his mind and thoughts in tranquility. By nature fond of solitary habitation, he found contentment resting in quiet groves.

This clarifies the Pratyekabuddha. That is to say, dwelling alone on a solitary peak, delighting in solitary tranquility, observing the transformation of all things, and personally awakening to non-arising—just as the king saw falling flowers and awakened to the Way, or the bhikṣu heard the sound of bracelets and realized the Truth.

They do not delight in preaching the Dharma, but manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to transform others. They appear in worlds where no Buddha exists, acting as the final flame of the Buddha-lamp.

Bodhisattvas at the initial stage of resolve (*prathamacittotpādika*) are able to preach the Dharma but cannot yet manifest supernatural powers; Pratyekabuddhas and Solitary Realizers (*pratyekajina*), however, are able to manifest supernatural powers.
Yet they are unable to preach the Dharma; only a Buddha-to-Buddha possesses both qualities.

Nevertheless, among the various pratyekabuddhas and solitary realizers, there are those who manifest supernatural powers and those who do not, as well as those who preach the Dharma and those who do not;
thus, these too cannot be standardized as one.
The body dwells in sublime tranquility; the mind delights in pure emptiness. Lodging alone upon a solitary peak, one observes how all phenomena disperse and perish.

While benefiting others has not been universal and self-benefit remains incomplete, one excels those below yet falls short of those above. Being neither of these classes, one takes the Middle Vehicle as one’s station.
Such is the way of the Pratyekabuddha.

A Pratyekabuddha takes solitude as his sole principle, like a deer; yet he is also able to guide disciples and lead a community. However, his benefit to others is not universal, and his own self-benefit is not yet perfected.

This is explained here according to the Shared Teaching (Pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-śāsana): the Pratyekabuddha first subdues the active outflows (kleśas), while slightly subduing the residual habit-energies (vāsanā).
When a bodhisattva reaches the stage of fruition, both their correct practice and habitual tendencies are completely exhausted. Based on these two matters, three types of persons are established.
Now, this person excels those below but falls short of those above; situated between the "eldest" and the "middle," they are therefore called a *pratyekabuddha*.

If one’s faculties and nature are fundamentally luminous and their original merit was established in past lives, then though their learning may not be extensive, understanding arises spontaneously through prior knowledge.

This clarifies that those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle all do so by virtue of what they have grasped in previous existences; having accumulated merit and cultivated virtue over many lifetimes, this realization truly does not arise from the accumulation of studies, questions, or debates.
The mind has no object of focus, yet it is able to benefit sentient beings. Its compassion is supreme, and it is not constrained by views of attachment.
Shibi said: "To have compassion without wisdom gives rise to views of attachment; to have wisdom without compassion falls into the stage of the Two Vehicles."
Now, by employing the wisdom that forgets artifice to guide the compassion that has no fixed object, one is thus a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śikṣā*).

The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "If one transforms sentient beings without giving rise to the thought of transformation, nor giving rise to the thought of non-transformation, such transformation is truly great."
Throughout the day one saves sentient beings, yet does not perceive any sentient beings who can be saved.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "One delivers all sentient beings to nirvāṇa, yet in reality there are no sentient beings who attain deliverance."

This is what is meant by that. Oneness and difference share the same purport; delusion and awakening originate from the same source. Since both person and phenomena are empty, one is called a Bodhisattva.

Shibi said: "Oneness refers to the illumination of the True (the ultimate), while difference refers to the illumination of the Conventional (the phenomenal). Although the True and the Conventional differ, their wondrous purport is not distinct."

The resolution of delusions is likewise so. For one's own benefit, great wisdom is primary; having already realized the two kinds of emptiness, for the benefit of others, great compassion comes first.
Wandering long through the six realms of existence, compassion and wisdom are exercised together; therefore, one is called a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the basis of their cultivation: the six perfections constitute the direct cause.
Both the Śrāvaka-Piṭaka (Āgama) and the Shared (Sādhāraṇa) Bodhisattvas cultivate these six perfections; they should be distinguished by means of two types: the phenomenal and the principle.
Here, we specifically speak of cultivating the six perfections according to the principle.
In practicing giving, one exhausts one's life and squanders one's wealth;
thus, one gives all three—body, life, and wealth. Practicing *dāna* in this manner, one cultivates the three enduring dharmas.
In observing the precepts, one commits no transgressions, even regarding minor infractions (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding the seven groups of pure precepts (*śīla-skandha*), even the smallest—namely, a *duṣkṛta* offense—is not violated; how much more so the greater ones?
Furthermore, it should be said that regarding both natural gravity (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and censurable offenses (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*), there is no violation in either case.

Through patience, one deeply realizes the absence of self; what harm can there be in being cut or dismembered? One remains composed amidst praise and blame, unmoved by the eight winds. As the Sūtra says:
"In the past, when my limbs were severed joint by joint, if there had been any mark of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.
Shibi said: "It is precisely because these four marks are empty that compliance and opposition do not [disturb the mind]."
On the stage of the *bhūmi*, one forms conceptions in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, it is called "profound clarity.

As for the eight winds—gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and insult, suffering and pleasure—one exerts diligence in seeking the ultimate Way as if one's head were on fire. Whether acting for oneself or transforming others, there is not a single moment’s interval [of distraction].

In this interval, be refined so as not to be distracted, and advance so as not to retreat. With such non-distraction and non-retreat, seek the Great Way with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire, and with the grief of one who has lost both parents.
Practice the two benefits simultaneously; even for a single kṣaṇa, do not allow even the slightest [negligence].
In this way, one may be called truly diligent.

As for *dhyāna*, it is the tranquility of body and mind; the subtle and profound practice of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) provides self-sustenance through abiding in silent concentration, while the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) benefit all beings.
The method for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) requires one to harmonize the body, the breath, and the mind. Upon entry, one harmonizes the coarse until it becomes subtle;

upon emergence, one harmonizes the subtle to emerge from the coarse; while abiding, these three matters are harmonized equally. This refers to the hundreds of thousands of *samādhis* known as entry, emergence, and abiding.
In Sanskrit this is called *ānāpāna*; here it is translated as "sending forth and sending away," which is to say, harmonizing.
This is the method for resting. It means that when a Bodhisattva abides, they cultivate tranquility and use meditative concentration to sustain themselves;
when they emerge, they employ the four modes of deportment to benefit sentient beings. There is nothing that does not constitute the work of benefiting both self and others.
Through wisdom, one thoroughly understands that dependent origination is by nature unarisen; all phenomena are thus, and the true source is ultimate stillness.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I declare them to be emptiness. Is this not precisely the absence of self-nature and non-arising?
By extending this understanding to encompass all things, one realizes that all phenomena are thus, and the true source is ultimately still.

Although they know that afflictions are not to be abandoned and that bodhi is not to be grasped, they are nevertheless able to refrain from realizing the unconditioned and thus pass through the long kalpas of birth and growth.

Within that which is not to be relinquished, I therefore relinquish it; within that which is not to be sought, I therefore seek it. Without realizing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I shall pass through the long kalpas of birth and growth.

Extensively cultivating the myriad practices, one observes all directions equally; below, this extends to the contemplation of the truths and conditions, and above, it encompasses the unique [Buddha-qualities].

The mind of great vows universally covers all beings, and the way of the four means of integration (catuḥsaṃgrahavastu) universally gathers them in. Taking the three realms as one’s home, it encompasses the four...
Born as a son, he unifies compassion and wisdom, adorns himself with both merit and insight, transcends the two vehicles, and stands alone at their summit;
such is the Way of the Mahāyāna.
This praises the Bodhisattva whose mind is universal, whose conduct is penetrating, whose lineage is great, and whose offspring are many;
for by uniting compassion and wisdom and adorning both merit and insight, he is able to transcend others and stand supreme, thereby accomplishing the way of the Mahāyāna.

It accords with the profound and wondrous principle of the Primordial Void (*xūyuán*).

One is not one; if it were not three, it would not be three. Three is not three; if it were not one, it would not be one.

Since even "one" is not truly one, then the "three" is fundamentally not three; thus, it is not three by its own nature. Since even "three" is not truly three, then the "one" is fundamentally not one;

It is not that the one is not one; the three do not remain. It is not that the three are not three; the one does not stand. In this non-standing one, there is fundamentally no three.
In these non-remaining three, there is fundamentally no one.
Now, the three causes establish the one; yet since the one is not truly one, how could the three remain? The one cause meets with the three;
yet since the three are not truly three, how could the one be established? Since the non-established one is itself empty, how can there be any three?
Thus, fundamentally there are no three. Since the non-abiding three do not exist, how can there be any one? Thus, fundamentally there is no one.
The One and the Three are originally non-existent; even non-existence is non-existent. When there is no non-existence, there is no original basis; therefore, it is supremely wondrous.
Although the One and the Three are non-existent, if they were to persist within non-existence, that non-existence would not be wondrous. Thus, one must negate even this non-existence.
If one truly negates that non-existence, then there will be no root for the One and the Three; only then can one reach the ultimate principle.

Although there are differences in their depth and shallowness, the animals are distinct while the river itself remains one. That the river is one—how could it become one only by following the various animals?
This is used as a metaphor that the principle is inherently one from the beginning; it is not made one through the convergence of people. Thus, the animals themselves...
They are distinct, yet the river itself is not divided. This serves as a metaphor for how, although there are three persons, the underlying principle does not become three.

Since the river itself does not constitute three rivers, how can one use the river to conflate it with the animals? And since the animals themselves do not constitute a single animal, how can one use the animals to represent three rivers?
The rivers and the lands are one; how can one river be used to conflate three animals? The principle is fundamentally non-different;
how can the principle be used to conflate the Three Vehicles? The animals are originally three; how can the three animals be used to constitute three rivers?
The capacities [of sentient beings] are fundamentally three; how can the Three Vehicles be used to constitute three principles?
The river is not the beast—what else could it be? (3) The beast is not the river—what else could it be?
(1). Shibi said: "Principle is not the function; it is inherently one. Function is not the principle; it is eternally three."
A single river alone encompasses three animals, yet the river itself has never become three; the three animals together tread upon one river, yet the animals have never been one.
This is a metaphor for how a single principle responds to three capacities, yet the principle does not become three because of those capacities. The three capacities observe it together...
The principle is one, yet the capacities [of beings] do not take that principle as being one.
That beasts are not identical reveals that their legs have varying lengths; that rivers are not three reveals that their waters have no fixed depth.
Water has no depth; this is like the non-differentiation of the Dharma. Feet have varying lengths; this is analogous to the clarity or obscurity of wisdom.
By applying the Dharma to the metaphor, it can be understood.
Thus, the Dharma fundamentally has no three; it is only people who themselves constitute three.
This can also be understood from the concluding text.

Thus we know that the Truths resemble a river. Whether human or beast, the Śrāvakas are the most inferior; they are the equals of rabbits.
Though they may rush along in haste, they can never reach the bottom of the waves; they cannot fathom its ultimate depth.
Since their own station is inherently low, why must they observe the current of the Truths and uniformly consider themselves to have attained only the Lesser Vehicle?

Shibei said: "Those of inferior wisdom do not penetrate deeply; when they contemplate it, they become small themselves. That which is produced by those of superior faculties—how could it be the same as something small?

If their wisdom-illumination is lofty and brilliant, and their capacity is equal to that of a fragrant elephant, then they can exhaust the source and reach the ultimate limit, becoming brilliantly great."
When the illumination of wisdom is lofty and brilliant, the wisdom that contemplates it is great; when its capacity equals that of a fragrant elephant, the rank one ascends is superior;
when one exhausts the source and reaches the ultimate limit, the principle realized is profound.
Thus we know that those who contemplate with inferior wisdom attain the fruit of a śrāvaka; those who contemplate with middling wisdom attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;

and those who contemplate with superior wisdom attain the fruit of a bodhisattva. The principle of our school is thus clear and manifest; how could it be something to be grasped through mere conjecture?

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Those who contemplate with inferior wisdom attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; up to those who contemplate with the highest-of-the-high wisdom, they attain the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Since this treatise discusses the three vehicles, it does not mention the "highest-of-the-high" [wisdom].
Therefore, the śrāvaka perceives suffering and abandons its origin; the pratyekabuddha awakens to the accumulation and dispersal of phenomena and contemplates detachment;

and the bodhisattva thoroughly understands the true source, knowing that the origin is fundamentally without combination. While these three types of persons alike perceive the Four Noble Truths, they differ in the fruits they realize.
There is only this single Four Noble Truths, yet the objects of contemplation differ for the three vehicles according to their respective three types of wisdom.

Those of the Śrāvaka-vehicle take the Truth of Suffering as primary; knowing suffering, they sever its origin. Those of the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle take the Truth of Origin as primary; awakening to the gathering and dispersal of origins, they contemplate emptiness.
Those of the Bodhisattva-vehicle take the Truth of Cessation as foremost; thoroughly penetrating the true source, they realize that the gathering [of conditions] is without synthesis. 4.
The Truths are identical, yet the realization of their fruits differs.
This is truly because there are varying depths of contemplation; it is simply that their relative heights and depths are revealed through mutual comparison.
By means of these varying depths of contemplation, one compares them against the Four Noble Truths to clarify their respective levels.

Therefore, those of the Lesser Vehicle practice the inferior; they do not cultivate what belongs to the Middle and Superior. Those of the Superior Vehicle practice the superior, yet they cultivate the Middle and the inferior.

Those of the Middle Vehicle practice the Middle and the inferior, but do not cultivate the superior. Whether one is superior, middling, or inferior depends on the person; it is not that the Truth itself makes them great or small.
The cultivation of the Three Vehicles is explained as being either direct or inclusive. Those of superior capacity cultivate the superior directly and inclusively cultivate the middling and inferior.

Those of middling capacity cultivate the middling directly and inclusively cultivate the inferior. Those of inferior capacity are only able to cultivate the inferior; they cannot cultivate the middling or the superior.
Although the three vehicles differ, they all converge upon the essential means for escaping suffering;

they collectively shatter the bonds of views and afflictions, and all transcend birth-and-death within the realm of limited duration. It is not by virtue of the clarity or obscurity of their contemplation of existence that there is superiority or inferiority in their liberation from suffering.

Although the Śrāvakas are minor [in rank], they have already dispelled the delusions of views and craving; thus, they possess no sorrow within the triple world, and their form of segmented birth has ceased.
Hereafter, I shall briefly clarify the merits of the Śrāvakas, while also adjudicating the stages of the sudden and gradual paths, in order to encourage their cultivation.
Intent. Now, this first clarifies that the Śrāvakas have already attained the severance of delusions and emerged from suffering;

they are illuminated by the three supernormal knowledges (*vidyā*), their eighty thousand kalpas are manifest before them, and they exercise mastery over the six higher faculties (*abhijñā*) within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

They pass straight through mountain walls as if traversing open space, sometimes walking or standing in mid-air, or sitting and reclining with ease; when floating upon a marsh, they move with lightness.
Like a goose feather gliding over the earth as if treading upon water, the power of the nine concentrations is perfected and the eighteen transformations follow the mind at will;
this clarifies that his merit and virtue are complete. Regarding the phrase "the three insights shine forth," it means that the three insights and six supernormal powers are all fully realized.
"Endowed with. Regarding the "nine concentrations," it is said that these supernormal powers (abhijñā) are produced by means of meditative concentration (dhyāna).
The nine concentrations and eighteen transformations are fully detailed according to the numerical categories of the Dharma.

However, when comparing the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka with the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi), there are points of equality and inferiority. In that they both eliminate the four abidings (catur-vāsa), they are equal.
But in their subduing of ignorance (avidyā), the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka is inferior; if even he is thus inferior, it goes without saying that the two vehicles (dviyāna) are so as well.

The text is derived from the *Fahua yuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra). Therein, it is judged that all four teachings possess Buddhas at the stage of fruition (*phala*). However, when discussing the stages of severance, suppression, cultivation, and realization, the difference between them is as vast as heaven and earth.

This is like the case where, while the borderlands have not yet been pacified, one may borrow a high office; yet when the rank and merit are formally determined, one’s actual position is truly low. Thus, comparing the Buddha of fruition in the Tripitaka teaching with a person at the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching: * **Severance:** The Tripitaka has severed the afflictions of the three realms; the Perfect Teaching has severed the delusions of the three thousand subtle gates. * **Suppression:** The Tripitaka suppresses the afflictions of the Desire Realm; the Perfect Teaching suppresses the delusions of the three thousand subtle gates.

* **Cultivation:** The Tripitaka cultivates the Four Noble Truths; the Perfect Teaching cultivates the Three Truths. * **Realization:** The Tripitaka realizes the Four Noble Truths; the Perfect Teaching realizes the Three Truths. Therefore, regarding the Buddha of fruition in the Tripitaka and a person at the level of the seventh faith in the Perfect Teaching: [the former] is like a high-ranking official in an unsettled region, while [the latter] is like one whose rank and merit are fixed, even if their actual position is lower. Thus, based on the Buddha of fruition in the Tripitaka and the person at the seventh faith in the Perfect Teaching...
Thus their relative superiority and inferiority are determined. Therefore it is said that they are equal in having eliminated the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*).

At this point, they are on the same level. However, regarding the suppression of ignorance (*avidyā*), the Tripiṭaka masters are inferior; for those of the Tripiṭaka do not even know that fundamental ignorance exists, much less are they able to suppress or sever it.
Thus, these persons of the sixfold purity of the faculties are considered inferior. Formerly, when the King Qian Zhongyi of the Five Dynasties reached this passage...

In this world, there is a class of people who have not cultivated roots of goodness in past lives and lack the wisdom of non-arising.

Though they possess superficial eloquence that gives rise to spirited debate, and they cite sutras and treatises to provide indirect interpretations and forced reconciliations, they do nothing more than deceive the ignorant and deaf, and repudiate cause and effect.
When circumstances accord with one's desires, joy gives rise to attachment; when they oppose one's will, distress engenders aversion. Such is the inherent nature of the three types of sensation.
To claim a rank equal to that of a Bodhisattva is to be like one who is inwardly displeased.
Having already verified their orthodoxy or heterodoxy through their understanding, we now further gauge their saintliness or ordinariness through their conduct.

If they rejoice when things accord with their wishes and become angry when they oppose them, they clearly possess the three types of sensation of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); how then can they call themselves Bodhisattvas?

The transgressions of the first category of precepts have not been avoided; moreover, the blemish of exceeding human limits continues to entangle him. While he does not cultivate what is practiced in the Mahāyāna, he further reviles the "Lesser Learning" (Hīnayāna).
Indulging his own impetuous eloquence for a time, the malady of slander resounds clearly.

The retribution of the three miserable realms and the wheel of suffering will persist through long kalpas. Alas! How lamentable! When these words are spoken, one is moved to profound sorrow and grief.
The first section concerns the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*). The transgressions of such individuals further entangle them;
it is said that these faults and rifts surround their persons in great numbers. Having failed to cultivate what is great, they moreover revile the small;
indulging their arrogant tongues in slanderous speech, they embrace the wheel of suffering for long kalpas—truly, how lamentable! To utter these words brings genuine sorrow.

However, for one who has realized their true nature, the more they encounter external objects, the more their illumination increases; for a person who has forgotten the mind, even favorable appearances do not enter their breast.
How much less could the perversities of the three karmas ever occupy their heart, even for a single drop of dust?
Cultivate by realizing the nature; when confronting objects, there is nothing that is not the mind-nature. By fully illuminating the nature, cultivation is perfected.

Seeing through the forgetting of the mind, what encountered circumstance is not suchness? The more one realizes suchness, the more one forgets "goodness. How could there be any wrong or deviance? How could even a drop of worldly dust ever stain it?
Therefore, those who mirror the Origin purify the three types of sensation at the source of the mind; those who wash away defilement sweep the seven branches of misconduct from body and speech.
If the three sensations are not purified, there is no means by which the Origin can be mirrored; if the seven branches are not swept clean, how can there be washing? This is what is most prized.
Those who dwell in the Way find joy solely in this.

Their insentient nature is untainted by the defilements of worldly karma; their conscious awareness is free from the vexations of even the smallest insects. Deep mountain streams are insufficient to match its purity;
flying snow cannot compare with its whiteness.
It can purify the three types of sensation and sweep away the seven branches [of misconduct]. Regarding insentient things, one naturally does not commit theft;

regarding sentient beings, one naturally does not commit sexual misconduct or killing. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If the mind does not even take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, or touch, then the three actions of the body and four of the mouth will necessarily have no cause for arising.
This pure and simple disposition cannot be fully described by metaphor.
Cultivating virtue is like a flock of birds raising their wings; they soar to the highest heights, reaching for the stars and moon. Abandoning evil is like a school of fish startled by a hook;
they plunge to the very bottom of the rivers and oceans.
Shibei said: "Cultivating virtue is like a bird soaring into the void, ever furthering the path of wisdom. Abandoning evil is like a fish avoiding the hook, exercising caution at every turn.
The primordial radiance feels ashamed that its illumination does not reach so far; the higher realms feel abashed as their karmic conditions dissolve."

Shibei said: "His wisdom and illumination are lofty and far-reaching; his discernment surpasses the primordial sun. As the conditions of the three realms of existence are extinguished, his merit exceeds that of the higher heavens.
With such understanding and practice, nothing can surpass him."
Object and wisdom merge to perfect the void; concentration and insight are balanced to achieve the sublime. Though the mulberry fields change, the mind remains unaltered;
though the seas and mountains shift, the will does not waver.
The Way resides within oneself; the characteristics of the world are constant. Though mountains and seas may undergo change, how could one’s will follow the shifting of things?

Thus, one can dwell amidst confusion without being disturbed by clamor, concentrating the spirit to manifest clear illumination. The source of the mind is bright and pure, and wisdom and understanding are boundless.

Shibei said: "To exhaust the capacity of one's ears and eyes in seeing and hearing—that which cannot be constrained by sounds and colors—is it not because these things are themselves inherently empty?
Therefore, external objects cannot burden one’s spiritual intelligence."
By contemplating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one penetrates True Suchness (*tathatā*); by examining the golden script, one relies upon the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Thus, within a single thought-moment, what dharma-gate is not fully contained?

One who practices the Perfect Teaching observes their own nature internally and accords with the definitive meaning externally. Since the nature is fully present in a single thought-moment, what dharma is not encompassed?

Therefore, one can realize that practicing good and practicing evil are themselves the inherent goodness and inherent evil of nature. When the mind-nature is thus interfused, there is no dharma that is not possessed;
such a person may truly be called one who has attained the definitive meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.

If their sublime wisdom has not yet manifested, their minds lack a standard of reference; their understanding does not accord with principle, and their practice lacks the transcendence of the mundane.
They deviate from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to follow ordinary sentiments, and turn their backs on the perfect expression to cling to provisional teachings.
In the complete cultivation of all matters, one must first awaken the wondrous wisdom. It is like a skilled archer whose arrow shafts buttress one another;

there is no shot that does not hit the mark. Mind after mind illuminates one another; there is nothing that does not transcend the defilements. For when the nature is illuminated, wisdom naturally becomes clear;
when wisdom is clear, the defilements naturally transcend it. If it were otherwise, how could one achieve this without the Dharma-body and prajñā?
How marvelous is the efficacious power of liberation!
Thus, the teachings were established according to the sequence of capacities, directed toward the fundamental source.
This concludes the exposition of the Buddha’s teaching on the gradual instruction of the Three Vehicles. As for those of perfect understanding and perfect practice, they do not...

This is necessary. If one understands [the truth] but does not accord with principle, or if one's practice lacks transcendence of the mundane, or if one opposes nature while following emotions, or turns one's back on the perfect to cling to the partial—then the Tathāgata cannot help but preach the teachings of the Three Vehicles according to the capacities and faculties of beings.

Therefore, I have set forth its fundamental framework and provided exhaustive detail regarding what has not yet been clarified. I have briefly stated the essential tenets concerning the various levels of depth;
as for the study of the Three Vehicles, one may understand their respective stages through their manifestations and echoes.
The Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles are exceedingly numerous and complex. Should one wish to understand them in detail, one must consult the original texts.
For now, I shall briefly outline the essential framework of these major works, so that beginners may understand their respective stages.
