Chapter Seven: The Non-duality of Phenomena and Principle Indeed, contemplation does not establish itself apart from its object, nor is the object integrated apart from contemplation. When both object and contemplation are simultaneously merged in stillness, one attains wondrous enlightenment.

Therefore, prior to the actual cultivation of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), the gateway of the non-duality of phenomena and principle (*dharmatattva*) is established as the essence from which the complete objective realm gives rise to wisdom.
Although the objects of the truths (*satya*) are three, they do not transcend phenomena and principle; although phenomena and principle diverge, their non-duality is the fundamental tenet.
Thus, the title "Non-duality of Phenomena and Principle" is set forth to manifest this foundation, and this wondrous realm is realized through the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
Its essence is the seamless integration [of the absolute and the phenomenal]. Its thesis is that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Since this serves as the object, it also serves as the contemplation; cultivation arises entirely from nature, and cultivation is entirely within nature—is this not what is meant?
If one does not place this before the three contemplations, then there will be no path for practice. Thus we know that the ancients compiled...
This collection truly darkens the great path.
Now, when wondrous awakening serves as a thoroughfare, mountains and rivers are not obstructions; yet when one is deluded by names and stalled by forms, even a hair’s breadth becomes a barrier.
The wondrous awakening on the thoroughfare is simply the complete realization that all dharmas are nothing other than the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*).
It is like the butcher Ding dissecting an ox: at the beginning of his work, everything he sees is nothing but the ox;

this serves as a metaphor for being deluded by names and obstructed by appearances, such that even the slightest thing before one’s eyes becomes a barrier. After three years, however, [he no longer saw the ox].
"One who sees the whole ox" refers to one who, because of its inherent nature, has never encountered the sinews, ligaments, or tough joints; how much less so the large bones?
This is used as a metaphor for the thoroughfare of wondrous awakening, where mountains and rivers are no longer obstructed.
However, the source of the myriad dharmas has always been the true reality (*dharmatā*); the realms of delusion, as numerous as dust motes and sands, have from the beginning been the True Vehicle.
Thus, while objective phenomena are boundless, Prajñā is limitless, because the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally true and is fully realized as perfected wisdom.
This is the correct explanation for the thoroughfare of wondrous awakening; it is the reason why mountains and rivers are not obstructed.

It states that the source of the myriad dharmas has always been the true reality (*dharmatā*), and that the realms of delusion, as numerous as dust motes and sands, have from the beginning been the True Vehicle (*saddharma*). These words, however, are extracted from the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The meaning is elucidated through the Tiantai school, and the merit is attributed to Prajñā. In practicing the Perfect Course (yuanxing), one must briefly clarify these three meanings:
first, principle (li); second, delusion (huo); and third, wisdom (zhi). This is because the wisdom of Prajñā on the stage of fruition of all Buddhas is thus boundless.

Regarding the objects illuminated by this [wisdom], the manifestations of things are boundless. The reason these manifestations are boundless is that the realms of delusion (*moha-gati*) are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The reason the realms of delusion are so numerous is precisely because they are the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the source of all phenomena (*dharma*).
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true reality of all phenomena."

Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): all phenomena (*dharmas*) consist of the nature-endowed ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) of sentient beings—conventional names (*prajñapti*), substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*), primary retribution (*vipāka*), and environmental retribution (*niśraya*).

These are the nature and characteristics of the three thousand [realms]. Within these ten dharma-realms, there are inherent goodness (*prakṛti-kuśala*) and inherent evil (*prakṛti-akuśala*), as well as cultivated goodness (*bhāvanā-kuśala*) and cultivated evil (*bhāvanā-akuśala*).
The nine realms inherently possessed are termed "inherent evil"; the Buddha-realm inherently possessed is termed "inherent goodness. Through cultivation, they are perfected.
The nine realms are called "cultivated evil," while the Buddha-realm is called "cultivated good.
Yet this dharma of inherent nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) is able to transform and create all phenomena within the course of daily life. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates; among all things in the world, there is nothing it does not create. It is like the mind...
The Buddha is likewise. As it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Nevertheless, although they are capable of creating, one must know that all remain unchanging while following conditions; they follow conditions without changing.

Thus, the nine realms of existence are capable of following defiled conditions to create the nine realms of existence. All phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants within delusion are called the "ten thousand."
"Dharmas" refers to all phenomena that are produced. "Dust-like sands of delusions and destinies" refers to the three defiled delusions that arise as conditions.

Delusion and defilement serve as the cause, while the myriad dharmas constitute the effect. Because the entirety of cultivated evil is identical to inherent evil, and because this inherent evil is pervasive and interfused, there is no dharma that does not enter into it.
It spontaneously encompasses the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm; therefore, the myriad...
The source of all phenomena is the reality-as-it-is (*tathatā*) from which they have always arisen; the myriad delusions and realms of existence are fundamentally the True Teaching.

Therefore, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to give rise to cultivation from the goodness of their nature, employing the boundless wisdom of *prajñā* to illuminate the infinite realm of phenomenal forms;
and from the infinite realm of phenomenal forms, they give rise to the boundless wisdom of *prajñā*.

Object and wisdom are fused as one; the beginning and the source are united to form the perfectly luminous Great Enlightenment. If one traces its achievement back to its origin, there is no other method involved than this:
it is simply because the fundamental reality of the Dharma-nature is intrinsically true, and through its thorough realization, wisdom is perfected.
The two characters "thoroughly realized" (*liǎodá*) are of paramount importance; let students reflect upon them.

It is like this: if one travels by way of a thoroughfare, ten thousand *li* can be expected; if, however, one encounters obstacles and strikes against ditches, one will remain within the confines of the local area all day long.
This is because one does not know that objects have boundaries beyond form, nor that ditches extend into the realm of infinite emptiness.

The two lines concerning "conduct through thorough paths" serve as a metaphor for the sublime awakening that touches all things. The two lines concerning "busy crossroads" serve as a metaphor for delusion and stagnation.
The subsequent two lines beginning with "because those who are ignorant" provide a critique that aligns with the principle of the Dharma;
for the deluded do not know that objects are the true mark (*dharmatā*), which is the boundary of the formless, nor that delusion is *tathatā*, the realm of ultimate emptiness. Thus it is said.
Therefore, if one studies and dwells in the Middle Way, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) can be anticipated.
The Middle Way is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it illuminates both emptiness and the provisional. The true mark is formless, yet it is form.

Having characteristics yet being without characteristics, one is thus able to train in and traverse the Middle Way. Then, mind after mind accords with reality, and the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) may be anticipated.
If, however, one clings to existence or stagnates in non-existence, one ultimately falls into extreme views; this is because such a person does not understand that existence itself is non-existent.
This is because there is no reality that is not non-existent.
Although ordinary beings perceive the existence of the myriad phenomena of the world as being existent, this very existence inherently possesses the characteristic of non-existence.
Although those of the Two Vehicles perceive the non-existence of Nirvana as being non-existent, this very non-existence inherently possesses... [the characteristic of existence].
It is not that there is no reality existing therein. Thus, while there are existence and non-existence, rightness and wrongness, one should abide in the Middle Way within their very substance.
This Middle Way, moreover, has never been without both existence and non-existence, such that the simultaneous illumination of both is perfectly manifest.
Since those who have not yet attained realization cling to existence and thereby stagnate in non-existence, how could they not fall into the extreme views?
The various forms and appearances of today, when investigated to their limit, are found to be no-phenomena; the roaring sounds and cries, when scrutinized to their end, are found to be wordless.

"Investigating to the limit" (*qiong*) is the same as "scrutinizing" (*jiu*). Just as in the Hīnayāna there is the analysis of form to reveal emptiness, and in Yoga there is the analytical dissection by the sword of wisdom.
The Mahāyāna possesses a substance that is like an illusion or a transformation. This extends to the thorough realization that the root of sound is entirely produced by conditions;
when sought within causes and conditions, it is utterly unobtainable. If form and appearance were not empty, how could one exhaustively investigate them and find them to be without characteristics?
If sound were not unreal, how could one investigate it and find it to be beyond words? Using the existent as an analogy for the non-existent, all things [are thus understood].

All are thus. Therefore, we know that clinging to existence and stagnating in non-existence both arise from emotional calculations. When one investigates the essence of phenomena, it is in reality neither existent nor nonexistent.
To be deluded regarding it is to say it possesses form and sound; to awaken to it is to realize its profound stillness and silence.
Shibei said: "In delusion, hearing does not transcend sound; seeing does not surpass form. In awakening, every color and every fragrance is none other than the Middle Way.
Thus, the Absolute Truth (paramārtha-satya) does not deviate from phenomena and principle; it is the original reality of the very substance of phenomena and principle. Wondrous wisdom..."
It is distinct from mere cognition; rather, the very nature of cognition is primordial wisdom (*ādi-jñāna*), the Middle Way, and the True Reality (*tattva*).
It is able to remain unchanging while following conditions, manifesting as sentient beings or Buddhas, as form or mind, as the basis or the primary, and as phenomena or principle.
Thus, both phenomena and principle are of the same nature; how could this be inconsistent with the principle that phenomena exist within the principle?
There is none. Thus, the essence of both phenomena and principle is fundamentally true. Now, wisdom is certainly the nature; likewise, awakening-knowledge is also the nature.
Since both are identical to the nature, how could wondrous wisdom alone be at variance with awakening-knowledge?
When the Great Master said to the Sixth Patriarch, "Even discrimination is not the mind," was there not a profound flavor in those words?

However, the wondrous purport transcends words; yet, we rely on words and phrases to elucidate that purport. The True Doctrine is devoid of characteristics; yet, we rely on names and forms to manifest its essence.
Above, I have briefly clarified the wondrous realm and the wondrous wisdom as the manifestation of the non-duality of phenomenon and principle. This is precisely intended—

The illumination of principle transcends verbal expression; wisdom forgets all that is relative. Therefore, one first clarifies the use of words to reach the point where words are forgotten, and relies on the presence of conditions to arrive at the state beyond all conditions.
If there were no words or texts, it would be insufficient to explain the subtle meaning;
if there were no conditions or oppositions, it would be insufficient to manifest the absolute. In both cases, one may attain the meaning through words, and having attained the meaning, forget them.
The statement says: "This reaches its profound depths.
It is like an elephant that is not the Snowy Mountain itself, yet uses the Snowy Mountain as a metaphor for the elephant; this merely takes what can serve as a metaphor."
How could one take the Snowy Mountains to be the elephant?

This borrows the dharma and the metaphor to address matters that cannot be made equivalent, using them to illustrate the principle that the hare and the leopard are not the same. The intended meaning is this:

if one were to claim that the Snowy Mountains resemble an elephant, one could not seek its tail or tusks within the mountains; likewise, one may apply this analogy to the provisional [teachings] regarding the sublime principle.
One must not cling to names and thereby demand their corresponding reality.

The Dharma of today is neither permanent nor is it clung to as existent; by means of the provisional non-existence, permanence is refuted. Its nature is neither annihilated nor is it clung to as non-existent;
by means of the provisional non-non-existence, annihilation is refuted.
Phenomena are fundamentally not eternal, yet ordinary beings cling to them as being existent. Phenomena are fundamentally not annihilated, yet non-Buddhists cling to them as being non-existent.

The Sage prescribes medicine according to the illness: he provisionally employs "non-existence" to shatter the view of permanence, and provisionally employs "non-non-existence" to shatter the view of annihilation.
Once the illness is gone, the medicine is forgotten. If one clings to the medicine and thereby contracts an illness, then the Sage...
Furthermore, there arises the teaching of "neither existence nor non-existence.
This is analogous to purity, which is neither water nor ash; yet, by employing water and ash to wash away impurities, one merely takes advantage of their capacity to cleanse.
"How could one achieve purity through water and ash? Shibi said:

"Water and ash are metaphors for that which can destroy; 'purity' is a metaphor for that which is revealed. The meaning is that the revealed [truth] relies upon the destroying [agent] as a provisional means."
That which is capable of refutation is not what is revealed;

thus we know that the Middle Way is non-biased. It uses the two extremes as a provisional means to distinguish the correct. Since "annihilation" and "permanence" are not [the truth], it relies on "non-existence" to clarify their falsity.

If both "existence" and "non-existence" are already seen to be inexpressible, how could "neither existence nor non-existence" be anything other than the truth? One can thus believe and know that this is the subtle penetration.
The ultimate source cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments.
This precisely clarifies the Middle Way; although it is manifested by provisionally employing the two extremes, it remains detached from existence and non-existence.

When the Middle is distinguished by means of the two extremes, it is detached from annihilationism and eternalism; when the Middle is elucidated by relying on non-existence and existence, it clarifies what is not [the extremes]. Once the principle is thus revealed—
The middle, too, does not exist. Therefore it is said: "If there is existence, if there is non-existence"—since these words are already false, how could "neither existence nor non-existence" be true?
One may thus know with certainty that the wondrous realization of the primordial source is not something that can be fathomed by ordinary sentiments.

This means that although [the teaching] provisionally employs existence and non-existence, it does not linger in existence or non-existence; although it manifests the Middle Way, it does not abide in the Middle Way.
Why is this? Delusion does not arise from ignorance; truth is not produced by wisdom. To penetrate delusion is called truth; to be confused about truth is called delusion.

How could it be that delusion changes in accordance with ignorance, or that truth turns in pursuit of wisdom? Truth and delusion do not differ; it is only ignorance and wisdom that are distinct from one another.
"Delusion" refers to the two extremes of existence and non-existence, or permanence and annihilation, as clung to by ordinary beings and non-Buddhists.
"Reality" refers to the Middle Way revealed by using provisional existence to refute non-existence and provisional non-existence to refute existence. Yet, that delusion is itself merely delusion.
It is not because of ignorance that delusion subsequently arises; the True is inherently true from the very beginning. Nor is it because of wisdom that the True is subsequently produced.
It is simply that when one realizes delusion is fundamentally empty, it is designated as "True"; when delusion is perceived as substantially existent, it is designated as "delusion.
How could it be that there is actually a delusion which becomes "delusion" only after following ignorance, or that the True becomes "True" only after pursuing wisdom?
Indeed, one must understand that truth and falsehood are fundamentally no different; they merely appear distinct due to the disparity between the ignorant and the wise.
Now, if one wishes to profoundly realize the ultimate source, one must first examine the distinction between ignorance and wisdom, and skillfully clarify the nature of truth and falsehood. If one...
Having clarified their reality and falsehood, one must further investigate their names and essences. If names and essences are distinguished, then reality and falsehood will naturally be discerned.
Once reality and falsehood are discerned, the gap between the ignorant and the wise becomes vast.
The preceding passage states that the false does not change according to delusion, and the true does not revolve with wisdom.

Nevertheless, delusion and wisdom cannot be left undifferentiated, and the true and the false cannot be left undiscerned. Should delusion and wisdom remain undifferentiated, [the distinction between them would be lost].
If this is so, how can folly be extinguished and wisdom brought forth? If one fails to distinguish between the real and the false, how can the false be severed and the real restored?
Thus, to examine folly and wisdom and to clarify the real and the false is the essential task of the gateway to cultivation.
Furthermore, one must investigate their names and grasp their substance; once name and substance are established, the Real [is realized].
When one falsely discriminates, the distinction between the ignorant and the wise is established.
Thus, the ignorant lack the capacity for enlightened wisdom, whereas the wise possess the reality of penetrating the ignorance of others.
Therefore, we know that without wisdom there is no means to clarify what is true and what is false; without wisdom, nothing can distinguish their names and essences.

This is intended to clarify the names and essences [of these states] as the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). However, names and essences are established based on the true and the deluded;
the true and the deluded are distinguished by means of wisdom (*prajñā*); and wisdom, in turn, is manifested in dependence upon ignorance (*moha*).
Yet, one does not yet know what is called ignorance and what is called wisdom. Therefore, it is first explained that the reason one is called "deluded" is as follows:
It is because of the capacity of non-apprehending wisdom that one is called "wise"; it is because of the reality of having penetrated folly that one is so designated.
Yet, why is it necessary to establish this wisdom? For without wisdom, there would be no means to clarify what is true and what is false.
It is because without wisdom one cannot discern their names and essences.

Why is this? There are cases where there is a name but no essence, and cases where a name is applied based on an essence; when names and essences are thus intertwined, they are truly difficult to investigate to the very end.
An inquiry arises: why must one employ wisdom to clarify the true and the false, and to distinguish between names and essences?
It is because within the world there are things that possess a name but lack an essence, and there are things that receive a name based upon an essence.
If one lacks the wisdom of clear discernment to differentiate them, then names and essences will become entangled in their origins, making it difficult to fathom the essence underlying a given name.
This is thoroughly understood.

Therefore, the substance is not the name, yet they cannot be distinguished; the name is not the substance, yet it cannot be applied without it. To speak of substance, one must necessarily rely upon its name;
to discuss the name, one must necessarily depend upon its substance.
Today, I shall first discuss the application of names based on the substance of phenomena. That is to say, there are dharmas that possess both name and substance.

For the substance is the actual entity underlying a name; thus, the substance is not manifested without its name. The name is a provisional designation applied to the substance; thus, the name is not applied without its substance.
Therefore, when speaking of the substantial entity, one must rely upon its provisional name; and when discussing the provisional name, one must necessarily depend upon—
In fact, the naming of an essence based on its characteristics has been so for a long time.
Those who today apply names outside of an essence merely name that which lacks an essence; how could there ever be an essence that truly corresponds to its name?
This clarifies that there is a name but no substance; it is merely applying a name to something outside of any substance.
It can only name that which lacks substance—how could there be a substance that lacks substance to correspond to this name? The following text uses a metaphor to illustrate this point.
It is like the case of a rabbit, which has no horns to which a name could be applied; this name merely designates its lack of horns. How could there be horns that correspond to that name?
For example, when people say, "A rabbit has no horns," this name simply names the absence of horns. Since there are no horns, there is nothing [to which the name refers].
How could there be a "horn" that lacks a horn as its substance yet corresponds to its name?
To apply a name where there is no substance is for the name to be a name without reality. If the name is a name without reality, then that which is named does not exist.
Since that which is named is non-existent, the naming agent cannot exist either.

The former clarifies that names are applied where there is no name; the latter clarifies that there is no substantial entity beneath the name. This explains that names are applied where there is no substance, for within a name there is no real name.

Why is this? Names are established fundamentally to designate their corresponding entities. If there is no entity, how can it correspond to its name? As for the statement that the entity is fundamental...
When one accords with its name, how can that which is nameless accord with its substance? Substance is not substance when it is beyond correspondence;
names are not names when they are beyond naming. Thus, is it only the substance that is fundamentally void? No, even names are originally quiescent.
Now, I wish to elucidate the non-duality of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*) as the essence of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
Since this true reality must rely upon names to be manifested, it follows conversely that without provisional names, there would be no means to name its true essence.
Thus, the presence of both name and essence constitutes the essential meaning of our present contemplation. One should therefore abandon empty names to seek the real name, and discard the empty...
Since the substance is attained through its actual reality, it is explained and clarified again and again regarding the names and substances, their emptiness and reality. Thus it is said:

"Names are established precisely to clarify their substance," and so forth. This is truly intended to abandon the empty and adhere to the real; therefore it is said: "That which has no substance is fundamentally empty, and that which has no name is fundamentally quiescent."
However, that names have no corresponding substance has been so from the beginning. As for what is called "the correspondence between name and substance," what could it possibly mean?
The first two lines conclude the preceding point that there are names without substance; the latter two lines introduce the subsequent argument that names are applied based on substance.

Now, substance does not name itself; it is named "self-substance" by borrowing the names of others. Names are not established by themselves; they are bestowed upon substance as "my name" by borrowing the substance of others.
Substance is the host and the essence; names are the guest and the provisional. Provisional names and the actual substance do not correspond to one another; therefore—
The substance does not name itself; it must rely upon provisional designations to name its own substantial reality. Provisional designations are not established by themselves;
they must rely upon this substantial reality to constitute the provisional designation of "self."
If the substance has not yet taken form, what would the name be named? If the name has not yet been established, what would the substance be made manifest by?
Nevertheless, although the manifestation of the substance relies upon its name, it is not the case that there is no substance simply because it is not named.
Before the substance has taken form, what name could there be to name it? It seems as though it were nameless. Before the name has been established, what substance could there be to manifest it?
It seems as though it were without substance. Nevertheless, although the substance has not yet taken form, it is not like a rabbit that lacks horns and thus lacks substance.
Although the name has not yet been established, it is not like the unestablished name of a rabbit’s horns, which do not exist. Therefore, it is said:

"While the substance is clarified through its provisional name, it is not the case that because the name is absent, the substance is non-existent. This precisely demonstrates that worldly phenomena possess both substantial reality and provisional names.

The establishment of a name must depend upon its substance; if there is no substance, then the name itself is fundamentally non-existent. Thus, it is not that the substance gives rise to the name, but rather that the name arises in relation to the substance.

This correctly clarifies the provisional name and its relationship to the substantial reality. By placing the name first and the reality afterward, it enables students to investigate names to reveal the reality, thereby awakening to the fact that dependent origination is fundamentally non-existent.
Thus, the principle of the emptiness of nature is revealed, serving as the primary prerequisite for entering the Path.
While the reality itself is not called "arising," the name arises with respect to the reality; this is what is termed the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya), wherein both name and reality exist.
This is the meaning.
In the present case, the substance precedes the name, while the name follows from the substance. For one who discerns it thus, the name is established in order to designate its substance;
therefore, we know that the substance is simply the source of the name.
The substance (*tǐ*) is the root, while names (*míng*) are the branches; thus, substance is the source of names.
Therefore, that from which names arise originates in substance. As for the primordial beginning of substance, upon what does it depend?
Regarding the phenomena of the world, there are only names and entities. Having investigated the names and understood their origins, one might ask:
what is the primary thread of the entity? The following text precisely clarifies this thread of the entity. Phenomena are fundamentally like silk; the causes of phenomena are like the threads.
As for the thread by which a name is acquired, upon what does it depend? If one can find that thread, one may exhaust the entire length of silk from a single cocoon.

Now, the substance does not possess my form; it assumes its substance through the convergence of conditions. Conditions do not possess my essence; they become conditions through the convergence with the substance.
Although the myriad dharmas are numerous, they do not go beyond the ten realms. Although the ten realms are many, they do not go beyond nature and appearance. As for nature—

That which has not yet taken form is called the essence (*tattva*). Once the nature (*prakṛti*) has manifested, it is called the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). However, nature does not exist apart from characteristics;

it relies on the convergence of conditions to constitute characteristics. This convergence does not occur by itself; it relies upon the nature and characteristics to constitute the convergence. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
Absolute truth cannot be established in isolation; solitary delusion cannot be formed.
It must depend upon the non-arising and non-ceasing [of the ultimate] uniting with arising and ceasing [of the phenomenal] to constitute the dharma of dependent origination.

Thus, not only are the false dharmas of the nine realms accomplished through dependent origination, but even the true dharmas of the Buddha-realm are likewise accomplished through dependent origination. Therefore, all four teachings...
This clarifies the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions;
therefore, I speak of the One Vehicle. This dependent origination pertains to the three periods of time. Regarding the past, that which has already been produced and completed consists of two links:

ignorance (*avidyā*) as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Regarding what has already been completed, this refers to the present world’s two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—arising from consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the condition.
Name-and-form. Conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling—these are the five branches [of the present].
The present result consists of these same five branches. The present cause consists of the three branches of craving, clinging, and becoming.
The future consists of the two links of birth and old age and death.

For now, we shall take the ordinary discriminative consciousness of the present moment as the object of contemplation to clarify dependent origination. This is precisely the mind employed when "applying the mind exactly" as described below;
it takes the faculty of thought (*manas*) as the cause and mental objects (*dharmas*) as the condition, with [consciousness] arising in between.
The arising of a single thought-moment of consciousness is called the dharma of dependent origination; this is what the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refers to as "dharmas produced by causes and conditions.
Such a consciousness originally arises based on the nature (*prakṛti*). When the nature remains unchanging and has not yet followed along with conditions, [it is thus].
Thus, when the substance does not manifest as my form, it reaches the state of being unchanging yet following conditions; at that time, it provisionally forms a substance by means of conditions.
However, conditions do not assemble of their own accord; they must depend on the nature-substance to constitute these delusive conditions.
If the substance has not yet taken form, with what could conditions meet? If conditions have not yet met, how could the substance take form?
If the substance has not yet taken form, then its nature has not yet followed conditions. If it follows conditions, then conditions have something with which to meet.
Since it has not yet followed conditions, even though there are conditions of defilement and purity, with what could they meet? If conditions have not yet met, then the conditions—

It is the state of non-pairing. If it were a state of pairing, its substance would have a manifest form. Since it is a state of non-pairing, although it possesses an unchanging nature, what form could it possibly take?
This clarifies that one takes [the nature] as the object of contemplation by means of following conditions; therefore, one first clarifies the state prior to conjunction as its fundamental basis.
As for "embodiment," it is formed through the convergence of conditions; as for "convergence of conditions," it is the convergence that forms the embodiment.
To "form an embodiment" means that within a single thought-moment of consciousness, one must necessarily fall into one of the ten dharma-realms; this is called forming an embodiment.
"Forming through the convergence of conditions" means that the mind arises only after the sense organs and their objects encounter one another. However, it is merely due to...
Conditions do not assemble of their own accord; they must depend upon the manifestation of the substance of their nature before they can assemble.

When they assemble through the manifestation of that substance, it is clear that there is no separate assembly apart from the manifestation itself. Since there is no separate assembly apart from the manifestation, the assembly is fundamentally non-existent.

The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) manifests its own form and signs, which subsequently arise through the convergence of conditions. As for "phenomena," the phenomena that are produced are not distinct;
they assume their forms by meeting with other factors, yet these forms are precisely the nature itself.
Is it not the case, then, that form has no separate convergence, and that this convergence is fundamentally non-existent?
When conditions meet, form arises; thus, when illumination meets, there is no distinct form. Since there is no distinct form when they meet, form is fundamentally non-existent.
Nevertheless, a solitary form does not stand alone; it must depend on the meeting of conditions before it takes shape.

That which takes shape through the meeting of conditions exists only as conditions and has no distinct form. Since there is no distinct form, one knows that form, too, is fundamentally non-existent. All of this is...
These two dharmas mutually negate one another, each manifesting its own non-existence in order to sever the attachments of people; it does not mean that the fruit lacks its dharma.
I privately maintain that the dharma which remains unchanging while following conditions certainly exists;

yet, since the nature is manifested through conditions, the nature has no self-nature, and since the conditions are established by means of the nature, the conditions have no self-nature. Since both lack self-nature, then as for the conditions...
Arising is non-arising; its nature is likewise inherently quiescent. Therefore it is said that they are fundamentally non-existent for this reason.
Thus, all phenomena arise from conditions and possess no self-substance.
Shibi said: "The nature of phenomena has no substance; it points entirely to ignorance. Ignorance has no substance; it points entirely to the nature of phenomena."
When the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) together universally produce all phenomena, this is termed "defilement.

When ignorance and the nature of phenomena universally respond to various conditions, this is designated as "purity. Although clear water and turbid water differ, the moisture of the clear and the moisture of the turbid are no different.
"All phenomena" refers to their essence; "arising from conditions" refers to their function. Since phenomena arise from a multitude of...
Arising through conditions, one knows that phenomena have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because their nature lacks an intrinsic self, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Since their nature is empty, although they meet through conditions, they do not exist;
yet since the conditions have met, although their nature is empty, they are not non-existent.
The first two lines conclude with the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). The subsequent four lines correctly name the self-emptiness of intrinsic nature:
it should neither be existent nor non-existent. Why? Because if it is empty of intrinsic nature, it should not be existent; yet, through the convergence of conditions, it should not be non-existent.
Neither existent nor non-existent: the principle of the Middle Way is thus revealed.

Therefore, existence as the convergence of conditions is existence that is not [inherently] existent; non-existence as the emptiness of intrinsic nature is non-existence that is not [inherently] non-existent. Why is this so?
The convergence of conditions is itself emptiness; therefore, it is said to be "not existent. Emptiness is itself the convergence of conditions; therefore, it is said to be "not non-existent.

That which exists as the convergence of conditions is precisely what is "existent," yet because its essence is constituted by the provisional assembly of various conditions, it is substantially non-existent despite being based on existence.
That which is non-existent as the nature of emptiness is precisely what is "non-existent," yet because it arises from delusion...
In terms of its essence, it is non-existent; therefore, although it is non-existent, it is in reality not non-existent. Thus, the commentary explains:
at the time of its manifestation, its nature is fundamentally empty, and thus it is said to be non-existent; at the time of its emptiness, it is able to exist in accordance with conditions.
Therefore it is said that they are not non-existent.
Now, when we say they are neither existent nor non-existent, this does not mean that apart from existence there is a separate non-existence,
nor does it mean that apart from non-existence there is a separate existence.
Now, as for the statement that things are neither existent nor non-existent: this precisely means that phenomena and principle are non-dual, which is termed the Middle Way;

therefore, it is called neither existent nor non-existent. This simultaneously negates the two extremes; it does not mean that apart from existence as the convergence of conditions, there exists a separate non-existence.
Nor is it the case that, apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there exists a separate "existence" called "neither existent nor non-existent.
Rather, these very phenomena—the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind—are simultaneously negated in their own essence; this is what is termed the Middle Way.
Thus, it is clear that dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, they are designated by the name "neither existent nor non-existent.
Herein, the name and the essence are explicitly concluded and revealed as the Middle Way. The name possesses the function of summoning the essence.
The essence possesses a reality that corresponds to its name, serving as the basis for the perfect cultivation of the three dharmas—śamatha and so forth—discussed in the subsequent text.
It is neither non-existence nor existence; since it is neither existence nor non-existence, it is also neither non-existence nor non-non-existence.
The preceding passage clarifies what this is; the present section negates what it is not.

That which is called the Middle Way—neither existent nor non-existent—does not merely consist of taking the state of neither existence nor non-existence as a basis and further adding a double negation, such as "not going toward existence" and "not going toward non-existence."
Why is this? It is because other sutras and treatises were intended for those who do not understand the essence of dharmas and whose emotional attachments have not been exhausted;
they must repeatedly negate even the "neither-nor" position, hence it is said: "not non-existent," and "not non-non-existent.

Now, we clarify that the dharma of conditional conjunction is such that existence is itself non-existence, and non-existence is itself existence. When these opposing natures mutually cancel one another, emotional attachments are completely exhausted, and the principle [is revealed].
There is nothing that is not manifest; why, then, must one repeatedly negate and discard?
If this is so, then it is not only that the path of language is cut off, but also that the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases—this is the ultimate, most perfect, and sudden Dharma that we revere.
It is precisely the phenomena produced by causes and conditions. They are empty in their very substance, because their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent.

They are existent in their very substance, because they arise through the convergence of conditions. They are the Middle Way in their very substance, because they are the convergence of conditions itself.
That which exists as non-existent is precisely the emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) existing as existent.

Such a Middle Way—how could it be discussed through words, or fathomed through thought? Nevertheless, there are the object, the contemplation, the nature, the cultivation, the phenomenon, and the principle.
Here, we are specifically speaking of the object, the nature, and the principle; as for the *śamatha* and so forth mentioned in the subsequent text, they correspond exactly [to these].
Precisely when the mind is applied, it is precisely without the application of mind; only then does one clarify its contemplation, its cultivation, and its practice.
Therefore, one should know that splitting this chapter and placing it as the tenth severs the vital veins and logical pathways so that they are no longer connected.
How can one not regret this? Those with the true eye will naturally be able to discern it for themselves.
○ Section Eight: A Brief Demonstration of the Partial and the Perfect;
within the precepts, there are three [aspects] that must be fully possessed.
Precepts have the meaning of preventing wrongdoing and ceasing evil. This is because the precepts of the three clusters are all capable of preventing and restraining all forms of evil and wrongdoing.
The first is the precept of restraining from unwholesome conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), which means the severance of all evil.
The precepts for restraining one's conduct consist of four points: first, one must not, for the sake of gain or offerings, praise oneself and disparage others;
second, one must not intentionally be stingy and fail to give to others; third, one must not, with a mind of anger, strike or revile sentient beings.
Fourth, one must not slander Mahāyāna sūtras. By upholding these four dharmas, there is no evil that is not abandoned;

therefore, this is called the "precept of restraining conduct" (saṃvara-śīla). Second is the "precept of gathering wholesome dharmas" (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla), which refers to cultivating all forms of goodness.
The precept of gathering wholesome dharmas refers to the practices one performs that are able to gather all wholesome dharmas.

This means that there are no wholesome dharmas performed by body, speech, or mind—nor those of the three types of wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, nor the dharmas of the six perfections such as giving—that are not collected and gathered.
Therefore, it is called the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas.
Third is the precept of benefiting sentient beings, which means vowing to deliver all sentient beings.

Regarding the "precept of gathering sentient beings," this refers to being able to gather in all sentient beings. The practice that enables such gathering consists of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Loving-kindness is defined as affectionate concern, for it is able to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings. Compassion is defined as... [text truncated]

Compassion (*karuṇā*) is so named because it can uproot the suffering of all sentient beings. Joy (*muditā*) is called "celebration," because it celebrates that all sentient beings have left suffering behind and attained happiness.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is defined as being without hatred or attachment, because one constantly remembers that all sentient beings equally attain this state of being without hatred or attachment.
By means of these four immeasurable qualities, one gathers in and sustains all sentient beings.
Regarding the three types within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they must be distinguished.
Shibi states: "Concentration takes as its meaning the correct discernment [of reality] that eliminates discursive thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and mental dullness (*styāna*).
First is the concentration of abiding (*sthiti-samādhi*), which refers to the wondrous nature that is natural and fundamentally unmoving.
This state of abiding in meditative concentration is designated by various names in different sutras: in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is called the Buddha-wisdom; in the *Śūraṅgama*, it is called the eternally abiding true mind;

in the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith*, it is called the nature of perfect enlightenment; in the *Nirvāṇa*, it is called the three virtues (*triguṇa*); and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is called the three [bodies].
Regarding the Truths and so forth, Jingxi said: "The Three Truths are the natural, inherent virtues of one's nature; they are precisely the wondrous mind of the person.
Those sentient beings who cultivate meditative concentration must first be able to realize this; only then can they fully employ their nature to initiate cultivation."
All cultivation resides within the nature.
Second, the arousal of concentration (*samādhi*): this means clarifying the mind and attaining stillness, so that it becomes lucid and its brilliance increases.
Shibi said: "The concentration of principle is fundamentally wondrous; one is deluded and does not know it. Now, reversing that delusion, one returns to cultivate the supreme concentration."
Clarifying the mind and ceasing delusions gives rise to the brilliance of lucid wisdom; increasing the Path and diminishing birth, this merit arises from induction.

The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states: "Prior to the Path, it is called 'intrinsic nature' (*svabhāva-gotra*); abiding within the Path of Buddha-nature, one brings forth the 'induced Buddha-nature' (*utpādya-gotra*).

I say that based on this, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) may be clarified: what was previously established as abiding is precisely the Three Truths (*tisro dharmatāḥ*). Although sentient beings possess them, they are obscured by afflictions.
*Fù*. Jingxi said: "The afflictions of seeing and thinking obstruct emptiness and stillness; the dust-like delusions obstruct transformation and guidance; ignorance clouds the Dharma-nature.

Now, by cultivating the [threefold] arousal, one uses the contemplation of emptiness to shatter all phenomena, the contemplation of the provisional to establish all phenomena, and the contemplation of the middle to unify all phenomena.
Once the darkness and delusion of the three delusions are removed, then the three virtues..."
When stillness and clarity become manifest, and the mind is settled and tranquil, one returns to stillness. When radiance is brought forth and clarity increases, one returns to clarity.
Through the cultivation of evocative meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one attains abiding meditative concentration; thus, one is able to accomplish the great task.
There is no merit greater than this.
Third is the completion of the task through concentration (*samādhi*). This refers to the water of concentration becoming still and clear, wherein all phenomena are reflected.
Shibi said: "Cultivating causes leads toward the fruit; when the task to be accomplished is perfected, that which follows the Path is called the 'Fruit Buddha-nature'. I say:
As for "accomplishing affairs," upon reaching the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), one is able to accomplish the great task of transforming and delivering sentient beings:

startling the world with the Way of Chan, proclaiming it through wisdom and eloquence, and manifesting through the unconditioned (*avyākṛta*) transformations—transforming again and again. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"When the marks of clarity are pure and refined, all manifestations do not become afflictions; they are all the pure and wondrous virtues of Nirvāṇa. This is it.
This is what is meant.
Regarding the three [aspects] within wisdom (*prajñā*), they must be distinguished.
Shibi said: "Wisdom takes the sense of spiritual discernment being unclouded as its definition."

The first is the wisdom of emptiness. This means realizing that the aggregates (*skandha*) are not the self; that within the aggregates there is no self, just as there is no hair on a tortoise or horns on a rabbit.

One is able to realize that the five aggregates are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and lack a sovereign master. This "non-existence" is like the non-existence of hair on a tortoise or horns on a rabbit.

Second is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This refers to the realization that all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), are conditioned by designations and lack substantial reality, being like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water.

One is able to realize that the five aggregates and all phenomena are conditioned by designations and are not real; this unreality is like the unreality of a reflection in a mirror or the moon in water.
Whereas the prior [example of] the non-existence of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns is a non-existence of essence (*asvabhāva-niḥsvabhāva*), now...

The non-existence of a mirror-image or the moon in water is a non-existence that lacks reality. Although the expression "two kinds of non-existence" is the same, the meaning of their two natures is eternally different.
Third is the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-jñāna*), which means realizing that both the object and the cognition are empty, and that even this emptiness is empty.

Regarding the two objects previously mentioned—persons and phenomena—one thoroughly realizes that all are empty. Although the objects are empty, the wisdom that realizes this emptiness is not non-existent.

Now, even that wisdom which realizes emptiness is itself empty; this is called "universal emptiness" (*ubhayābhāva-śūnyatā*). Therefore, it is termed the "wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Regarding the three types within "seeing," one must recognize them.
Shibi says: "Seeing" means the conceptualization of length where what is not itself is taken as such.
First is the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*): this refers to seeing emptiness while [mistakenly] seeing it as non-empty.
The "one who perceives emptiness" refers to one who is able to realize that both persons and phenomena are empty. Although that which is perceived is empty, the perceiver is not empty;
thus, the view of emptiness is established.
Second is "non-empty vision. This means that one sees what is not empty, yet the seeing itself is not non-empty.
As for "non-empty vision," it refers to being able to thoroughly comprehend both the empty and the non-empty. Although that which is seen is indeed non-empty...
Yet one is able to see that which is not non-empty; thus, it constitutes the vision of non-emptiness.
Third is the vision of the emptiness of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This refers to seeing the self-nature while seeing that it is not a [substantial] nature.
Regarding the vision of the emptiness of nature: this means being able to clearly perceive the self-nature. Although that which is seen is a nature, the one who sees it...
It is not a nature; thus, it is established that views are without nature. First, there is the arising of views regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
second, the arising of views regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and third, the arising of views regarding the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent. This is because one has not yet forgotten the subject and object, and thus has not transcended absolute dependence. Although...
One perceives the Three Truths, yet conversely clings to fixed views.
Among the three [aspects] within the partial, one must exercise discernment.
The three virtues discerned herein constitute the most urgent and essential practice of meditative cultivation. To awaken to this, then that which is cultivated...
All things are perfectly complete. To be deluded regarding this, everything one cultivates becomes partial.

If one follows the distinctions made in the *Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, first concerning the Hīnayāna and subsequently concerning the Mahāyāna, the scope of what is encompassed—both vertically and horizontally—is extremely vast and the discussion is exceedingly broad.
Regarding this point, the old commentaries likewise employ the distinctions between Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna to eliminate partiality. However...

None of these should be cultivated as gateways, for they do not know the Great Principle. As for that Great Principle, it lies precisely in the capacity to contemplate and the object of contemplation;

when the subject and object are in perfect accord, one removes oneself from dust and leaves behind defilement, thereby illuminating the Three Virtues. Specifically, the three truths that are the objects of contemplation are called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
the three contemplations that are the capacities of contemplation are called Prajñā; and the perfect accord between the subject and object is called Liberation (*vimukti*).
Thus, both the "transverse" (zōnghéng) and "non-transverse" (bù zōnghéng) perspectives are explained based on this.

Regarding the presence or absence of the three virtues—where there is the Dharma-body but lacks Prajñā and Vimukti—one must explain it by means of both the transverse and non-transverse doctrines. First, according to...

Regarding the three aspects of the object (*ālambana*): the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*) observed therein belongs to the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*); the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) belongs to the virtue of Prajñā; and the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) belongs to the virtue of Liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*).

Regarding the three aspects of the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): the Contemplation of the Middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) belongs to the virtue of the Dharma-body; the Contemplation of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) belongs to the virtue of Prajñā;

and the Contemplation of the Provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) belongs to the virtue of Liberation. Regarding the three aspects of the harmony between the subject and object (*grāhaka-grāhya-saṃyoga*): the Innate Purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*)... [text continues]

Nirvāṇa belongs to the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Perfectly pure nirvāṇa belongs to the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*). Skillful means-pure nirvāṇa belongs to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
When it is said here that there is a Dharma-body but lacks wisdom and liberation, this is discussed from a vertical perspective:
it means one knows that the Dharma-body of the three truths is inherently present, yet one is unable to fully manifest its nature to give rise to the three types of cultivated wisdom.

How could there be the realization of the threefold liberation free from entanglement, wherein subject and object are in perfect accord? Therefore, there is the Dharma-body, yet it lacks the liberation of prajñā.
Speaking in terms of the horizontal perspective: regarding the object, one knows the existence of the truth of the "middle alone," which does not coincide with the two extremes;
regarding contemplation, one merely cultivates the Middle Way view, being unable to simultaneously realize emptiness and the provisional. Thus, there is the dharma of the Middle Way.

If one possesses a body but lacks *prajñā* and liberation, how could one possibly achieve the three truths and the three contemplations, or attain the perfect realization of the three liberations at the stage of fruition through the union of object and wisdom?
I maintain that herein, "horizontal" refers to the three within the one, while "vertical" refers to the three in their sequential order;
furthermore, "horizontal" refers to the three dharmas, while "vertical" refers to the relationship between object and contemplation, or the grasped and the grasper.
Second, there is prajñā, yet there is no liberation-dharmakāya.

Regarding this from a vertical perspective: although there is the prajñā of emptiness-observation that illuminates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it cannot illuminate the dharmakāya of the Middle Way;
how then could the object and the observation be in accord to realize the liberation of intrinsic purity? Regarding this from a horizontal perspective: there is...
If one practices the three contemplations yet cannot thoroughly illuminate the realm of the three truths,
how could one possibly accord with the Dharma-body to attain liberation?
Without the liberation from the three realms of existence, there can be no wisdom of the Dharma-body.
Regarding the vertical perspective, there are worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth;

yet, being unable to illuminate the Dharma-body of the Middle Way to cultivate Prajñā, how could they possibly achieve supramundane liberation through the harmonious convergence of object and contemplation?
Regarding the horizontal perspective, the partial teachings of the three vehicles possess liberation at the level of the fruit, yet they do not know the Perfect and Sudden [teaching].
Because of the duality of object and wisdom, there is no true *prajñā* and *dharmakāya*.
Since there is one and not two, it is not perfect; because it is not perfect, it is not the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*).
Whether arranged vertically or horizontally, having one and lacking two cannot accord with the wondrous nature of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Furthermore, among the three [types of] partial [perfection], one must distinguish them.

In the former case, there is one [aspect] lacking and two present; in the latter case, there are two [aspects] present and one lacking. In both instances, they do not constitute completeness; therefore, it is necessary to distinguish between them.
First, there is the dharma-body-prajñā (dharmakāya-prajñā) without liberation.
Speaking in terms of the vertical progression, one is able to give rise from the nature of the dharma-body to the cultivation of prajñā; therefore, there are two.
There are two [aspects]. One should distance oneself from defilement and be liberated from dust; yet, because one is as if obscured and lacks clarity, there is no liberation.
Speaking in terms of the horizontal [perspective], one is able to illuminate the True and the Middle within emptiness; however, this is merely a partial cultivation and not a complete cultivation.
Therefore, the conventional truth lacks the provisional contemplation that leads to liberation.
Second, there is liberation through *prajñā*, which lacks the Dharma-body.

Discussing this in terms of the vertical progression: one is able to use the empty wisdom of *prajñā* to illuminate and perceive the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandhas*), thereby crossing over the suffering and distress of the afflictions of views and thought.
Yet they cannot thoroughly illuminate the Middle Way; therefore, they lack the Dharma-body.

The former ceases; its cessation induces cognition. The latter is cognition; cognition continues the cessation. Thus, the succession of arising and ceasing is the path of saṃsāra. Shibi said:
"The preceding thought ceases and induces the succeeding cognition; the succeeding thought arises and continues the preceding cessation. This is the nature of arising and ceasing.
Non-interruption is precisely saṃsāra. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "Moment after moment they continue in succession, revolving and returning;
all manner of grasping and rejecting are saṃsāra. I say that although the arising of faults differs [from the arising of afflictions], the binding of faults and saṃsāra are one and the same.
What is now called "knowing" does not require knowing that one knows; it is simply knowing.

The former [passage] already excluded what is not [the case], while the present text clarifies what is. As for the term "knowing," it refers merely to a single, numinous clarity of solitary knowing, devoid of subject and object, and transcending all relativity.
Thus, the preceding does not connect with the ceasing, and the succeeding does not give rise to it. The preceding and succeeding are severed and discontinuous;
in the interim, it stands alone. Know this simply as such. As for "knowing": it exists without the preceding connecting with the ceasing, and it knows without the succeeding giving rise to it.
The former ceases and the latter is known; there is neither interruption nor continuity. The wondrous essence in the interim is spiritually solitary and self-contained.
Without regard for its own substance, it vanishes in accordance with the moment. Once the essence of knowing has already ceased, one is suddenly enlightened as if entrusting oneself to the void.
Shibei said: "If you look back, you again fall into subject and object; if you do not look back, it is like leaning against the great void.

After a brief moment of profound stillness, one perceives only that there is nothing to be attained. This very perception of non-perception—this awareness that is without awareness—is what distinguishes one from wood or stone."
Suddenly it is like empty space; what, then, can be attained? It is not that there is a total absence of awareness, nor is it that there is a total presence of awareness.
Rather, it is awareness itself being without awareness—this is the awareness of non-awareness. Therefore, it is distinct from wood or stone.

This is the state of the initial mind. It is dark and silent, with all discursive thought severed; for a moment it is like that of a dead person. Subject and object are suddenly forgotten, and even the slightest conditions are completely purified.

People take discursive thought to be their very self; when discursive thought is severed, they are like the dead. This is merely a temporary cessation of the afflictions of the mundane world, occurring for a brief moment.
It is thus. It is not like those who die forever; if one were to die forever, one would enter nirvana—would that not be joyful?
I privately maintain that at the very moment of first resolving for enlightenment, one achieves perfect awakening and accomplishes the body of wisdom, not through awakening by means of another.

With a single thought, one turns the light back upon itself and is identical to what was originally attained. Only through the sudden awakening of perfect cultivation can one leap directly beyond, transcending both subject and object.
Suddenly forgotten; every subtle speck of dust is utterly purified.
It is profoundly still and empty, as if one were without cognition. Yet this nature of non-cognition is different from wood or stone;
it is simply that there is no deliberate thinking, not that there is no true knowing. Therefore, the nature of non-cognition is distinct from wood and stone.
This is the point for beginners; it is difficult to comprehend.
This concludes the preceding intent; it is difficult for those newly learning to understand.
It is the continuation of *śamatha*.
When entering the initial stage of the mind, three [states] should not be present: first, the unwholesome, which refers to contemplating the causes and conditions of the five worldly desires;

second, the wholesome, which refers to contemplating various mundane virtuous matters; and third, the indeterminate, which refers to neither contemplating the wholesome nor the unwholesome, remaining in a state of silent, dull stagnation.
Regarding these three kinds of mindfulness: speaking of them briefly, the first exists in evil persons, the second in good persons, and the third in neutral persons.
Speaking of them further, all three exist in all people; they differ only in degree.
Since they all constitute obstacles to the Path, one should eliminate them.
Furthermore, for a person first cultivating the mind, after entering the gate, they must recognize five types of mindfulness: first, intentional arising; second, habitual practice;
third, continuity; fourth, distinct arising; and fifth, immediate stillness.
This is a general indication; the following provides the detailed explanation.
"Arising thought" refers to the arising of mental reflection upon the five worldly desires as well as various virtuous matters.
"Habitual recollection" refers to remembering through the absence of deliberate intent, suddenly reflecting upon matters such as good and evil. "Continuous mindfulness" refers to...
Through long-standing habituation, thoughts suddenly arise; one perceives the mind wandering and scattering, yet fails to restrain it, allowing it to continue as before.

When contemplation does not remain stable and another thought arises, this means one recognizes that the preceding thought was distracted. Thereupon, one immediately gives rise to a sense of shame and remorse, along with a mind of repentance and reform.
"Immediately entering stillness" means that at the very moment of first sitting, one no longer contemplates worldly matters such as good, evil, or the indeterminate;
because one exerts effort in this very state, it is called "immediately entering stillness."
The first three moments of mindfulness are the same as the previous two; they differ only in that they lack the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state.
Regarding the single moment of habitual practice, it occurs frequently among beginners. Two moments arise due to continuity, which occurs for those who are indolent.
A separate single moment arises for those with a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*). A single moment of stillness arises for those who are diligent.
The latter two moments of thought are indeed as definitively determined.

As for the former three moments of thought, while they may be so on the surface, when examined more closely, there are those for whom the first three moments of the initial resolve are suddenly eliminated, and there are those who, having practiced for a long time, experience fluctuations that occur spontaneously.
In sum, this can be resolved by two statements: it exists for those who are indolent, but not for those who are diligent.
If one achieves perfect understanding and realizes that mindfulness is fundamentally empty, then one knows that illusion is itself liberation; no further expedient means need be employed.
If it is otherwise—like a gourd bobbing on water, turning and rolling in mutual dependence—what can be done?

Through habitual practice and continuity, thoughts arise and are produced separately; thus, the four [objects of] mindfulness constitute the illness, while the stilling of even one thought constitutes the medicine.
Although the medicine and the illness differ, they are collectively subsumed under the single term "mindfulness."
A separate thought arises; although it is judged to be a sickness, it is nonetheless a sickness within the medicine.
However, speaking in terms of its correspondence with a single thought-moment, it should not exist; yet, speaking in terms of the preceding four stages of breath-cultivation, it cannot be absent.
Thus, taking stillness as the medicine, one has not yet transcended thought. Although medicine treats illness, how does it compare to being without illness? Not using medicine is the ultimate cure.
Ah! Furthermore, as for both being termed "mindfulness" (念): this refers to the time of sitting meditation when the tranquil object is most appropriate.

Upon this object, one should contemplate it with stillness and illumination so as to become free from mindfulness. How much more so, then, when one has not yet abandoned mindfulness—how could this not still belong to the realm of mindfulness?
When these five thoughts come to rest, it is called "correspondence with a single thought. A "single thought" is the self-nature of numinous awareness.
Shibi said: "When the five thoughts have entirely ceased, a single thought manifests before one. This 'single thought' refers to non-thought. Non-...
A single thought of mindfulness is the very source of numinous awareness. As the Sūtra says: "One who quiets the mind and reaches the source is therefore called a śramaṇa.
Thus, the five types of mindfulness are the branches of this single thought, while this single thought is the root of the five.
Shibei said: "The five mindfulnesses do not exist apart from a single mindfulness, nor does a single mindfulness arise without depending upon the five mindfulnesses.
They are bound together as aspects of beginning and end that require one another; they should be understood as being no different from water and its waves."
Furthermore, when a single thought-moment arises in conjunction [with the mind], one must recognize six kinds of analytical distinctions: first, recognizing the illness;

second, recognizing the medicine; third, recognizing the remedy; fourth, recognizing the arising of faults; fifth, recognizing what is right and wrong; and sixth, recognizing the primary and auxiliary practices.
This has been briefly indicated above; the following text provides its own explanation.

First, regarding the "sick," there are two types: first, conceptualization (*ālambana*), and second, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). As for conceptualization, it refers to both wholesome and unwholesome thoughts.
Although they differ from one another, neither constitutes liberation; therefore, they are collectively categorized and termed "conceptualization. As for the indeterminate:
Although they do not take good, evil, or other such phenomena as their objects, both are nonetheless not the true mind; rather, they are merely states of dull stagnation.

These two types are called "illnesses. In the preceding passage, when illness was explained, there were three [aspects] that should not exist; now, furthermore, these three are condensed into two: namely, dullness and movement.
This is because they constitute the primary opposition between the medicine and the disease, namely alertness (*xing*) and stillness (*ji*).
Regarding the second medicine, there are also two kinds: first, stillness-within-stillness (*jijij*), and second, alertness-within-alertness (*xingxing*).

Stillness-within-stillness means not being mindful of external objects such as good or evil matters. Alertness-within-alertness means that the states of dullness, abiding in indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) consciousness, and so forth do not arise. These are the names of these two kinds.
As for medicine:

although the manifestations of disease are many, they do not lie outside the categories of emptiness and fullness; although the classes of medicinal substances are numerous, how could they exceed those of tonification and depletion?
Heaven and Earth produced them, and the King of Physicians followed this principle without erring by even a hair’s breadth.
Regarding the third, "antidotes" (pratipakṣa): one uses tranquility to counteract discursive thought, and clarity to counteract dull stagnation.
By employing these two medicines to overcome these two ailments, they are called "antidotes."

A skilled physician prescribes medicine based on the illness and likewise devises a treatment plan accordingly. Illness has causes that are either deficient or replete; medicine possesses powers of supplementation or depletion.

When one is muddled or stagnant and loses the reality [of the mind], one depletes it with clarity and alertness (*śamatha*). When one is distracted by discursive thought and loses oneself in toil, one supplements it with stillness and tranquility (*vipaśyanā*).
Tiantai said: "Cessation (*śamatha*) is the initial gateway for subduing the fetters; contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is for severing them."

Concentration is the essential means for dispelling delusion; tranquility is the excellent resource for nourishing the mind and consciousness; and insight is the wondrous technique for stimulating spiritual understanding.
How great is the King of Physicians! He may truly be called divine, sagely, and skillfully adept.

The fourth, the arising of faults (*doṣotpatti*), refers to the following: after a long period of stillness, a state of dull stagnation arises; after a long period of alertness, discursive conceptualization arises.
Because this is like a disease being provoked by medicine, it is called "the arising of faults."
One who practices the perfect cultivation must understand the faults of "breaking through" (po-guo). There is the case where that which can break through is not equal to that which is broken through;

this is like taking the medicine of tranquil clarity to treat the illness of delusion and distraction. There is also the case where that which can break through is equal to that which is broken through;

this is like tranquility giving rise to long-term dullness and stagnation, and clarity giving rise to long-term discursive thought and conceptualization. At the beginning, was this not indeed the power of breaking through? Now—
This would instead result in what is to be refuted.

Fifth, regarding the discernment of right and wrong: if one is silent and still yet lacks alertness, this is a state of dull stagnation; if one is alert yet lacks silence and stillness, [this is likewise a defect].
This is merely objectifying thought; it is neither alert nor tranquil. This is not only objectifying thought, but it also enters into a state of dullness and remains there.
That which is both tranquil and alert, which is not only vividly clear but also profoundly still—this is the wondrous nature that returns to the source.
Of these four lines, the first three are incorrect and the last one is correct; therefore, it is said: "Consciousness is [the Buddha]."
No. In the first three phrases, one either takes medicine and thereby creates illness, or the medicine and the illness do not correspond; thus, afflictions arise.
Only in the fourth phrase does one take medicine because of the illness; when the medicine takes effect, the illness is cured, and the primal spirit becomes full.
It is real; furthermore, its essence and function are not isolated from one another. Therefore, it is called the wondrous nature that returns to the source.
Regarding the sixth point, the primary and the auxiliary: taking alertness (*xingxing*) as the primary and stillness (*jiji*) as the auxiliary—these two matters are inseparable in their essence.
Discussing these two dharmas: in terms of essence (*tǐ*), they are both essence; in terms of function (*yòng*), they are both function. This is spoken with reference to their mutual necessity.
If one discusses essence and function in terms of stillness and arousal, would it not be that quiescence (*jì*) is the essence and alertness (*xīng*) is the function?
It is like the relationship between space and the sun: throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they illuminate equally.
At that time, space is not different from the sun, and the sun is not different from space; yet is it not the case that essence and function must necessarily coexist?
Nevertheless, while empty space is still, the sunlight is in motion. Is this not because space constitutes the essence and the sun constitutes the function? This is simply due to one...
When one takes mindful spiritual awareness as the sovereign, one cannot help but regard clarity as the essence and stillness as its function.
Furthermore, in the "Distinguishing the Partial from the Perfect" section, when discussing the three virtues, the dharma-body is again taken as the essence and prajñā as the function.
It is like a sick person who walks with the aid of a staff; walking is the primary action, while the staff serves as an assistance.
When such a sick person wishes to walk, they must first take up the staff before they can proceed.
This can be understood through the preceding analogy.
It is likewise for one who cultivates the mind: first, one must cease discursive thinking so that the mind becomes tranquil;

next, one should maintain alertness so as not to fall into dullness, ensuring the mind is vividly clear. This state of being both vividly clear and tranquil is called a single essence; they are no longer different.

At that time, the essence of the mind is fundamentally quiescent; it is through the conditions of discursive thought that weariness arises. The nature of principle is fundamentally luminous; it is through the conditions of deluded activity that drowsiness arises.
Now, if one wishes to restore [the mind] from this weariness and agitation, it will not be effective without profound stillness; and as for drowsiness, it cannot be overcome without alertness.
Neither is sufficient on its own; the two require one another, and neither can be dispensed with. However, there is a sequence in their application and a distinction in their therapeutic function.

Since this treatise concerns the initial entry into the gates of meditative concentration, it must begin by discarding worldly afflictions. Therefore, the cessation of discursive thought must be prioritized.
