It is like a sick person who wishes to walk; it is impossible without a staff. At the very moment of walking, one is able to proceed by relying on the staff.
It is the same with the person performing the function: the distinct and the quiescent cannot exist at different times. Although there are two names, their substance is not separate.
Shibei said: "Vigilance is like walking; stillness is like leaning on a staff. These two must complement one another;
*śamatha* is held in the hand. He further said: "Discursive thought is a sickness; indeterminate states (*avyākṛta*) are also a sickness. Stillness is the medicine; vigilance is also the medicine.
Stillness destroys discursive thought, while vigilance treats indeterminate states. Stillness gives rise to indeterminate states, while vigilance gives rise to discursive thought. Stillness..."
Although one can use *xingxing* (alertness) to remedy chaotic thoughts, it may in turn give rise to neutral states (*avyākṛta*).

Although one can use *xingxing* to remedy these neutral states, it may in turn give rise to chaotic thoughts. Therefore it is said: "Alertness within stillness is correct; neutral stillness is not. Stillness within alertness is correct;
alertness within chaotic thought is not. Stillness serves as an aid; alertness is the primary practice. Reflect upon this.

These six sections—classifications, general principles, diagnosing illnesses, identifying medicines, counteracting [afflictions], the arising of errors, and the primary and auxiliary [teachings]—enable the student to master each prescription and remedy.
By applying them with adaptability according to the specific circumstances, there will be no failure to achieve efficacy.
Furthermore, following this analytical clarification, it is necessary to clearly recognize the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
Shibi says: "The purpose of this passage follows from what was stated previously: that the self-nature of numinous awareness (*lingzhi*) is the single thought-moment.

Fearing that those of shallow learning might fail to realize that the single thought-moment is non-thought (*wunian*), and that this non-thought which is itself thought is the self-nature of numinous awareness, they instead mistakenly identify [it with something else]."
To claim that there is a "knowing" which exists because of conditions and objects is to speak of a "spiritual knowing. Such a view is profoundly erroneous.
Therefore, this text refutes it by means of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Specifically, that which discriminates vividly and is associated with clear consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); that which experiences and receives [objects] within the mind is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

The aggregates (*skandha*): the mind taking this principle as its object is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) operating upon this principle is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
and that which defiles the true principle is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The meaning of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) is twofold: first, the five aggregates of birth-and-death;

second, the five aggregates of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). The five aggregates of birth-and-death exist within the nine realms. The five aggregates of the nature of phenomena are realized only by the Buddhas. Furthermore, the five aggregates of birth-and-death are also of two kinds:

the five aggregates of segmented existence (pariccheda), which exist among the six classes of ordinary beings; and the five aggregates of transformational existence (nirmāṇa), which exist among the three types of sages.
The five aggregates of the segmented [existence] are further divided into two types: the five aggregates of a single lifetime, which exist as the fruition of karmic retribution;

and the five aggregates of a single moment, which exist as objects of mental apprehension and deliberation (*ālambana*). What is analyzed in the present text refers precisely to these five aggregates of mental apprehension and deliberation. These serve as the cause for [the arising of deluded thoughts].

A single lifetime constitutes the fruit. If one has not yet escaped this, how can one accord with numinous awareness? If one does not accord with numinous awareness, how can one transcend birth and death?
Therefore, it is necessary to recognize this [delusion] and shatter it.
These five aggregates (pañca-skandha), in their entirety, are but a single thought-moment (ekakṣaṇa). This single thought-moment, in its entirety, is completely the five aggregates.
Taken as a whole, they reside within a single thought-moment; when differentiated, they are divided into form (rūpa) and mind (citta).
Seeing clearly within this single thought that there is no sovereign master, one possesses the wisdom of emptiness.
Since people take the notion of a sovereign master as their fundamental meaning, seeing this absence of a master brings one into accord with the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
To see [all things] as like illusions and transformations is precisely the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Since "phenomena" takes the aggregates (*skandhas*) as its referent, seeing them as illusory and transformative brings one into accord with the emptiness of phenomena.
Therefore, you must recognize these five contemplations as well as the sixfold analysis; I hope you will not disdain them.
Shibei said: "Those who do not see it regard it as mere weeds and brush. If one does not provide a detailed demonstration, how can students know?
It is like taking pure gold: one clearly identifies the rubble and counterfeit jewels and discards them all; even if one does not recognize the gold itself, [the impurities are removed]."
The golden essence manifests of itself; why worry that it cannot be attained?
At the beginning, gold and sand are mixed together; in the middle, the sand is sifted out and the gold remains; in the end, there is only gold and no sand.
If one can simply remove the sand until it is exhausted, even if one does not recognize the gold, the golden essence will manifest of itself. Contemplate this by applying the analogy to the Dharma.
This can be known from the *Vipaśyanā-gāthā*.
In the Sanskrit language, *vipaśyanā* means "contemplation" (*guan*). To explain it vertically, its meaning corresponds to the provisional (*prajñapti*); to explain it horizontally...

To speak of this: the meaning [of the Three Truths] opens up the three contemplations, namely emptiness (śūnyatā), the provisional (prajñapti), and the middle (madhyama). For now, I shall explain them vertically. There is the sense of illumination and the sense of the provisional.

Furthermore, there are three names for contemplation: the contemplation that penetrates, the contemplation that reaches through, and the contemplation that is non-contemplation. These are explained in detail in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* within the section on "Explaining Names, Substance, and Characteristics."
Now, objects are not understood apart from wisdom, and wisdom does not arise apart from objects. Objects consist of both phenomena and principle;
wisdom is likewise the same. To understand the phenomenal objects of the world and to realize that they arise through correct causes and conditions is conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
To understand that the essence of causes and conditions is fundamentally empty—devoid of person and self—is the wisdom of true emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā-jñāna*). To understand that emptiness is...

"Entering the provisional" refers to the wisdom of entering the provisional, which consists in knowing the illness and identifying the medicine. "Thoroughly penetrating the two extremes" means that they are simply the Middle Way; this is the wisdom of the Middle Observation (*madhyamaka*).
Now, in clarifying the object and the wisdom, it is said for the time being that conditioned co-arising is itself emptiness, establishing this as the supramundane wisdom of emptiness.

Therefore, the subsequent text merely states that "the nature of dependent origination is emptiness" and that "form is itself emptiness," establishing these as the initial steps for cultivating the mind.
By citing one case as an example for the other two, what need is there to explain them all? Now, the myriad phenomena of the universe are shared by all upon this broad earth;
whether one realizes this or not is the distinction between the wise and the foolish. To be foolish is to drift along with sensory objects.
The flow gives rise to the discrimination of objective conditions; because it arises again and again, it is called "birth. This birth serves as the cause of the cycle of birth and death.
Wisdom, however, observes dependent origination and thereby restrains it; it realizes the emptiness and vacuity of the nature of things.
Though there is existence, it is not existent; this constitutes the path to Nirvana. In this way, object and wisdom rely upon one another, through which they are both understood and brought forth.
When cognition arises, it arises by means of apprehending an object; when the object is apprehended, cognition arises and apprehends.
When the object has not yet been apprehended, cognition ultimately does not arise; when cognition has not yet arisen, the object ultimately is not apprehended.
Therefore, one knows that the arising of cognition occurs only after the object is apprehended, and the apprehension of the object occurs only because of cognition.
Wisdom arises and realizes. This realization has nothing to realize. Realization arises from the object; yet that which gives rise to it has no power to give rise.
If the object were not empty, it could not be realized; if so, how could the arising of wisdom realize it?
Now, since wisdom arises and realizes, the object is fundamentally empty from the beginning, and thus there is realization without anything to be realized. If wisdom were not empty...
If it could arise, then how could the object be what brings about its cognition? Now, since cognition arises while the object is already cognized, wisdom is fundamentally empty of itself;
thus, that which arises has no power to cause its own arising.
That which gives rise has no power to give rise; though it is wisdom, it is not existent. That which is realized has nothing to be realized; though it is an object, it is not non-existent.
If there were a power to give rise, then wisdom would belong to existence. If there were something to be realized, then the object would belong to non-existence.
Since there is no power to give rise, wisdom is not existent. Since there is nothing to be realized, the object is not non-existent. It is neither existent nor non-existent.
Then the object is empty and the wisdom is quiescent; being both empty and existent, the object is pure and the wisdom is luminous.
Non-existence is not non-existent, and existence is not existent. When existence and non-existence are simultaneously illumined, the wondrous awakening is serene and detached.
Regarding the mutual clarification of existence and non-existence concerning the object and wisdom discussed above:

it is not that there is a separate existence apart from non-existence, nor a separate non-existence apart from existence. It is simply that non-existence is itself not non-existent, and existence is itself not existent.
That which is non-existent is not non-existent; non-existence is itself existence. That which is existent is not existent; existence is itself non-existence.
Since the beginning is thus a double negation, the end is a double illumination. Through such wondrous awakening, the myriad burdens vanish into thin air.

Just as fire becomes even more fiercely blazing when it obtains fuel, the fuel is a metaphor for the many objects that give rise to wisdom, and the fire is a comparison for the sublime wisdom that cognizes those objects.
Shi Bi said: "True wisdom illuminates objects like fire burning fuel. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Form is great; Prajñā is also [great]."
Great! Its words say: "To realize the emptiness of nature is not bondage; though relying on the provisional, one does not cling.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Failing to realize that objects are but mind, one gives rise to various kinds of discrimination. If one gives rise to discrimination, then [one is bound]."
One is bound by objects. Once one realizes that objects are merely mind, conceptual discrimination no longer arises. When discrimination does not arise, one is no longer bound by objects.
To realize that all is but emptiness is to reverse this process; thus, although one may still perceive provisional objects, [one remains unbound].
Furthermore, the mind remains unattached.
It simultaneously illuminates both existence and non-existence; the mind of the Middle Way is thus clearly manifest.
To realize the emptiness of nature is to illuminate emptiness. To accord with the wondrous provisional is to illuminate existence. This is simultaneous illumination. Having realized emptiness...

One reaches [the truth] by means of conditions that are provisional. These conditions that are provisional arise from the realization of emptiness; this is the simultaneous negation [of both extremes].
This simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination is established within the perfect Middle Way.
If wisdom comprehends an object, that is precisely the emptiness of the object within wisdom.
This does not mean that wisdom arises because the object does not exist; rather, it means that when wisdom arises, it arises by comprehending the object.
This is because wisdom is able to comprehend emptiness only because the object is fundamentally empty from the outset, such that wisdom can subsequently comprehend its emptiness.
"Just as the eye perceives that flowers are empty, this perceiving of the emptiness of flowers is the eye itself.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The seeing and the conditions for seeing, together with the perceived appearances, are like flowers in the sky; fundamentally, they do not exist at all."
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "To know that these are like flowers in the sky is to be free from the cycle of transmigration. The meaning of these two sūtras is clear;
one may thus apply the metaphor directly to the Dharma.
If wisdom realizes wisdom, this is precisely the emptiness of wisdom.
Although wisdom realizes that objects are empty, the wisdom itself remains and is not yet realized. It is like lighting a fire from wood: when the fuel is exhausted, the wood still remains;
once all the fuel has been consumed, the wood also naturally perishes. Thus, having already realized the emptiness of objects, one further uses wisdom to realize that very wisdom.
To thus realize the wisdom of wisdom is what is called "the wisdom that knows emptiness."
Just as the eye perceives that the eye is empty—this being the perception of the emptiness of the eye—the application of this principle to other phenomena can be understood accordingly.

Although wisdom perceives that objects are empty and perceives that wisdom itself is empty, it is not the case that there is no wisdom that perceives objects; while the objects are empty, wisdom still persists.
This restates and concludes the first section. Although that which is observed is empty, that which observes still remains.
When one realizes that both object and wisdom are empty, there is no longer an object or wisdom that is not realized.
"Realizing that both object and wisdom are empty" concludes that both object and wisdom are equally empty; "there is no longer an object or wisdom that is not realized" means that...
In general, it can be said that if one is able to do so, then although there is neither object nor subject, there is nothing that is not understood.

It is like the eye perceiving that the flower is empty and perceiving that the eye itself is empty; it is not that there is no understanding of the flower and the eye, for the flower, the emptiness, and the eye still exist.
When one realizes that the flower is empty, the eye is also empty; if the flower is not realized as empty, the eye is not realized.
The first two lines illustrate that both the objective realm and the cognition thereof are empty. The third and fourth lines reiterate the error of failing to realize the observing cognition.
The fifth and sixth lines clarify the correctness of the emptiness of both realm and cognition. To realize the flower is the [realization of the] realm.
It is emptiness. When the eye is empty, wisdom is empty. That the eye does not perceive flowers is a metaphor for the absence of objects and the absence of wisdom;
there is likewise no non-perception.
Furthermore, all phenomena are entirely dependent upon causes and conditions. That which is produced by causes and conditions is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Intrinsic nature" refers to the quality of phenomena arising from themselves. People do not understand this and cling to the notion that things arise from themselves.
If effects could indeed arise from themselves, they would not require causes and conditions. When examined through correct reasoning, no such thing exists in the world.

Regarding the statement that "not a single dharma arises apart from causes and conditions": for example, visual consciousness arises internally from the sense organ (the eye) and externally from the objective field (visible forms).
When these two are combined, consciousness arises between them. Apart from these two, visual consciousness fundamentally does not exist.
Is it not therefore the case that the eye as consciousness lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? Since its arising lacks intrinsic nature, its nature is empty. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
"Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I say they are empty. To investigate the emptiness of intrinsic nature, these two phrases are required.

If one wishes to contemplate within the perspective of the provisional (parikalpita), there are further the latter two phrases: namely, "they are also called provisional names," and "they are also the meaning of the Middle Way.
This is the essential tenet of the Tiantai school's transmitted tradition. Recently, some have said: "If one relies on the intent of the teachings..."

Generally speaking, every verse consists of four lines to establish its meaning. That the Wise One (the Buddha) divided these into three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) seems like an unnecessary elaboration.

I say this: if the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*) are attained within a single moment of mind, this also originates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; how could Nāgārjuna also be guilty of such elaboration?

Furthermore, scriptures such as the *Ratnakūṭa*, *Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-uttaratantra* (or *Yingluo jing*), *Awakening of Faith* (*Nirvikalpa-samādhi-sūtra*), and *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* all clarify the three [wisdoms].
Consider this: if it were as you have refuted, then even the sincere words from the golden mouth of Śākyamuni would be rendered redundant.
One who acts as a patriarch must possess at least one eye of the Dharma; otherwise, one cannot avoid being like Xu Liu, who went off with only one shoulder of a wooden board.
If one phenomenon is thus, all phenomena are likewise.
Among all phenomena, there is none that exists with an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) apart from arising through causes and conditions.
Since object and wisdom follow one another, how could they not be quiescent?

Wisdom is empty because it illuminates objects; objects are quiescent because they are realized by wisdom. These two dharmas follow one another, such that both subject and object vanish together. Why is this?
Because the nature of phenomena arising from causes and conditions is without differentiation.
Although phenomena arising from causes and conditions possess distinctions, the nature of causes and conditions is fundamentally without distinction.
For example, although waves may have a thousand variations, the nature of water is non-dual. This non-dual nature is precisely the true nature.

The present cycle of the three realms, the ascent and descent through the six paths, the distinction between the pure and the defiled, suffering and joy, and the differences between the ordinary and the holy—
all clearly demonstrate that there are distinctions within the dharma of causes and conditions.

All [karmic results] arise from the three types of action, the four modes of deportment, and the objects encountered by the six sense faculties. According to one's inclinations, one creates karma, and thus the retributions differ:
through goodness one experiences happiness; through evil one experiences suffering.
This clarifies the origins of the distinctions among causes and conditions.
Therefore, a sutra states: "Good and evil are the causes; suffering and pleasure are the fruits.
This can be understood by citing such scriptural evidence.
One should know that phenomena have no fixed characteristics; they are assembled according to conditions. Since conditions do not belong to a self, they are said to be empty of intrinsic nature.
Because they are empty, they are not distinct [from one another]; all phenomena are thusness.
Consider, for instance, the four great elements: insentient beings conglomerate them to form mountains and peaks; sentient beings conglomerate them to form physical bodies;
through precepts and goodness, they conglomerate them to become humans or devas; and through wickedness and rebellion, they conglomerate them to become ghosts or animals.
Is this not because dharmas have no fixed characteristics, but are constructed according to conditions? Sentient thoughts are fundamentally empty; sin and merit have no master. One—
All natures are empty. What, then, is not suchness?
Therefore, a sutra says: "Form is itself emptiness; the same applies to the other four aggregates.
Form is illusory form, and emptiness is true emptiness. When deluded, one takes all true emptiness to be illusory form; when awakened, it is entirely...
Illusory forms realize true emptiness.
If this is so, then why should it be only the ordinary beings who arise through conditions? Even the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles all exist through conditions.
Shibi said: "The dependent origination of the ten realms is divided into two parts: ordinary beings and sages. The six destinies are defiled conditions; the four noble ones are pure conditions."
Although defilement and purity differ, their dependent origination is the same; it is like clear water and turbid water—their waves and moisture are no different.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions."

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions; for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught. This means that for śrāvakas, the Four Noble Truths are the condition-arising;
for pratyekabuddhas, the twelve links of dependent origination are the condition-arising; for bodhisattvas, the six perfections are the condition-arising;
and for the Buddha-realm, the Buddha-vehicle—the great white ox-cart—is the condition-arising. Furthermore, one must understand this clearly.
The Avataṃsaka [Sūtra] is able to manifest the ten dharma-realms in accordance with defiled or pure conditions.

Only through the principle that "the unchanging follows conditions, yet while following conditions it remains unchanging" does one truly accord with the school of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Therefore, when the myriad affairs of state converge in profusion, for one who realizes this, there is nothing that is not a *dharma-śālā* (place of practice).

In daily life, whenever encountering conditions or facing objects, everything is a phenomenon born of causes and conditions; yet that which is born of conditions lacks inherent nature, being entirely empty in its very essence.
This total emptiness is itself the *śānti-mārga-śālā* (the tranquil place of the path), the true site of *araṇya* (solitude). Thus, one who can realize this—
What, then, could there be that is not *bodhi*? Form and appearance (*rūpa*) are boundless;
for one who awakens to them, there is nothing that is not *prajñā*.
Since the objective realm relies upon wisdom to be integrated, and wisdom follows the realm to pervade it, form and appearance pervade the *dharmadhātu*, and thus *prajñā*...
It also pervades the entire dharma-realm. What was previously called the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the principle of the originally existing dharmakāya;
what is now called "prajñā" refers to the wisdom of the bodhi realized through cultivation. When object and wisdom are perfectly interfused, this principle is established.
By means of the trap one catches the fish; thus, empty words are not in vain. This has already been clarified in the previous section on pervasive perfection.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Because form is boundless, one should know that prajñā is also boundless.
Were it not for the realization that the object constitutes wisdom, how could both be made boundless?
Why is this? It is not that the object is not known because it is not wisdom, nor that wisdom does not arise because it is not the object.
When wisdom arises, it knows the object; when the object is known, wisdom arises and knows. Wisdom arises and knows, yet there is nothing to be known.
It knows the object and thus arises, yet its arising has no agent of arising.
Reiterating the preceding text to clarify the principle that there is nothing that is not the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) regarding Prajñā:
when there is no "producer" of birth, internal wisdom is profoundly still; when there is nothing to be "realized," external objects are as they truly are (*tathatā*).
The internal wisdom is fundamentally quiescent; that it is not quiescent is due to the fault of failing to realize the emptiness of objects. External objects are fundamentally suchness;
that they are not suchness is due to the fault of lacking the wisdom capable of realization. If one understands that birth is incapable of producing anything, [then one has realized this].
There is nothing to be realized; how could there be any wisdom that is not quiescent, or any object that is not suchness?
As quiescence is without differentiation, object and wisdom are darkly one.

The suchness of the object is the suchness of wisdom; the quiescence of wisdom is the quiescence of the object. They have been a single essence from the beginning; now, one awakens to the fact that arising is non-arising.
Birth is realized as being without realization; object and wisdom are merged in one, like a silent stillness without distinction.
Thus, the Dharma-body and Prajñā are darkly united and indivisible.
All myriad burdens are utterly extinguished, and the wondrous principle remains.
Tiantai said: "Direct liberation is not [mere] liberation; true liberation must necessarily possess the Dharmakāya and Prajñā.

This is entirely due to the perfect interfusion of object and wisdom, such that the subject and object are non-dual. Thus, one is able to transcend the mundane world and overcome all burdens, soaring high on the wings of wisdom."
Therefore, a sutra says: "Prajñā is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know. Thus, this wondrous principle is not knowing;
it knows by means of non-knowing.
Although Prajñā employs knowing as its function, if one retains that knowing, it is not true Prajñā. Only...
That which is non-knowing yet knows all that can be known—such knowing is to know through non-knowing.
*Upaśama* (Sanskrit):
*Upaśama* here means "cessation and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). It is also called the "wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way. It resides within cessation and contemplation.

This belongs to the inclusion within the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun). It is precisely the aforementioned two contemplations: it is vertical while being horizontal, and horizontal while being vertical;
it is both the simultaneous negation and illumination, and neither negation nor illumination.

Now, as for the stabilization of chaos and the divergence of paths, the source of movement and stillness is not dual. As for the separation between the foolish and the wise, the root of clarity and darkness is not different.
Movement and stillness, clarity and darkness—these are the ailments. That which gives rise to the stabilization of chaos and the divergence of the foolish and wise are all but tributary streams.
Examining their source and root, there is none that does not arise from the nature of clarity and stillness.
Observing their branches and tributaries, they all appear different; observing their source and root, they are all the same. When one is ignorant and deluded, one follows the flow and drifts away:

through stillness, confusion arises; through clarity, agitation arises. When wisdom awakens, one traces the flow back to its source: by breaking through agitation, one achieves stillness; by breaking through [delusion], one returns to clarity.

Taking darkness for light. Therefore, wishing to clarify the principle that *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) are non-dual, [this text] designates the sources of the states of darkness, movement, and light.

Among the masses who are deluded, they follow darkness and turn their backs on light; they abandon stillness to seek movement. Among the multitudes who have attained awakening, they turn their backs on movement and follow stillness; they abandon...
They seek illumination while remaining in darkness.

The multitude who are deluded are not without illumination; they simply turn their backs on illumination and follow darkness. They are not without stillness; they simply seek movement and abandon stillness.
This is why they are called ignorant and deluded. The multitude who have awakened are not without movement; they are able to turn their backs on movement and follow...
Stillness is not the absence of darkness; rather, it is the ability to relinquish darkness in order to seek illumination, which constitutes the awakening of wisdom.
When illumination arises, ignorance is transformed into prajñā; when stillness is established, distraction is stilled and samādhi is achieved.
How is it that clarity can transform ignorance into wisdom? How is it that stillness can quell distraction to form concentration?
It is because the source of movement and stillness is not two, and the root of light and darkness is not distinct. Therefore, one may be bound and one may be liberated.
Generally, one is turned by things, which leads to obscurity and agitation; yet if one can turn things, [one attains liberation].
Thus, it becomes stillness and clarity.
Stability is established by turning away from movement; wisdom arises by abandoning darkness.
Since stability is established by turning away from movement, one must not fail to turn away from movement. Since wisdom arises by abandoning [darkness], one must abandon it.
Darkness: thus, darkness must not fail to be relinquished.
Darkness and movement are bound together within the cage;
as for darkness and movement, why need they be rejected? It is because they are able to bind one to the cage of birth and death.
This is why. Stillness and clarity tend toward that which lies beyond phenomena;
since stillness and clarity already tend toward that which lies beyond the phenomena of affliction, what need is there for them to return?
Furthermore, that things cannot delude him is due to the efficacy of wisdom (*prajñā*); that distractions cannot move him is due to the efficacy of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
How can stillness and clarity be restored? How can concentration and wisdom be perfected? It is because, having attained the Great Substance, one is able to give rise to the Great Function.

As for its function: when the great function manifests before one, things cannot delude them and afflictions cannot disturb them. If one traces back to its cause from afar, its efficacy arises from *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Concentration and wisdom mutually support stillness and clarity; ignorance and distraction entwine each other in darkness and movement.
When concentration and wisdom support one another, the fundamental substance is still and clear; that which is still becomes ever more still, and that which is clear becomes ever more clear.
If ignorance and distraction entwine, the original mind is dark and agitated; that which is dark becomes ever darker, and that which is agitated...
Yet, the more one moves, the more one stirs.
One who can remain still amidst movement brings disorder to order. One who can attain clarity amidst darkness brings folly to wisdom.
Thus, there is no difference between the essence of darkness and movement; through this, stillness and clarity accord with the Way. The source of folly and chaos is likewise [non-differentiated].
They differ. In this regard, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) share the same principle.
That which is still amidst disorder is like empty space, which fundamentally possesses neither motion nor stillness. When the wind arises, there is motion; when the wind ceases, there is stillness.
Yet the wind also arises dependent upon space; thus it exists when the robe is brushed against it, but is absent when the garment hangs down. To brush [the robe]...
Its hanging down depends upon man; is this not precisely movement within stillness and stillness within movement?
That which is both darkness and light is also like empty space, which fundamentally has neither light nor darkness; when the sun rises, it is bright, and when the sun sets, it is dark.
Yet the sun also abides by depending upon space; thus, when it is uncovered, there is light, and when it is covered, there is darkness.

Whether it is uncovered or covered depends upon the person. Is this not the case where light itself becomes dark, and darkness itself becomes light? The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise so; this can be understood through synthesis. Therefore it is said:
"The essence of darkness and movement is without difference; the source of delusion and confusion is not [other than that]."
It is thus. In this way, stillness and clarity thereby unite with the Way; concentration and wisdom thus share the same source.
When the source is the same, there is unconditioned compassion; when there is concentration and wisdom, one is tranquil yet ever-illuminating.

When the essence [of samādhi and prajñā] is identical, concentration and wisdom are unified; this corresponds to the unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) of the Middle Way, wherein both concentration and wisdom are simultaneously forgotten.

When it concerns concentration and wisdom themselves, they are quiescent yet constantly illuminating; this corresponds to the compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*) and the compassion based on phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), wherein both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*) are simultaneously forgotten.

Quiescence while constantly illuminating constitutes the simultaneous granting [of both]; unconditional compassion constitutes the simultaneous taking away [of both]. Because of this simultaneous taking away, there is *upekṣā*;
because of this simultaneous granting, there is *vipaśyanā*.
"Bestowing both" refers to the twofold illumination of the Middle Way. "Withdrawing both" refers to the twofold negation of the Middle Way.
Thus, each of the three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā has its own corresponding counterpart.
By means of *śamatha*, although it is quiescent, it is constantly illuminating.
*Śamatha* carries the meaning of "calm. However, the essence of the *dharmatā* does not stand in isolation; therefore, although it is quiescent, it is constantly illuminating.
By means of vipaśyanā, although there is illumination, it is ever-quiescent.
Vipaśyanā carries the sense of contemplative observation; yet, the essence of dharmatā does not exist in isolation.
Therefore, although there is illumination, it is ever-quiescent.
Because of *ubhaya* (both), it is neither illumination nor stillness.
*Ubhaya* refers to the equality of cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). Since it is neither stillness nor illumination, it is simultaneously illumination and simultaneously stillness.
The present text, in order to reveal the Middle Way, provisionally speaks of its twofold negation.

Because it is constantly quiescent while illuminating, it is said that the conventional is identical to the ultimate. Because it is constantly illuminating while quiescent, it is said that the ultimate is identical to the conventional.
It is neither quiescent nor illuminating; thus, [the Buddha] remained silent at Vaiśālī.

This precisely concludes by returning to the three truths of the ultimate, the conventional, and the middle, thereby clarifying the three contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle that constitute our primary doctrine.
Therefore, although *śamatha* corresponds to cessation (*śamatha*), it is also termed the contemplation of emptiness; although *vipaśyanā* corresponds to...

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is also termed "contemplation of the provisional" (*jia-guan*). Although *ubhayatobhāga-vimokṣa* (liberation through both parts) pertains to both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is also termed "contemplation of the middle" (*zhong-guan*).

This is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) culminates in the ultimate, and its meaning reaches its limit in three aspects; this applies even to afflictions and bodhi, as well as to prajñā and nirvāṇa.
It is likewise limited to these three alone. Alas! The Great Way is luminous and clear, manifest to the ears and eyes; yet one hears it and does not believe, sees it and does not practice.
Thus, one wanders aimlessly without sight and willingly remains lame while gazing at the path—then there is truly nothing I can do for such a person.
○ The Tenth of the Ten Gates of Contemplating the Mind:
Furthermore, regarding the ten gates of contemplating the mind: first, it describes the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); second, it reveals the essence of the contemplation;
third, it speaks of its correspondence; fourth, it warns against arrogance; fifth, it cautions against negligence and indolence; sixth, it reiterates [the preceding points].

1. Contemplating the essence; 2. Contemplating the nature; 3. Contemplating the characteristics; 4. Contemplating the function; 5. Contemplating the substance; 6. Contemplating the principle; 7. Clarifying right and wrong; 8. Distinguishing the purport of the teachings; 9. Realizing contemplation in every encounter; 10.
Wondrously acceding with the primordial source.
Regarding the arising of the ten gates: in all practices of the hundredfold cultivation, one must first awaken to the reality of the principles of the Truths (*satya*) in order to enter the Way;

only then can one attain the essence of the contemplative gates and fully give rise to cultivation from within the nature (*prakṛti*). If one can cultivate in this manner, one will certainly attain resonance (*yoga*).
If there is no such resonance, then those who are diligent will fall into the error of overweening pride (*abhimāna*), while those who are indolent will lapse into negligence.

No. The previous presentation of the essence of contemplation was concise in expression yet comprehensive in meaning; this subsequent presentation of the essence of contemplation is complete in principle and exhaustive in dharma.
Only when the broad and the concise follow one another will there be a path for cultivation and a method for seeking the jewel.

Furthermore, I fear that in the cultivation of the mind, there may be many divergent paths, where some might mistake the non-true for the true, or take the true for the non-true. Among such matters of right and wrong, it is most appropriate [to clarify this].
Clearly understand that all gateways of meaning rely upon the expressed intent. Only when there is realization of this expressed intent does one accord with the Buddha-mind;

thus, every single practice-gateway is none other than perfect penetration. If it is so, then one encounters conditions on the left and right, and wherever delusion is encountered, it becomes contemplation.
One will not cling to contemplation at the expense of the ultimate intent, nor will one be confused about the principle by being bound to words.
First, regarding what is called "the nature of things" (*dharmatā*):
"the nature of things" means spontaneity. It refers to the fact that all phenomena are thus; their essence is naturally so. This is indeed the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The nature of things is unchanging while following conditions; all phenomena follow conditions by their very nature without undergoing change.

Now, the nature of the mind is empty and pervasive; the source of movement and stillness is non-dual. True Suchness (Tathatā) transcends thought; the notions of conditional calculation are no different from it.
The "nature of the mind" and "True Suchness" differ only in their terminology. "Empty and pervasive" describes its essential quality. This mind is True Suchness.
Throughout the three periods of time and across the ten directions, empty space is utterly devoid of a single thing; it is all-pervasive and free from the slightest obstruction.
It is like a great mass of fire to which nothing can approach from any side, incinerating all conceptual thoughts and conditioned shadows.

Therefore, it is said that the nature of the mind is void and penetrating, and true suchness transcends all deliberation. Nevertheless, we currently observe that sentient beings possess discursive thought and mental objects.
The mind moves when stirred and is still when at rest. Those who perceive the mind-nature and True Suchness as two distinct things do so because they are deluded and fail to awaken to themselves.
What is meant by "delusion"? And what is meant by "awakening"? One must know that there is no separate delusion;
delusion arises solely from the very place where the Buddhas have awakened. Likewise, there is no separate awakening. Furthermore—

Awakening is achieved precisely within the delusions of sentient beings. Therefore, if one traces all movement and stillness back to their source, they are no different from the source of the mind-nature’s empty penetration.
If one traces all conditional calculations back to their root, they are not distinct from the mind of True Suchness that transcends thought.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all..."

O Great Bodhisattva, within this self-abiding samādhi, you see that both the seer and the conditions for seeing, along with all perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and its conditions are originally the wondrous, tranquil, and luminous essence of bodhi.
How could there be "is" or "is not" within them? Thus, the nature of the mind is empty and pervasive; true suchness (tathatā) transcends all thought.
It is like a clear, cloudless sky; yet the conceptual thoughts and anxieties of sentient beings cause it to appear obscured and turbulent, much like pressing upon the eye and seeing phantom flowers.
When one presses the eye and the flowers appear, are there actually flowers? Or are there no flowers at all?
Is there, then, truly arising and ceasing, motion and stillness? Or is there truly no arising and ceasing, motion and stillness?
Yet, the flower is emptiness, and emptiness is the flower. This is like motion and stillness being the void-penetrating nature of the mind;

and conditioned conceptualization being the transcendence of thought within True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore it is said: "This seeing and its conditions are fundamentally the wondrous purity of Bodhi."
This is the luminous essence. How could there be "is" or "is not" within it? If one clarifies this meaning, its purport becomes radiant.
When deluded views proliferate and race about, if one exhaustively investigates them, they are found to be nothing but a single, profound stillness.
This uses present phenomena to verify the aforementioned principle.

If the source of movement and stillness were distinct from the vacuous penetration of the mind-nature, and if the thoughts of conceptual attachment were different from the true suchness (tathatā) that transcends deliberation, why would this be so?

For if deluded views proliferate and run wild, when one employs the methods of contemplation to exhaust and investigate them, these very deluded views dissolve and melt away in their own place; there is only this One.
It is quiescent and empty yet true. To verify this through such evidence, one knows it is certainly not false.
The numinous source has no form; when reflected upon, it appears in a thousand differences.
This "numinous source" is precisely what was described above as the essence of the mind-nature, the *tathatā*. It is called "empty and penetrating" because—

It is because of the cessation of discursive thought (*cintā*). Therefore, it is said to be "without form" (*a-rūpa*). When movement and stillness, as well as the conditions for conceptualization, have not yet taken form, it is like a mirror on a stand reflecting objects without error;
nothing can escape its form. Is this not so because the nature of mind is empty and pervasive, and true suchness (*tathatā*) is beyond discursive thought?
The first phrase verifies that the source from which thoughts arise is identical [to the nature of mind]; the second phrase verifies that freedom from thought is a vast illumination.
Though there are a thousand differences, the name "Dharma-eye" is established; though they are one in stillness and not distinct, the title "Wisdom-eye" persists.
When both principle and measure are simultaneously extinguished, the function of the "Buddha-eye" is fully realized.
This is because the great function of the fruition-virtue manifests before one; it clarifies that all is inherently possessed within the causal mind of sentient beings.
Just as the Dharma-eye can discern the conventional, this is entirely due to the source of the causal mind being formless; yet when discerned, it appears in its thousandfold differences.

Just as the Wisdom-eye can illuminate the ultimate truth, this is entirely due to the deluded perceptions of the causal mind racing about in confusion; yet when investigated, it is found to be nothing but—
First is Quiescence. That the merit of the Buddha-eye reaches its ultimate perfection is entirely due to the single quiescence of the causal mind:

the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and the wisdom of phenomena (*jñeya-jñāna*) which, in their thousandfold differences, are both dissolved and attained therein. This is what is meant by "the cause transcending the ocean of fruition" and "the fruition penetrating to the source of the cause."
Therefore, the three truths are a single realm; the principle of the Dharmakāya is eternally pure. The three wisdoms are a single mind; the illumination of Prajñā constantly shines.
Realm and wisdom merge in profound stillness, while the response of liberation accords with capacities. Neither vertical nor horizontal, the Way of the Perfect *I* is fundamentally unified.
Thus we know that the wondrous nature of the three virtues is perfectly harmonious without any discord.

What has been explained above is indeed a discourse on the fundamental meaning; yet it is better to discard the literary form to grasp the substance and conclude by returning to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

This is precisely the non-duality of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*), a concise demonstration of the partial and the perfect. Within the correct cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this is the profound and essential goal:
the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) as the single realm of the three truths, and the Prajñā as the single mind of the three wisdoms. Herein, realm and wisdom merge in silent harmony.

This is the liberation [attained by] unifying them. Indeed, the Way of the Perfect *i* (the character for "three") is neither vertical nor horizontal precisely because the object of contemplation belongs to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This is one truth within the perfect middle of the three truths (*triratna*). It is like that single, most supreme dot at the center of the circle.
However, as for this truth, because raising one immediately entails the three, it is directly the Dharma-body rather than merely the Dharma-body. This is because...
The Dharma-body necessarily possesses both prajñā and liberation, because within this Middle Truth, the ultimate and the conventional are one.
The contemplation that is able to observe belongs to prajñā; it corresponds to one of the three contemplations of the "True Emptiness" (zhēn-kōng).
It is like the single dot on the left side of a circle. Since this first contemplation embodies the three by raising up the one, it is directly prajñā and not non-prajñā.
If Prajñā-pāramitā necessarily possesses the Dharmakāya and liberation, it is because this contemplation of emptiness is simultaneously provisional (prajñapti) and the Middle Way.
When subject and object merge in profound stillness, it belongs to liberation; at this stage of the three liberations, it belongs to the "liberation of skillful means" (upāya-śuddha-vimukti).

This is analogous to the single dot on the right side of a circle. Since this first liberation is "one that raises the one and thereby includes the three," it is not merely "direct liberation" (mukhya-vimukti).
Liberation. Liberation necessarily possesses the Dharma-body and Prajñā, because this very liberation is itself the Dharma-body and Prajñā.
To point directly and intimately to it: it is the single thought-moment of the present person, wherein all phenomena are inherently complete.
The distinctions between the primary and secondary [realms] are liberation; their abiding within that single thought-moment without differentiation is Prajñā.
That which is a single thought-moment is all phenomena; that which is all phenomena is a single thought-moment.
This is the Dharmakāya, which is the object of contemplation. That which is able to contemplate these three is Prajñā.
When the subject and object merge in profound stillness, transcending both thought and discourse, this is Vimukti.
The single mind is profound, vast, and inconceivable. What essential path could there be that is not this?
That which is the profound and vast single mind extends vertically through time and horizontally across space;

there is no state of mind that is not the threefold wisdom, no object that is not the threefold virtue, and no sensory realm that is not the threefold liberation. Thus it is subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of thought. Upon encountering it—

Objects encountered in the environment are none other than the essential means for transcending birth and death. With every step taken and every thought arising, how could one not enter the path to Bodhi?
Therefore, those who take the mind itself as the Way may be said to have found the source by following the current.
Sentient beings arise from the truth into delusion, like water flowing from its source. Practitioners return from delusion to the truth, like tracing a stream back to its source.
Therefore, for those who practice well and enter the flow, it is precisely by remaining within the flow that they attain the source.
To return before one has gone far is like abandoning the current to seek the source separately; the further one seeks, the more distant one becomes.

The "current" is the single thought of the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*); the "source" is the single thought of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way (*śūnyatā-pratītyasamutpāda-madhyamā*).
Therefore, it is said that "taking the mind as the Way" can be described as seeking the source by following the current.
Second, regarding the emergence of the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): it is simply knowing that a single thought-moment is both empty and not empty, neither empty nor not empty.
"Contemplation" refers to the three contemplations; "essence" refers to the locus from which the three contemplations arise and are established.
"Simply knowing a single thought-moment" means there is no need to rely on principles to sever the nine grades [of afflictions], nor to seek a pure *tathatā* apart from this single thought-moment.
A single thought is emptiness; what *prajñā* is not fully present? A single thought is non-emptiness; what liberation is not there?
A single thought is neither empty nor non-empty; what *dharmakāya* is not perfected?

This is the transmission of the Great Master, the single school of Tiantai: contemplating delusion within the five aggregates, where afflictions are themselves bodhi, and birth-and-death are themselves nirvana.

[The character] "pan" (槃). Regarding the principle of the inherent perfection of nature (*xingju*), the old commentary wishes to change the character "zhi" (祇) to "ying" (應); how could such a person know the fundamental tenet?
Thirdly, concerning that which corresponds to it:
Emptiness shatters the views and afflictions, corresponding with prajñā; the provisional shatters the dust-like delusions, corresponding with liberation;
the middle shatters ignorance, corresponding with the dharmakāya.
When the mind is in accord with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), what cause is there for sorrow or joy regarding censure, defamation, praise, or honor?
When people encounter circumstances of adversity or favor, joy and anger entangle their hearts because their minds are not empty.
If one attains the emptiness of mind, one does not rejoice because of praise and honor, nor does one grieve because of censure and defamation, because the mind is empty.
This is because there is nothing to which one is attached.
When the body is in accord with emptiness, whether it is cut by a blade or smeared with incense, what suffering or joy can there be?
Neither joy nor anger manifests on the countenance. The eminent sages of antiquity and those who cultivate patience were all able to practice this.
One might think that being cut by a blade is not painful; yet one fears that it may be impossible to endure it through sheer force of will.
Consider the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, who, when King Kali severed his body and dismembered him limb by limb, remained free from affliction. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"At that time, if there were any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, he would have given rise to anger and resentment. This is because...
When the body is in accord with emptiness, one is able to act in this way.
When the conditioned environment is in accord with emptiness, then regarding giving and plundering, what is gained and what is lost?
The "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*) refers to all objects of enjoyment upon which the primary retribution of the human body depends.
If a gentleman in his ordinary station can remain self-satisfied regardless of wealth, honor, calamity, or hardship, he has already been able to forget gain and loss and set aside joy and anger;
how much more so for one who practices dhyāna and whose retributive environment is in accord with emptiness—how could gain and loss disturb such a person?
How wondrous is the mind!
When the mind accords with both emptiness and non-emptiness, then attachment and views are entirely forgotten, and compassion universally saves.
That attachment and views are both forgotten is the power of emptiness; that compassion universally saves is the power of non-emptiness. At the beginning, it was thus...

First, one turns from the provisional to enter emptiness; next, one turns from emptiness to enter the provisional. Thus, one is able to dwell neither in the unconditioned nor fail to benefit the various realms of existence.
When the body accords with both emptiness and non-emptiness, internally it is like a withered tree, while externally it manifests dignified deportment.
Corresponding with emptiness: within, it is like a withered tree leaning against a cold cliff, where not a breath of warmth remains through the three winters. Corresponding with non-emptiness:
without, it is like mountain flowers encountering the power of spring; though their roots lie deep in the crags, they nonetheless bloom.
When the dependent retribution accords with both emptiness and non-emptiness, one forever cuts off greedy seeking. As for the provision of wealth and resources, Shi Bi said:
"Greed and seeking have already been extinguished; this principle accords with emptiness. Provision and relief are constantly bestowed; these phenomena accord with the provisional."
Master Sengzhao said: "The gate of Prajñā contemplates emptiness; the gate of Upāya engages with existence.
When the mind accords with that which is neither empty nor non-empty—neither empty nor not empty—then the true mark (dharmatā) is first revealed, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
The Lotus Sūtra states: "To open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "Opening" (kai) stands at the beginning;
this is because when a bodhisattva first shatters ignorance, they first perceive the true reality (bhūtatathatā), thereby becoming able to accord with the Middle Way.

The body and emptiness are neither empty nor non-empty; they correspond to that which is neither empty nor non-empty. Thus, when a single mote of dust enters right concentration (*samāpatti*), all motes of dust arise from samādhi.
Shibi said: "One mote of dust and all motes of dust refer only to the environment of dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*); within a single mote of dust, one enters and emerges."
They enter and exit simultaneously; they neither enter nor exit. Within the environment of dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), they exercise mastery in every single respect;

it is likewise so within the physical body of primary retribution (*upādāna-vipāka*). As for *samādhi*, this is translated as "right reception" (*samyak-pratigraha*); for it is precisely because one does not receive any [defiled] sensations that it is called "right reception."

The dependent retribution and emptiness/non-emptiness correspond to that which is neither empty nor non-empty. Thus, there are fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions that adorn the land for the transformation-born.
As for these fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions, they are the land of actualized retribution adorned by the self-enjoyment body, wherein it dwells. This is precisely...
By means of this, one adorns the land through self-effort; by means of this, one adorns the land through transformation-birth.
Fourth, as for those who harbor arrogance toward the superior: if it were not so, then they would not be in accord.
Tiantai uses the six identities (liu ji) to distinguish the stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuan wei). Because they are "identical," one does not give rise to discouragement;

this pertains to the matter within the first two gates. Because there are "six," one does not give rise to overweening pride (māna); this pertains to the matter within the gate of correspondence (xiangying).
Thus, we know that the single gate of correspondence already encompasses the clarification of the stages.
The fifth admonition is for those who are negligent: To cross the sea, one must board a boat; without a boat, how can one cross?

To cultivate the mind, one must enter into contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); without contemplation, there is no means to clarify the mind. If the mind is not yet clarified, when will realization (*yoga*) be attained?
Reflect upon this and do not rely on yourself.
Although the parable says, "Without a boat, how can one cross? its intent is to encourage people to board the vessel.

Although the Dharma discourse says, "Without contemplation, there is no way to clarify the mind," its intent is to urge people to enter into contemplation. This is because these warnings against indolence are for the sake of knowledge.
Regarding the observation of others' discourse: it is not for the sake of those who do not yet understand.
The sixth section, which reappears as the "Observation of the Essence," merely knows that a single thought is both empty and non-empty, neither existent nor non-existent;
it does not know that the very thought is itself empty and non-empty, neither non-existent nor non-non-existent.
One knows only illumination, but does not know stillness. Because illumination itself is negation, it is both empty and non-empty, and thus a double negation.

Because stillness itself is illumination, it is a double illumination. "Neither departing nor existent" is precisely the illumination of emptiness; "neither departing nor non-existent" is precisely the illumination of existence.
As for the previous mention of the essence of contemplation, that was merely to manifest the Middle Way directly; now it is presented again to emphasize the practice of contemplation.
As for its essence, it is not established even in the middle; whether existing or perishing, it cannot be named. This is the attainment of the ultimate mystery.
Seventh, clarifying right and wrong: the mind is not existent, nor is the mind non-existent; the mind is not "not existent," nor is the mind...
It is not that it is not non-existent.
This is the purpose of this chapter: to clarify the reason why the essence of contemplation is presented again. For it is said that because the mind is not existent, it is emptiness;
because the mind is not non-existent, it is non-emptiness; and because the mind is not non-existent, it is not "not-existent."
The mind is not non-existent; therefore, it is not "not non-existent.
To say it is existent or non-existent is to fall into the extreme of existence. To say it is neither existent nor non-existent is to fall into the extreme of non-existence.

This explains the reason for what preceded: why is it that the mind is not existent, and why is it that the mind is not non-existent? It is because [to claim] it is existent or non-existent [is a fallacy].
This is because one would thereby fall into [the extreme of] existence. Why is it that the mind is not non-existent? Why is it that the mind is not non-non-existent?
Because by being neither existent nor non-existent, one would thereby fall into [the extreme of] non-existence.
It is thus. This is merely the negation of right and wrong; it is not yet the negation of "negating right and wrong," nor is it the affirmation of "negating the negation.

Shibi said: "To bind one's fingers [in a gesture] while negating both right and wrong is still a negation that relies on its opposite; it is not yet the absolute affirmation that transcends all relativity."
Now, by means of the "double negation," one refutes the two "affirmations.
It is not that the preceding mind is neither existent nor non-existent; rather, this "neither" which is neither existent nor non-existent serves to refute both existence and non-existence.
This "is" refutes that which is "not-is," yet it remains "is.
This "is" is precisely the "is" of both existence and non-existence. Since it neither affirms nor negates, is this not indeed "not-is"?
Is this still "neither"?
Furthermore, by means of "double negation," one breaks through both negations.

"Double negation" means double non-being. This refers to the two instances of non-being mentioned previously: that the prior mind is not non-existent with respect to existence, and that it is not non-existent with respect to non-existence.
By destroying "neither existence nor non-existence," one neither destroys nor does not destroy; this is "is" and "is not.

This "is not" is precisely the "is not" of the prior "neither existence nor non-existence. Since one has already negated both [existence and non-existence] through that negation, and has thus moved beyond negation itself, then—

"This exists. Is this not so? It is neither "not breaking" nor "not non-breaking"; it is precisely "is. Shibi said: To provisionally establish it as "is" involves the danger of falling into infinite regress;
when one reaches the conclusion below, it returns to becoming the subject of calculation itself.

"It is so. This 'it is' is precisely the 'it is' that is neither 'it is' nor 'it is not. It has not yet reached the state of 'not being not' or 'not being not-not,' nor 'not being,' nor 'not being not.
Shibi said: From 'It is so' downward, he concludes the two preceding layers; from 'It has not yet reached' downward, he explains the preceding layer to refute what was [asserted]."
He establishes the capacity [of the teaching], yet this too he refutes; thus he says: "Not non-non, not is-is. Below, he explains the two preceding layers:
the illness has departed but the medicine remains, yet this too he refutes; thus he says: "Not not-is."
The delusion of "is" and "is not" is subtle and difficult to perceive.
Shibi said: Question: Does this delusion obstruct principle (*li*) or obstruct phenomena (*shi*)? Answer: It can obstruct principle, but it does not obstruct phenomena.
This arises because ignorance fails to comprehend and thus recklessly calculates "is" and "is not. If the governing darkness were extinguished, "is" and "is not" would both vanish.
Ming. With a spirit clarified and anxieties stilled, he examined it minutely.
Shibi said: "Right and wrong are profound and subtle; their meaning is most refined. To observe them, they have no form; to seek them, they leave no trace."
If one’s eye of wisdom were not bright and clear, how could one dispel such views?
Eighth, regarding the distinction between the expression (*śabda*) and the meaning (*artha*):

"expression" refers to that which expresses, while "meaning" refers to that which is expressed. One desires that, at the beginning, one realizes the meaning by means of the expression, and in the end...
One catches the rabbit to forget the snare; therefore, it is necessary to exercise discernment.
Nevertheless, the ultimate truth is ineffable; one resorts to words and phrases to clarify its meaning.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Dhāraṇī is without letters, yet letters manifest dhāraṇī."
The essential principle is not contemplation; one relies upon the cultivation of contemplation to realize its essence.
Shibi said: "Wisdom and principle are not practice; they are formed through the permeation of practice. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Although it is originally gold,"

In the end, it was finalized as the "accomplishment" (chengjiu). Now, [some] say that the "purport" (zhi) is the direct cause (zhengyin), the "thesis" (zong) is the revealing cause (liaoyin), and the "contemplation" (guan) is the conditional cause (yuan-yin).
I say this is not so; one should take the purport as the direct cause, while both the thesis and contemplation are taken as the revealing cause. This is because of this thesis.

This is not the primary tenet among the five stages; rather, it is the tenet of the ultimate goal (*abhiprāya*). Its meaning belongs to *vibhāga* (analytical understanding). Both *vibhāga* and *vipaśyanā* (contemplation) belong to the *vijñapti-hetu* (the cause of realization).
If one clarifies the *pratyaya-hetu* (the causal condition), one adopts the auxiliary methods of the path (*mārga-dharma*).
If the purport is not clear, then the words are not precise; if the central tenet is not grasped, then the contemplation is not profound.

When principle is attained within, words are attained without; there has never been a case where the form is straight yet the shadow is not upright, or where the principle is clear yet the words are inappropriate.
When the central tenet is realized in the mind, the contemplation becomes profound in practice; there has never been [a case where this fails].
If the sound is harmonious but the resonance does not follow, it is because the fundamental principle has been grasped while the contemplation lacks depth.
Only through deep contemplation can one truly grasp the fundamental principle; only through precise words can one necessarily clarify their underlying intent.
In the beginning, one contemplates the profound by means of the fundamental principle (zong), and articulates the definitive meaning (di) by relying on the purport (zhi).

In the end, through contemplation, the fundamental principle is further realized, and through words, the purport becomes increasingly clear. Once the purport and the fundamental principle are thus clarified and realized, how could the words and the contemplation still persist?
Shibei said: "When principle is clarified, words are discarded; when wisdom is realized, contemplation perishes. Furthermore, the ultimate aim is principle and the school is wisdom;
words are the teaching and contemplation is practice. One should know that the manifestation of principle depends on words, and thus words are forgotten;
the illumination of wisdom depends on contemplation, and thus contemplation is forgotten. To forget the trap once the rabbit is caught—this is truly how it is."

Ninth, as for those who "turn every encounter into contemplation" (*chùtú chéngguān*) without having yet mastered the aforementioned entryway: whatever cultivation they undertake is like wearing tattered rags or walking amidst thorns.
When one has resolved that there are obstructions at every point of contact, then as one encounters conditions and confronts objects, every path becomes a site of contemplation;
it is like the wind moving through space, meeting with no obstacles whatsoever.

Now, to restate the words and re-emphasize the essence of contemplation (*guan*) is intended to clarify that the fundamental principle remains unchanged. Regarding the term "contemplation," there are shifts according to different contexts.
Shibi said: "If the words shift, the teachings established may number in the thousands; how could this deviate from the core intent? If the contemplation shifts, the practice cultivated..."

There are ten thousand varieties [of teachings]. That they find peace and ease in their fundamental source is truly because principle and wisdom share a common origin, while capacities and conditions follow divergent paths.

Therefore, the words encompass both the provisional and the real, and the contemplation includes both the shallow and the deep. To clarify the fundamental tenet and manifest its subtle essence, one should first contemplate according to the words.
To shift one's words means that the principle remains without discrepancy; to alter one's contemplation means that the essential meaning does not differ.

Shibi said: "If words shift, the teachings become distinct, yet when the principle is revealed, there is no difference. If contemplation changes, the practice deviates, yet when wisdom is clarified, it does not differ."
The principle of non-differentiation is *li* (principle). The principle of non-disparity is the *zong* (tenet).
Shibi said: "The principle of non-differentiation is the tenet. Because this tenet is entirely *li*, it is said to be "identical with *li*.
The principle of non-disparity—because this *li* is entirely wisdom—it is said to be "the tenet. When principle and wisdom are suchness (*tathatā*), the discourse of contemplation ceases.
The fundamental principle is one, yet there are two names; "Contemplation" (*guan*) is spoken of merely as its introductory prelude.
Shibi says: "The essence of the fundamental principle is one, yet two names are established, like a mirror and its light, which likewise manifest two designations."

Through words, one attains the principle; by means of contemplation, one accords with the fundamental source. Since wisdom and principle are equally illuminated, words and contemplation serve as skillful means.
Regarding the tenth [stage], "Miraculously Accordant with the Primordial Source":

Now, a person who has awakened to the mind would never cling to the contemplation while remaining deluded about its ultimate meaning; how could a person who thoroughly understands the teachings remain stuck in words while being confused about the principle?

For one who has awakened to the mind, cultivation arises by fully embodying the nature; thus, the ultimate meaning is itself the contemplation. When cultivation is fully embodied within the nature, [the two are inseparable].

Thus, contemplation is itself the ultimate meaning. Therefore, one does not cling to contemplation and thereby lose sight of the meaning. One who penetrates the teachings uses the trap to catch the fish;
they will certainly not cling to the trap as being the fish. When the essence is realized, names are forgotten; they will certainly not follow the name and forget the essence.
Thus, one does not become stuck in words and thereby confuse the principle.
When principle is clarified, the path of language is severed; how then can words provide a discourse upon it? When the essential meaning is realized, the movements of the mind are extinguished;
how then can contemplation conceive of it? Shibi said:
"Words cannot discourse upon it, for principle is fundamentally beyond names. The mind cannot conceive of it, for wisdom is originally free from deliberation."
Tiantai said: "The mouth wishes to speak, yet words fail; the mind wishes to contemplate, yet thoughts vanish. I say:
The Master’s teaching on the principle of wondrous contemplation takes as its primary tenet that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Therefore, in the tenth chapter, "Wondrous Accord with the Original Source," the ultimate point of return is precisely such as this.
"That which cannot be conceived by mind or expressed in words" may be called a wondrous accord with the center of the universe. Shibi said:
"Since phenomenal dharmas are empty, there are no characteristics that are not exhausted; since the rational nature is true and real, there is no essence that does not manifest."
Therefore it is said: "He wondrously accords with that which lies within the cosmic sphere.
